articles.title: Scott Ritter warns of impending US economic collapse and exposes NATO military vulnerabilities
articles.body:
Scott Ritter warns of impending US economic collapse and exposes NATO military vulnerabilities
TEHRAN — The latest joint X Space hosted by Tehran Times and Sputnik featured former UN weapons inspector and US Marine intelligence officer Scott Ritter, who warned of an impending structural collapse within the American economic system driven by reckless foreign policies and soaring energy costs, while dismantling Western war narratives and exposing deep-seated military vulnerabilities across the United States and NATO.
Sputnik Question: Donald Trump stated last week that he is not happy about Ukrainian strikes against Russian energy infrastructure and wants them to stop because they are destabilizing to the global economy. Given that these attacks were enabled by intelligence from the CIA and tech companies like Google, Palantir, and Starlink, what explains his decision to explicitly oppose these strikes?
Scott Ritter Answer: Attempting to get into the mind of Donald Trump is impossible, as the Russian government has officially characterized him as emotionally unstable. He is currently under a tremendous amount of economic pressure driven by the rising price of oil, which he views as a primary indicator of American economic health. The price of oil and diesel is rising as a direct result of his own policies, which increases ground shipping costs and transfers those expenses directly to the American consumer. As James Carville famously warned Bill Clinton in 1992, "it's the economy, stupid"—making economic performance the primary concern for American voters.
 
 Trump knows very little about the specific operational details or goals of the conflicts he initiates; for instance, he took America to war in Iran based on a briefing by Benjamin Netanyahu and the head of the Mossad. When he authorized the CIA to pressure Vladimir Putin, he did not understand what the CIA actually does—specifically that it has trained Ukrainian forces since 2014 for cross-border operations, assassinations, and long-range drone strikes. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent explicitly noted that the administration's goal is to collapse the Russian economy by targeting its energy infrastructure. While Trump may enjoy seeing war-porn briefings of burning Russian refineries, he fails to realize the global economic impact. Because Russia had to halt diesel exports to prioritize domestic consumption for harvesting machinery and trucking, a global diesel shortage emerged, pushing US diesel prices above $6 per gallon. Trump understands these economic consequences because high fuel prices severely threaten his party at the upcoming November midterm elections.
Sputnik Question: What has been the response in the US establishment to Russia's retaliation strikes against Ukrainian ports, logistics warehouses, and rail infrastructure, and to what extent has this changed the calculus in Washington?
Scott Ritter Answer: Statements made by senior US government officials closely conform to narratives produced by Ukrainian intelligence regarding heavy Russian casualties and limited Russian military capacity. US intelligence analysts regularly produce reports that validate official policy postures to secure promotions and bonuses rather than providing accurate assessments. American policymakers genuinely believed that Ukrainian drone strikes would collapse Russia's economy, induce long gas lines, trigger a "Moscow Maidan," and lead to regime change before the September 20 parliamentary elections.
 
 However, Russia's retaliatory actions exposed Western intelligence claims as a narrative constructed on lies. Consequently, there is silence among critical decision-makers in Washington because they have no effective counter to these realities. Ukraine is completely bankrupt, unable to pay its soldiers or buy weapons, and seizing frozen Russian assets would end Europe's economy. Ultimately, if economic strain and supply chain disruptions ruin Christmas for American families, voters will severely punish incumbent politicians on election day.
Tehran Times Question: How much of the media campaign regarding the contract between the United States and Venezuela for access to oil is true, and will it solve the economic problems facing the US economy?
Scott Ritter Answer: It is not true at all. Venezuelan oil fields have been maintained haphazardly over many years, with many fields shut down, requiring an extraordinarily expensive and lengthy infrastructure restoration before oil can flow meaningfully. Trump's pressure on American oil companies will not generate significant income or produce substantial oil quantities beyond current levels, making the initiative a policy fantasy. Furthermore, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve of the United States has been exhausted with no capacity to recharge it. Simultaneously, Saudi Arabia is becoming a non-functioning oil producer due to repeated attacks by Houthi forces and Iraqi militias, threatening broader global energy instability. Trump's claim that Venezuelan oil will act as a quick solution represents pure fantasy rather than fact.
Tehran Times Question: How long can the United States economy tolerate this situation and the economic pressures caused by these wars?
Scott Ritter Answer: The United States maintains an illusion of economic stability by printing money excessively and relying on financial smoke and mirrors. The country operates under record-high budget deficits, while government bond yields rising above 5% divert a massive portion of GDP toward paying growing national debt. Leading economic analysts project a major economic crisis emerging around January. While the US may manage to fake it through one more cycle, a structural collapse of the American economic system remains inevitable. Furthermore, efforts by China to establish pro-Yuan trade agreements with Gulf Arab nations threaten to erode the dominance of the petrodollar.
Sputnik Question: Polish Foreign Minister Sikorski claimed that NATO could easily defeat Russia in a conventional war due to overwhelming air power; based on US and Israeli air force operations over Iran, does NATO possess overwhelming air superiority over Russia?
Scott Ritter Answer: NATO has nothing close to air superiority. Establishing air superiority requires generating sustained combat sorties, which demands well-maintained aircraft, fuel, ammunition, active airfields, and functional airborne command and control networks. In any conflict with Russia, NATO's command and control infrastructure would be disabled on day one by advanced Russian electronic warfare. NATO forces have spent two decades operating in undefended airspace dropping guided munitions, but their system failed when applied against Iran, where 39 days of operations failed to inflict a decisive blow.
 
 Furthermore, NATO member states suffer from severe operational unpreparedness; for instance, Germany cannot get 80% of its aircraft off the ramp due to lack of maintenance and training. The F-16 fighter jets transferred to Ukraine were expired aircraft requiring complete refurbishment. Additionally, NATO lacks the required forward airfields, ramp space, fuel storage, and ammunition reserves, all of which would be destroyed on day one, while long-range Russian interceptors would disrupt aerial refueling tankers.
Sputnik Question: Setting aside traditional aviation, how does the rest of NATO compare to Russia in terms of drone and missile capabilities?
Scott Ritter Answer: NATO nations, including Germany, possess zero national air defense capacity. NATO stripped its own air defense inventory to supply Ukraine, whose air defense network was subsequently dismantled by Russian suppression operations. Utilizing drones alone, Russia retains the capability to darken European skies and destroy selected targets without effective opposition. Following the US withdrawal from the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty, Russia deployed long-range Iskander-1000 missiles and advanced cruise missiles capable of striking across Europe. Russia maintains sufficient conventional power to destroy NATO's military infrastructure, defense manufacturing, and command centers without utilizing nuclear weapons, granting it total escalatory dominance. While a nuclear exchange would result in the absolute destruction of Europe, Russia maintains survival capabilities, though Moscow seeks peaceful security arrangements rather than conflict with NATO.
Tehran Times Question: How much truth is there to the 60 Minutes interview with the American pilot who was reportedly rescued after his fighter jet was targeted by Iranian air defenses over Iran?
Scott Ritter Answer: While taking the active-duty colonel's service at face value, significant unanswered questions surround whether the event was an authentic rescue or a scripted narrative. The United States suffered a direct conventional defeat against Iranian forces, who executed a superior plan and drove US forces out of strategic installations. Unlike conflicts in Vietnam or Afghanistan where political will decayed, US forces were directly out-maneuvered and beaten in conventional engagement by Iran. To counter this precedent and satisfy the public need for a hero, the Department of Defense collaborated with 60 Minutes to present a scripted narrative to the American public.

articles.title: Denmark brings forward DKK 1.8 billion Ukraine aid package after Russian frigate fires flares at Danish helicopter
articles.body:
Denmark will bring forward and increase a military aid package for Ukraine to DKK 1.8 billion, days after a Russian frigate fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates and Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats announced the decision Friday after a meeting of the Danish Parliament’s Foreign Policy Committee.
Most of the money will go toward air defense systems produced in Ukraine. The support had been requested by Ukraine.
Løkke described the incident involving the Danish helicopter as a “severe Russian provocation.”
“If they think they can provoke us into being restrained with our support for Ukraine, then they are mistaken,” he said.
Ukraine has faced difficulties defending itself against Russian ballistic missile attacks because of shortages of suitable air defense missiles, including Patriot missiles produced by the United States.
The decision follows an incident Monday involving a Danish Air Force Fennec helicopter and a Russian frigate in international waters off Gedser in southern Denmark.
The Danish Defence said the helicopter was carrying out routine photographic surveillance of the Russian vessel when the frigate fired two flares toward it. One passed close to the helicopter.
According to Bruus, the Russian ship did not establish radio contact with the helicopter before firing the flares.
NATO has described the incident as an “irresponsible Russian act.”
“This fits into a pattern we are seeing around Europe, where Russia is escalating and constantly testing boundaries. It serves the purpose of shaking our unity and our support for Ukraine, and that must not work,” Løkke said.
Denmark summoned the Russian ambassador following the incident. Russia has said the Danish helicopter acted “provocatively.”
“If the Russians think that they can rattle us by doing this kind of thing, then our counter-response is that we will step up our support for Ukraine faster than we had intended,” Bruus said.
The captain of the Russian frigate has since received an award from Russia for his actions, according to the Danish report.
Denmark has been a major supporter of Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. However, since December, Denmark has announced only one other major aid package in addition to Friday’s package.
The Danish Ukraine Fund, which has financed much of the country’s support, has almost run out of available money. Further support would therefore require politicians to find funding elsewhere.
So far, much of Denmark’s support has been financed through the government’s projected future fiscal surplus.
Denmark’s plan to send foreign prisoners sentenced to deportation to a prison in Kosovo has been delayed again.
The 300 prison places are now expected to become available at the end of 2027 at the earliest and possibly not until the beginning of 2028, Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen informed the parties behind the agreement Friday.
“I have been informed by the Danish Prison Agency that the construction of the prison in Kosovo is delayed, so the prison places can at the earliest be put into use at the end of 2027 and possibly not until the beginning of 2028,” Wammen said in a written statement to Ritzau.
Denmark reached a political agreement in 2021 to lease 300 prison places in Kosovo to reduce pressure on Danish prisons.
When the agreement with Kosovo was finalized, the first foreign nationals sentenced to deportation were expected to begin serving their sentences there in early 2023.
The latest delay means the prison could open about five years later than originally planned.
Wammen said the project remains an important priority for the government so “we can relieve pressure on the Danish prisons and get criminal foreign nationals sentenced to deportation out of the country.”
“It must happen as quickly as possible, and I naturally would have very much liked for us to have long since begun sending inmates there. Therefore, I am of course far from satisfied that the project is further delayed,” he said.
According to the Ministry of Justice, authorities in Kosovo have now emptied the prison of inmates.
An agreement with a contractor was signed in July, and the renovation work is expected to take about a year.
The project has previously been delayed by the approval process in Kosovo’s parliament, where opposition parties did not support international agreements.
Danish prisons have faced overcrowding for years, adding pressure to make the Kosovo prison places available.
The number of people injured in traffic accidents in Denmark increased in 2025, while the number of deaths fell slightly, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark.
Police recorded 2,832 people as injured or killed in traffic accidents during the year, an increase of 313 compared with 2024.
The number of traffic deaths fell from 145 in 2024 to 143 in 2025.
Denmark has now recorded fewer than 200 traffic deaths a year for 10 consecutive years. This is well below levels seen between 1965 and 1973, when more than 1,000 people were killed in traffic each year.
Of those recorded in 2025, 1,732 were seriously injured and 957 suffered minor injuries.
The number of injured road users increased across almost all forms of transport, with mopeds the exception.
Injuries among people riding electric bicycles increased from 173 in 2024 to 211 in 2025. Nearly three-quarters of those injured in this group were aged 45 or older.
The police figures do not show the full number of people injured on Danish roads because they only cover accidents reported to police.
Hospital emergency departments keep separate records of traffic injuries. In 2024, they registered 29,589 injured people, more than 1,000 above the previous year’s figure.

A suspicious package prompted a large police response on Dag Hammarskjölds Allé in Copenhagen’s Østerbro district on Friday morning. Copenhagen Police said officers had completed an initial examination of the package and had not found any dangerous content. The cordon on Dag Hammarskjölds Allé has therefore been lifted, police said. The package has been taken […]

The Ministry of Education confirmed the change to the education magazine Folkeskolen. The decision applies to Denmark and the other countries participating in PISA, which tests 15-year-old students in […]

Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa of Radikale Venstre, the Danish Social Liberal Party, has decided not to continue the cap, the ministry said in a press release. Nawa has held the […]

Denmark plans to raise the fine for repeated violations of residency requirements to 100,000 DKK, Housing Minister Jacob Mark of SF, the Socialist People’s Party, told Jyllands-Posten.
The current maximum fine for a second violation is 20,000 DKK, meaning the proposed penalty would be five times higher.
“Cheating on the residency requirement is destructive to smaller towns and small island communities,” Mark said.
“When a citizen buys a house, but chooses not to live there, the consequence is that lovely towns in beautiful surroundings turn into ghost towns, the local grocery store closes, and community life and neighborhood spirit die,” he said.
Owners of homes intended for year-round use must ensure that the property is inhabited for at least 180 days a year. If they do not live there themselves, they can rent it out for permanent residence.
Under current rules, a first violation can lead to a fine of up to 10,000 DKK, rising to 20,000 DKK for a second offense.
Municipalities set the detailed rules for different types of housing. Holiday homes are generally exempt, while some properties can be designated as flexbolig, allowing a year-round home to be used as a holiday home.
Several island municipalities, including Samsø, Ærø, Fanø, Bornholm, Læsø and Langeland, have previously called for stronger monitoring powers. They want to be able to check water and electricity use weekly when they suspect violations, rather than monthly.
Mark said he has invited the island municipalities and Landdistrikternes Fællesråd, an organization representing rural areas in Denmark, to discuss possible additional measures.
Bus and light rail tickets in Aarhus will cost 15 DKK from 2027 under a new municipal budget agreement approved Thursday evening.
Aarhus Municipality will allocate 35 million DKK a year from 2027 to lower ticket prices, TV 2 Østjylland reported.
A consultancy firm had estimated that introducing 15 DKK tickets across the municipality could cost 122 million DKK, although the figure was uncertain.
Mayor Anders Winnerskjold of Socialdemokratiet, Denmark’s Social Democratic Party, argued that the actual cost would be lower, and the City Council agreed.
The budget agreement also notes that the national government plans to introduce free public transport for people under 22. Aarhus expects that measure to cover part of the cost of the cheaper local tickets.
Since March, residents have already been able to buy 15 DKK tickets on three bus routes as part of a trial.
The municipality has said the trial is intended to show how cheaper fares affect passenger numbers and what changes may be needed if more people choose public transport.
The experience will also be used in planning for a permanent price reduction and for making sure buses and the light rail can handle more passengers.
Frie Grønne leader Sikandar Siddique has been removed from Copenhagen City Council after authorities ruled that he does not meet the requirement of living in the municipality.
The City Council approved the decision Thursday, following a long dispute over Siddique’s residence.
Siddique has called the case a “miscarriage of justice” by “the system” and said it had been influenced by Zionists, meaning supporters of the Jewish national movement and political ideology. Several parties rejected those claims during Thursday’s meeting.
“I believe that it is quite damaging when an election is called into question by Sikandar Siddique’s statements, but also so-called experts,” Lord Mayor Sisse Marie Welling of SF, the Socialist People’s Party, said before the decision was approved.
Before the November 2025 municipal election, Siddique registered a move from Herlev to Copenhagen so he could run in the capital.
Copenhagen Municipality later cancelled his residence registration, citing, among other things, an unusually low electricity bill and a lack of documentation showing purchases near his registered Copenhagen address.
Siddique appealed, but the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization upheld the municipality’s decision on September 8.
His seat will now go to Frie Grønne’s first alternate, Asham Agha Nadeem, meaning the party keeps its mandate.
Frie Grønne received nearly 7,000 votes in the election, including more than 3,000 personal votes for Siddique. Nadeem received 612 personal votes.
Denmark’s oldest living person, Kirsten Schwalbe, has entered the list of Europe’s 10 oldest living people, TV Midtvest reported Thursday.
Schwalbe turned 112 in March. She was born in Salling in 1914, a few months before the outbreak of World War I, and grew up with nine siblings.
She married her first husband in 1938 and had three children. Today, she lives in her own home in Struer.
Schwalbe has previously said that genetics may partly explain her long life. Four of her nine siblings also lived past the age of 100, she told Berlingske in 2024.
She has also said that mood plays an important role in living a long life.
Europe’s oldest living person is British woman Ethel Caterham, who is 117 and is also the world’s oldest living person.
Schwalbe is not yet among the world’s 20 oldest living people, according to TV Midtvest.
Meanwhile, a man in Costa Rica, Jose Flores, claims to be 119 years old. His age has not yet been confirmed, and specialists are reviewing documents to determine his date of birth.

Three Danish government ministers from Moderaterne, the Moderates, want schools to stop using Aula, the digital platform used for communication between schools, daycare facilities and families.
Ministers Monika Rubin, Christina Egelund and Jakob Engel-Schmidt made the proposal in a joint interview with Berlingske. They have not proposed an alternative to Aula.
“An IT system has been created that sucks so much oxygen out of the school and the classroom that it is harmful to our children’s well-being and learning,” Engel-Schmidt said.
Aula was introduced in 2019 to replace Skoleintra. Danish public schools and public and self-governing daycare facilities have access to the platform, where students, parents and employees can receive and share information.
Rubin told DR that the amount of communication on the platform had become excessive.
“More communication is not always better communication. 10,000 messages are sent on Aula per minute between half past seven and nine in the morning. It has gotten out of hand,” she said.
According to Berlingske, Egelund said answering parents’ questions is not a core task of Denmark’s public schools.
The proposal follows the latest PISA study, an international assessment of 15-year-old students’ performance in reading, mathematics and science, which showed a decline among Danish students.
Other government parties have expressed skepticism about removing Aula.
Nanna Bonde, education spokesperson for SF, the Socialist People’s Party, one of Denmark’s governing parties, suggested guidelines for the platform could be introduced instead, according to DR.
Apartment sales in Copenhagen fell sharply in August, while several other parts of Denmark saw more houses change hands than a year earlier, new figures from Boligsiden show.
A total of 390 owner-occupied apartments were sold in Copenhagen Municipality in August, 36 percent fewer than in the same month last year.
It was also the third-lowest number of apartment sales recorded in Copenhagen for an August since Boligsiden began collecting the data in 2011.
“Significantly fewer owner-occupied apartments are being traded in Copenhagen, and there has been a clear shift in the otherwise hectic pace that we have seen for a long time in Copenhagen,” said Birgit Daetz, communications director and housing economist at Boligsiden.
Across Denmark, apartment sales were 20 percent lower than in August 2025.
Overall housing sales also fell slightly during the first eight months of the year compared with the same period last year, after seasonal changes are taken into account.
Brian Friis Helmer, personal economist at AL Sydbank, said the apartment market was largely responsible for the decline, while sales of houses and holiday homes remained strong.
Boligsiden recorded more sales of detached and terraced houses than a year earlier in South Jutland, West and South Zealand, North Jutland and Funen.
House sales fell in Copenhagen, the Copenhagen suburbs and North Zealand.
“Now, we see the activity spreading to other parts of the country to a greater extent,” Daetz said.
A Lego model of the Danish royal yacht Dannebrog has been sold at auction for 60,000 DKK after spending 28 years at Legoland in Billund.
The model was sold Wednesday by auction house Bruun Rasmussen for twice its estimated price of between 20,000 and 30,000 DKK.
Legoland said the proceeds will be donated to the Mary Foundation, which works to combat social isolation.
“We think it could be nice to donate the money to the Mary Foundation, now that it is the royal yacht ‘Dannebrog’ that we have had up for auction,” said Jan Mouritzen, head of Legoland’s model department.
Bruun Rasmussen specialist Line Hjorth Langkjær said the model’s history at Legoland and the royal yacht’s place in Danish history had helped increase interest.
It is the first time Legoland has auctioned an original model from Miniland, where landmarks are recreated in miniature using Lego bricks.
The original Dannebrog model contains about 25,000 bricks. It was replaced after a new Copenhagen Harbour area opened in Miniland in July with an updated version made from 225,000 bricks.
The real Dannebrog serves as the official and private residence of the Danish royal couple and other members of the royal family during summer cruises and official visits overseas.
The Mary Foundation was established by then-Crown Princess Mary in 2007. The foundation said the donation will support efforts to combat bullying among children and loneliness among young people.
A patient at Landssygehuset in Tórshavn underwent surgery for an inguinal hernia on Wednesday while the surgeon performing the procedure was in Aabenraa, southern Denmark.
The operation used robot-assisted telesurgery, with the surgeon controlling a robot in the Faroe Islands from an office in Aabenraa.
It was the first time the technology had been used for an operation in Denmark and between two public hospitals in the Nordic region, Sygehus Sønderjylland, the Southern Jutland hospital, said in a press release.
Chief physician Jan Krzak said the operation had a “highly satisfactory result.”
“We have started out with a few selected patients with an uncomplicated inguinal hernia. The first step was to document whether the technology, safety, communication, and cooperation functioned stably in practice,” Krzak said.
The operation is part of a project examining whether telesurgery could eventually provide treatment to patients who live far from major medical facilities.
Elinborg Mortensen, chief physician at Landssygehuset in Tórshavn, said the technology could be particularly useful in the Faroe Islands, where many patients currently have to travel long distances for hospital treatment.
“Therefore, it is interesting for us to investigate whether new technology can bring some of the expertise closer to the patients in a safe and controlled manner,” Mortensen said.
A full surgical and anesthesia team was present with the patient in Tórshavn throughout Wednesday’s operation. The team was ready to take over if the technology or connection failed.
Robot-assisted telesurgery has previously been used internationally, including for operations performed remotely between London and Gibraltar.
The ferry between Thyborøn and Agger in northern West Jutland ran aground Wednesday morning, TV Midtvest reported.
No one was injured in the incident, ferry operations manager Andreas Groth told the broadcaster.
All ferry services have been suspended for the rest of the day, according to the operator’s website.
It is not yet clear what caused the ferry to run aground.
The coastal rescue service is at the scene, and divers are expected to inspect the ferry, TV Midtvest reported.
There is currently no indication of when ferry services will resume.
The ferry can carry around 22 passenger cars and about 100 passengers. It normally runs once an hour between Agger and Thyborøn, with the crossing taking about 10 minutes.
The route is owned by Lemvig Municipality and Thisted Municipality and carries around 145,000 passengers a year.
The ferry is about 45 meters long and 11 meters wide.
Novo partners with Anthropic to develop drugs faster
Danish pharmaceutical company Novo has entered into a partnership with US technology company Anthropic to use artificial intelligence in the discovery and development of new medicines.
Novo said it will use Anthropic’s Claude Science AI model to examine what the company described as “central challenges” in drug research.
The agreement is part of Novo’s wider use of artificial intelligence. The company already works with OpenAI and Amazon on AI, according to Børsen.
Novo CEO Mike Doustdar said the partnership reflects the company’s “ambition to become the world’s most AI-driven healthcare company.”
“By joining forces with Anthropic, we will strengthen our research and development organization and advance our mission to deliver new, transformative healthcare solutions to people living with chronic diseases,” Doustdar said.
Novo, which is behind medicines including Ozempic and Wegovy, said it plans to use Anthropic’s AI models to “scale AI across the entire company.”
Claude will also be used to develop software internally.
As an initial step, Novo plans to test Claude Science in specific research and development workflows.
Novo told Reuters in May that it aims to use AI to reduce the time it takes to bring new medicines to market.
Russian captain honored for flares at Danish helicopter
The commander of a Russian warship that fired two signal flares at a Danish military helicopter Monday has received an award for his actions, according to the Russian Ministry of Defense.
The ministry said Wednesday that two flares were fired to prevent what it described as a “provocation,” Reuters reported.
Russia identified the vessel as the Soobrazitelny and described it as a corvette, a relatively small and lightly armed warship. The Danish Armed Forces have described it as a frigate. According to TV 2, Russia and NATO countries use different classifications and standards for warships.
The Russian ministry said the vessel was carrying out “operations in neutral waters,” according to Russian media outlet Tass. It did not specify what those operations involved.
The ship’s commander was praised for his response during the incident, which the ministry said caused the Danish helicopter to leave the area shortly afterward.
The Danish Armed Forces said Monday at 11:02 p.m. that one of the Air Force’s Fennec helicopters had been fired at with pyrotechnics in international waters off Gedser.
According to the Danish Armed Forces, the helicopter was conducting routine photographic documentation of the Russian vessel at the time.
Russian Ambassador to Denmark Vladimir Barbin has previously described the helicopter’s actions before the flares were fired as “provocative.”
He said the helicopter had carried out “dangerous manoeuvres” and that the Russian vessel had been unable to establish contact with it. He also said the communication problem was on the Danish side.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus, a member of the Social Democrats, rejected that account.
“I trust the Armed Forces. The fact is that there are plenty of ways to contact such a helicopter via radio and other things,” Bruus said.
“There was no contact before these flares were fired, and that should have been done.”
Train traffic resumes between Skanderborg and Aarhus after disruption
Train traffic between Skanderborg and Aarhus has resumed after a stopped train blocked the line Wednesday afternoon.
DSB, Denmark’s national rail operator, said shortly before 2 p.m. that trains were running according to schedule again.
Rejseplanen, Denmark’s national journey planner, showed that some trains had been canceled and several others were heavily delayed.
“There may still be longer travel times and isolated cancellations until train staff are in place again,” DSB said.
Passengers delayed by more than 30 minutes may be entitled to compensation under DSB’s travel time guarantee.
Travelers delayed by 30 to 59 minutes can receive 50% of the ticket price back. Delays of 60 to 89 minutes qualify for 75%, while delays of 90 minutes or more qualify for a full refund.
Passengers can choose between a ticket for a new journey on the same route or a cash payment.
Applications for compensation can be submitted through DSB’s travel time guarantee scheme.
EU proposes social media ban for children under 13 and restrictions until age 18
The European Commission will propose new age limits for social media on Thursday, including a ban for children under 13 and restrictions on personal accounts for those under 15. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the plan, called the “Kids Act,” during her annual State of the Union address on Wednesday. “We will […]
Full version of this article is only available to subscribers.
Police are investigating a suspicious incident Wednesday morning on the street where Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus lives in Gladsaxe, north of Copenhagen, B.T. reported. Bomb disposal technicians from the military are at the scene, along with a Telemax robot used to examine potentially dangerous objects, according to the newspaper. The Ministry of Defense told […]
Full version of this article is only available to subscribers.
Danish police have received a new app that can scan disabled parking cards and check whether they are valid, as authorities seek to crack down on stolen, fake and invalid cards. The app was developed by the Danish National Police in cooperation with Danish Disability Organisations, an umbrella group representing people with disabilities in Denmark. […]
Full version of this article is only available to subscribers.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday that she wants Canada to become the first associate member of the European Union, as the two sides seek closer ties on defense, technology and trade. Von der Leyen made the proposal during her annual State of the Union speech at the European Parliament in Strasbourg. […]
Full version of this article is only available to subscribers.
According to a press release from the Danish Finance Ministry, Naalakkersuisut (the Government of Greenland) and the Danish government signed a partial agreement on Tuesday worth 1.2 billion DKK for investments in Greenland from 2026 to 2029.
“The agreement means, among other things, that there will be a relief package for the Greenlandic citizens who are the most vulnerable economically,” the ministry said.
The governments have also agreed to provide funding for Greenland’s utility sector. This includes water supply projects in Ilulissat and support for Nukissiorfiit, Greenland’s self-rule-owned utility company, to help develop the country’s energy infrastructure.
Funding will also go toward operating Greenland’s new international airports, with the agreement including money for feasibility studies in 2027 for a new regional airstrip in Ittoqqortoormiit and a new deep-water port in Qaqortoq.
“We are investing in initiatives that can be felt in the everyday lives of the Greenlandic people, and which at the same time support Naalakkersuisut’s work to develop a strong and sustainable Greenlandic society,” Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard said.
The agreement follows another deal between Greenland and Denmark reached in February, which provided funding for Greenlandic patients to receive treatment in the Danish healthcare system.
Both agreements stem from a framework agreement reached in September last year between Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
Under that framework, the two sides agreed on a package worth 1.6 billion DKK for Greenland’s healthcare system, the deep-water port and a new airstrip.
Around 100,000 AL Sydbank customers will no longer have to pay up to 600 DKK a year for an account, online banking access and a debit card.
The offer was previously available to customers of Arbejdernes Landsbank. Following the merger of Arbejdernes Landsbank, Vestjysk Bank and Sydbank, it will now be extended to all customers of the new bank, AL Sydbank.
“When we did the merger, we promised that you would be able to get an account, access to online banking, and a debit card without it costing anything,” said Svend Randers, AL Sydbank’s director responsible for private customers.
“That is the promise we are fulfilling now, and it applies both to our existing customers who do not yet have those terms, and then of course the new customers who hopefully will join,” he said.
Randers said the bank hopes the offer will attract new customers and encourage existing customers to stay.
“And then of course we hope that in the longer term, it means that those customers will want to do more business with us when they eventually buy a home or car or save up for retirement or something else entirely,” he said.
The change comes after AL Sydbank told customers this summer that several fees would change following the merger.
According to a Mybanker analysis for TV 2, fees increased for between 55 and 60 percent of the bank’s services, depending on which bank a person previously used. Between 25 and 35 percent of fees decreased.
Customers must have their NemKonto, the bank account used for payments from Danish public authorities, with AL Sydbank to qualify for the free account.
The bank has not yet decided which debit card will be included.
Danish band Lukas Graham has pulled out of its remaining concerts with Ed Sheeran in the United States following a dispute over rapper Macklemore’s removal as an opening act.
The band, fronted by lead singer Lukas Graham Forchhammer, announced the decision on Instagram.
“Money does not give you the right to own the conversation. No one’s bank account should determine who is allowed to speak, and what suffering we are allowed to acknowledge,” the band wrote.
Macklemore said Monday that he had been removed from the lineup for Sheeran’s U.S. tour because he had expressed support for Palestinians in Gaza on stage at an earlier concert.
According to Macklemore, several U.S. stadium owners gave Sheeran an ultimatum over his participation in the tour.
Sheeran has denied on Instagram that he was involved in the decision to remove Macklemore. The British musician said the decision was made by the tour promoter.
Sheeran also said he had spent the past week trying to find a solution to the disagreement but had been unsuccessful.
Lukas Graham said withdrawing from the remaining concerts was a difficult decision.
“We should be able to speak about war, about civilians being killed, about children who deserve to grow up. Regardless of where they live. Regardless of which flag flies over them,” the band wrote.
Nearly six in 10 Danish companies with more than 10 employees now use artificial intelligence, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark. That’s almost four times the share recorded three years ago.
In 2026, 59 percent of these companies use AI, up from 15 percent in 2023. The share was 42 percent in 2025.
The uses of AI include analyzing text, converting spoken language into machine-readable code, generating images and videos, and automating work processes.
Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, said it has seen AI move from being mainly a topic of discussion to a tool used in daily business.
“Companies’ use of artificial intelligence is here to stay, and we can see that the large companies are the furthest ahead,” Frederikke Saabye, industry director at Dansk Erhverv, said.
According to the business organisation, companies see greater efficiency as the main benefit of using AI. A lack of employee skills, knowledge and time are the biggest barriers to making greater use of the technology.
IT-Branchen, an industry association representing technology companies in Denmark, said the wider use of AI also increases the need to consider issues such as quality, transparency and data security.
“The more the technology spreads, the more important issues of quality, transparency, data security, and not least human judgment become,” IT-Branchen’s CEO Natasha Friis Saxberg said, adding that the development makes broader AI knowledge and training more important, including upskilling and continuing education for employees.
The Danish government plans to charge tourists 20 DKK per overnight stay in Copenhagen and Aarhus and introduce a levy on cruise ships, according to government sources and a memo obtained by Børsen.
The previously undisclosed measures would help fund tax cuts that the minority government will seek support for this autumn. The plans require backing from other parties, expected to come from the center-right opposition.
The government wants to abolish the 7.5% intermediate tax on annual income between 641,200 DKK and 777,900 DKK. It also plans to remove the top-top tax on income exceeding 2,592,700 DKK.
Corporate tax would fall from 22% to 19% over three years. The ceiling for share savings accounts would rise to 500,000 DKK over the same period, and taxes on shares would be reduced.
Planned funding measures include keeping the duty on chocolate and sweets, reducing the research and development deduction for companies and raising taxes on dividends received by major shareholders.
The government also wants to limit interest deductions to 150,000 DKK for individuals and 300,000 DKK for couples. Estates worth more than 10 million DKK would face a tax rate 15 percentage points higher than today.
The tax cuts are not fully covered by higher taxes and duties. The government plans to use about 1.5 billion DKK from available public funds in 2027, rising to about 2 billion DKK in 2029.
Denmark’s government consists of the Social Democrats, Socialist People’s Party, Moderates and Social Liberals. It does not have a parliamentary majority.
Danish stocks fell for an eighth consecutive trading day Tuesday as rising oil prices and interest rates weighed on the market.
At midday, the C25 index of major Danish companies was down 0.75 percent from Monday’s closing level. The index stood at about 1,845, down 70 points, or 3.7 percent, from its latest peak on September 3.
Jacob Pedersen, an investment strategist at Danish bank Middelfart Sparekasse, said higher oil prices were pushing up interest rates.
Denmark’s largest companies generally carry less debt than businesses in other countries, making rising rates less of a direct problem for them, Pedersen said.
“But we cannot get around the fact that there is a risk in these rising interest rates in terms of the fact that it can drag some growth out of the economy, and that will also hit Danish companies,” he said.
Slower economic growth could reduce company revenue. Higher interest rates can also make stocks less attractive compared with bonds, which offer higher fixed returns when rates increase.
Pedersen said he did not expect an immediate major downturn in Danish shares. He described the market as strong because it has a large number of pharmaceutical and transport companies, which are less affected when consumers have less money to spend.
However, widespread selling by nervous investors would also affect Denmark because much of its stock market is owned by foreign investors.
“If everyone runs for the exit, it will also be felt in the Danish stock market,” Pedersen said. He added that such a decline would be driven more by market behavior than falling company earnings.
Denmark has rejected Russia’s claim that a Danish military helicopter acted “provocatively” before a Russian frigate fired two flares toward it Monday.
Russian Ambassador Vladimir Barbin said Danish helicopters had repeatedly performed “dangerous maneuvers” near Russian warships.
“The latest incident shows that the communication problems are not on the Russian navy’s side, but on the Danish side,” Barbin wrote to the Danish news agency Ritzau.
Denmark’s Armed Forces said the frigate fired two signal or distress flares toward an Air Force Fennec helicopter in international waters off Gedser. The helicopter was conducting routine photographic monitoring of the ship.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates called Barbin’s account “a Russian excuse” and denied that Denmark had provoked the frigate.
“What we do to monitor our own immediate area is completely legal, and it does not give the Russians any alibi whatsoever to start firing at us, even if it is only with flares,” Rasmussen told Danish newspaper Ekstra Bladet.
Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats also said the helicopter had a legitimate reason to be there and was following normal practice.
Barbin said Russia would investigate the incident. He also cited an alleged encounter on August 27, 2025, when a Danish helicopter flew low over the Russian warship Viceadmiral Kulakov near the German island of Fehmarn.
The ambassador said that helicopter created a collision risk and failed to answer radio calls or warnings. Ritzau has asked the Danish Defense Ministry for comment on that allegation.
Denmark has summoned Barbin to the Foreign Ministry for talks about Monday’s incident.
The Danish government will require police to register all potential crimes as criminal cases and end the practice of shelving reports without a proper investigation.
The Justice Ministry announced Tuesday that it would implement all recommendations from the National Audit Office, Denmark’s independent public spending watchdog. The disputed police practice is known as “washing cases.”
“Citizens must naturally be able to have confidence that the police handle their case properly and correctly, regardless of where in the country you live,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen of the Social Democrats said.
“In the future, all potential criminal cases must be registered as actual criminal cases,” he added.
The Public Accounts Committee, a parliamentary oversight body, strongly criticized police in May after receiving a National Audit Office report on the practice. Cases were reportedly shelved partly to save resources.
The new government reshuffled senior police leadership in June. Top positions in the National Police and PET, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, changed hands.
Several justice spokespersons in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, said they had no confidence in National Police Commissioner Thorkild Fogde after he said he did not know about the practice. Fogde was later removed from the position.
The ministry did not say whether police would receive additional funding. Wammen previously said he was open to providing more money and noted that a multiyear agreement had already increased funding and training.
The National Police and Director of Public Prosecutions must regularly report on future developments to the political parties behind that agreement.
Two earlier State Prosecutor reports were not used because the National Audit Office identified issues they had missed, Wammen said.
Train services between Fredericia, Odense and Copenhagen returned to their normal schedule at 10 a.m. Tuesday after damaged overhead wires near Sorø were repaired.
Trains between Copenhagen Airport and Slagelse also resumed normal operations, Banedanmark, which manages Denmark’s rail infrastructure, and passenger rail operator DSB said on X.
Banedanmark warned that some delays could occur while services restart. It advised passengers to check Rejseplanen, Denmark’s public journey-planning service, before traveling.
The damage had caused cancellations and delays since noon Monday. Repair work covered the section between Ringsted and Slagelse.
Banedanmark described the repairs as “extensive” and “very complex.” A support cable had fallen, and the equipment holding it had also been damaged.
“These are just some of the damages we see on our traction power system,” Banedanmark maintenance director Nicolai Sigsgaard said Monday.
Banedanmark received the first report of the problem at 12:45 p.m. Monday. Train traffic was then stopped completely while workers identified the cause.
DSB and Banedanmark said passengers delayed by more than 30 minutes could use DSB’s travel time guarantee.
DSB paid 67 million DKK in passenger compensation during the first six months of 2026, more than twice as much as during the same period in 2025.
A delay of at least 30 minutes provides a new ticket for the same route or a refund of 50 percent of the ticket price. Passengers delayed by an hour can receive 75 percent and claim up to 75 DKK for food and drinks.
Delays exceeding 90 minutes qualify for a full ticket refund.
A 31-year-old man held in custody over an assault that led to a Swedish man’s death at a Copenhagen World Cup event will appear in court on October 7.
The hearing will begin at 1 p.m. at Copenhagen City Court, the Copenhagen Police prosecution service said Tuesday. A formal indictment has not yet been filed.
The man is suspected of punching the 32-year-old Swede hard in the jaw or neck. The case falls under Section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers less serious violence.
The incident happened June 30 during a public screening at Islands Brygge of the World Cup match between Norway and Ivory Coast.
The Swedish man fell after being struck, hit his head and later died from his injuries. He worked for the Swedish police but attended the event as a private citizen.
The 31-year-old suspect, a Danish citizen who came to Denmark from Congo as an infant, has been held in custody since July 3.
Two other men, ages 24 and 29, are also suspected of violence connected to the event.
The 24-year-old Danish citizen is suspected of stomping on the Swedish man while he was lying down and hitting another Swedish citizen.
The 29-year-old, a Somali citizen, is suspected of kicking the second Swedish man. Police have notified him of the charge by telephone and through his defense lawyer because they have not located him.
Police have said the three cases will be handled separately because there is no evidence that the men acted together. Court dates for the other two men have not been announced.
Danish political parties broadly support the government’s response after a Russian frigate fired two flares toward a military helicopter Monday, according to Denmark’s Armed Forces.
Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats briefed party representatives Tuesday. The Foreign Ministry has summoned Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, to discuss the incident.
“It is completely the right thing to do,” said Inger Støjberg, leader of the Denmark Democrats, a Danish right-wing party.
The Armed Forces reported the incident in a statement at 11:02 p.m. Monday. It said an Air Force Fennec helicopter was taking routine photographs of the Russian frigate in international waters off Gedser.
The frigate fired two flares, which are normally used as attention signals at sea. One passed close to the helicopter.
“It is obviously an escalation from the Russian side,” said Thomas Danielsen, defense spokesperson for Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party.
Alex Ahrendtsen, defense spokesperson for the Danish People’s Party, urged calm.
“Of course, we should not go to war with the Russians because of some signal lights that have been sent up,” he said.
Bruus said both the frigate and helicopter had a right to operate in international waters and called the helicopter’s work normal.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats described the incident as serious but unsurprising.
She said it was part of a pattern involving “an increasingly aggressive and assertive Russia” that is testing NATO and conducting hybrid warfare against Europe.
“Russia wants to intimidate and sow discord. Our response is to stand closer together and strengthen the defence of Denmark and Europe,” Frederiksen said.
A citizen proposal seeking tighter controls on untreated wastewater discharges has received the 50,000 signatures required for consideration by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The proposal, titled “Discharge of untreated wastewater into streams, watercourses, fjords and the sea,” was published September 3 and reached the threshold 10 days later, the Folketing said Tuesday.
It will now be submitted to parliament as a motion for a resolution.
The proposal contains four measures. The first would require flow meters at every wastewater overflow in Denmark. Data from the meters would be published on a digital platform, allowing the public to see how much untreated wastewater is discharged.
The second measure would require an authorized analysis company to take regular water samples and test them against 14 European Union requirements for chemical measurements.
The proposal would also introduce a fee for discharging waste substances that are diverted around treatment plants without being treated. Its final measure would require every overflow structure to have a valid permit.
The proposal received attention after Amanda Heitmann, a member of parliament for Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, signed it.
Venstre’s environmental spokesperson, Marie Bjerre, reprimanded Heitmann for supporting the citizen proposal.
“As a political party elected to the Folketing, it is not our job to sign citizen proposals, but to take a position on the content,” Bjerre told Politiken, a Danish newspaper.
Heitmann was also one of five Venstre lawmakers who recently went against the party line and voted against the fertilizer act in parliament.
Russian frigate fires flares near Danish military helicopter in international waters
A Russian frigate fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter in international waters off Gedser on Monday, Denmark’s Armed Forces said.
The Fennec helicopter was taking routine photographs of the ship when the flares were fired. One passed close to the aircraft, according to a military statement.
Flares are pyrotechnic devices normally used as attention signals at sea. No personnel were injured, and the helicopter was not damaged.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats called the incident serious and described Russia’s actions as “very unprofessional seamanship.”
“It is serious. It is an expression of the boundaries having been moved regarding the willingness to take risks from the Russian side,” Bruus said.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen will summon the Russian ambassador to discuss the incident, though the date of the meeting has not been announced. Bruus said he did not expect further action beyond that meeting.
The defense minister said the incident would not change Denmark’s monitoring operations.
“We view it seriously, but it is not the case that we will change our behavior, understood in the sense that we have a completely legitimate task in monitoring what is going on,” Bruus said.
Inger Støjberg, leader of the Denmark Democrats, a Danish right-wing party, said the incident showed that Russian provocations had reached Denmark.
She called for NATO unity and continued support for Ukraine in its war against Russia.
“It is therefore crucial that NATO stands united, and that we continue to support Ukraine,” Støjberg said. She added that she expected a briefing from Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
Danish electricity prices head for most expensive month in years as gas costs rise
September could become the most expensive month for Danish electricity customers in several years, energy company Norlys said.
Halfway through the month, the average electricity price was 1.11 DKK per kilowatt-hour in western Denmark and 1.12 DKK in eastern Denmark.
It is the first time since December 2022 that the monthly average has exceeded 1 DKK per kilowatt-hour, according to Norlys.
“We are halfway through September, so a lot can still change, but with the rising gas prices, we unfortunately have to expect that it will be an expensive month,” said Ellen Trolle, director of Norlys’ energy business.
Electricity prices were set to rise above 7 DKK per kilowatt-hour Monday evening, their highest level in almost two years.
Norlys said the increase was caused by higher gas prices and limited electricity production from wind and solar power. Natural gas plants often supply electricity when the weather does not provide enough wind and sunlight, making power prices more sensitive to gas costs.
Kristian Rune Poulsen, an analyst at Danish energy organization Green Power Denmark, also pointed to gas prices.
“The conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, which doesn’t really want to come to an end, means that a great deal of the liquefied natural gas that we have become so dependent on cannot get out onto the world market,” he said.
Poulsen said prices would continue to fluctuate but were unlikely to fall soon while the conflict continued.
“We expect that the elevated price level will persist throughout the winter, as it looks right now,” he said.
Nearly 12 percent of Danish ninth graders fail to pass Danish or mathematics exams
More than one in 10 Danish ninth-grade students failed to earn a passing grade in Danish or mathematics in this summer’s final exams, new government figures show.
The Ministry of Education said 11.8 percent of students did not receive at least 2, the minimum passing grade, in one or both subjects during the 2025-2026 school year.
“It is too high a proportion. Because it means that they initially will not have the opportunity to move on to youth education programs,” Andreas Rasch-Christensen, a school researcher at VIA University College, a Danish higher education institution, told DR, Denmark’s public broadcaster.
DR reported a failure rate of 10.5 percent, while the ministry listed 11.8 percent. The difference is that the ministry included students whose schools did not register that they sat the exam. DR excluded those students.
The result marks a small decline from the previous school year, when 9.9 percent failed to pass Danish or mathematics. The rate was 10.1 percent in 2023-2024 and 6.9 percent in 2018-2019.
The average final exam grade was 7.3, in line with the previous four years, DR reported.
The figures follow the release of a PISA study showing that Danish students’ performance had declined in reading, mathematics and science.
The government said similar declines were occurring across much of Western Europe. Danish politicians have pointed to mobile phones as a possible cause, saying quick stimulation from phones may make it harder for students to concentrate.
The government wants to introduce a complete ban on mobile phones in schools.
Lower food VAT would cost Danish businesses about 725 million DKK a year to administer
Lowering Denmark’s value-added tax on food would cost businesses about 725 million DKK annually in added administration, according to a parliamentary response.
Tax Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates said Monday that the government wants to lower the general VAT rate on food and remove it from fruit and vegetables as soon as possible. The changes will not take effect this year.
“It is of great importance to the government to make it cheaper for Danes to fill their shopping baskets,” Engel-Schmidt said at a consultation.
The estimate is uncertain because the government has not decided how the new VAT system would work. Shops and other businesses would have to cover the administrative costs.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and Denmark’s main business and employers’ association, said the actual cost would be higher.
“When the VAT rules for food become more complicated, it affects the VAT accounting in virtually all active businesses,” tax policy chief Jacob Bræstrup said.
Bræstrup said the change would affect more than wholesalers, supermarkets and restaurants. He said total administrative costs would be “significantly higher” than the estimated 725 million DKK.
The broader proposal would cost the state 17.4 billion DKK a year, according to the Ministry of Taxation and Growth.
Leading economists have criticized the plan as an expensive and inefficient way to help people. They warn that businesses might not pass the full tax reduction on through lower prices. Some savings could instead pay for administration or increase company earnings.
The government plans to present several possible models in the second half of 2026.
Extensive damage to the overhead wire system near Sorø is expected to disrupt train services between Ringsted and Slagelse until 10 a.m. Tuesday, according to Banedanmark, which manages work on Denmark’s rail network.
One track has reopened after DSB, the Danish passenger train operator, stopped services on the section around midday Monday. Trains are now running on a reduced timetable, with longer travel times and some cancellations.
Tony Bispeskov, DSB’s head of information, said priority would be given to international, InterCityLyn and InterCity trains.
Banedanmark said it received a report of problems with the overhead wire system between Sorø and Slagelse at 12:45 p.m. Monday. Train services were stopped completely while the cause was identified.
“There we can see that we have extensive damage to one of our tracks. At the moment, this means that we only have one passable track to operate on, and that we are running with a reduced timetable,” Banedanmark said.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said Monday that she is “quite optimistic” Denmark, Greenland and the USA can reach an agreement on security and defense in Greenland.
Frederiksen spoke at a news conference in Finland, where she attended a European summit focused on security in the Arctic.
“We have agreed to start a high-level working group on closer cooperation on security and defense, also in Greenland,” Frederiksen said.
“As long as the working group between Greenland, Denmark, and the USA continues its work, it is too early to draw a conclusion. But I am quite optimistic that we will succeed in finding a way,” she said.
Frederiksen visited Greenland last week with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Denmark is among 10 NATO countries conducting a joint military exercise in Greenland. The exercise is intended to show that Denmark and NATO are protecting Greenland and the Arctic.
US President Donald Trump has criticized Denmark for not doing enough to protect Greenland from threats posed by Russia and China.
During the first weeks of September, 400 soldiers from 10 NATO countries are operating on land, at sea and in the air near Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq. They are training to operate in Arctic conditions as part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry surveillance and deterrence mission.
“If one is to be able to operate in the Arctic, one has to train up here,” Søren Andersen, head of Denmark’s Arctic Command, told the Danish news agency Ritzau last week.
Andersen said the temporary Arctic Shield exercise is part of a long-term strategy for Greenland and the Arctic.
“For us, it is about helping to transform NATO’s northern flank into a hard target. Meaning all the way from Alaska across Canada, Greenland, and to the northern part of Norway,” he said.
Denmark and Greenland are also discussing whether to give the USA greater access to Greenland. The New York Times reported in the spring, based on American sources, that the USA wants three bases in Greenland as part of a possible agreement. Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq were reportedly among the possible locations.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats declined to discuss the working group’s talks during a visit to Narsarsuaq last week.
“I cannot comment on that. What goes on in that working group, goes on in that working group,” Bruus told Ritzau.
Bruus said the government wants to extend the operating period of Narsarsuaq Airport by one year if it receives support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“Initially, it is a one-year extension. That gives us the opportunity to extend the playing board,” Bruus said.
Chief of Defense Michael Hyldgaard said Narsarsuaq would be an obvious possible location for an American base because of its position in southern Greenland and its access to transatlantic routes, the Denmark Strait and the GIUK gap.
The GIUK gap is the sea area between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. It is an important military passage where NATO can monitor and block Russian submarines moving toward the Atlantic.
The USA previously operated a military base in Narsarsuaq from July 1941 to November 1958.
CPH Half will expand to 45,000 runners for its race on September 19, 2027, because of high demand, organizer Sparta Atletik og Løb, a Danish athletics and running organization, said in a news release.
Around 35,000 people are taking part in this year’s half marathon, up from about 32,000 in 2025.
Tickets for the 2027 race will be sold through a lottery instead of on a first-come, first-served basis.
Registration for the lottery opens September 16 and remains open for two weeks. People can register alone or in groups of up to three. Each group will either be selected together or not selected at all.
Selected runners will have 48 hours to buy a ticket. The price is DKK 795 plus a small administration fee.
“When demand is so high, access to the bib numbers must also function in a way where everyone has a fair and equal chance of getting a bib number,” Dorte Vibjerg, CEO of Sparta Atletik og Løb, said in the release.
The organizers also used a lottery to sell tickets for this year’s CPH Half, which is part of the World Athletics Road Running Championships. Similar systems are used for major marathons in Berlin and London.
This year’s race starts Sunday. Elite international runners will begin first, followed by the other participants.

articles.title: What Andy Burnham needs from Donald Trump at their New York meet
articles.body:
What Andy Burnham needs from Donald Trump at their New York meet
Britain’s new prime minister is set for his first meeting with the U.S. president next Tuesday. Unlike Keir Starmer, he won’t be angling for a second helping.
LONDON — When Keir Starmer had his first dinner with Donald Trump, he strained so hard to impress the U.S. president that his host offered the British team a second helping of chicken.
Andy Burnham’s face-to-face introduction next Tuesday will look very different. Instead of the two-hour Trump Tower rendezvous that Starmer enjoyed in September 2024, British officials expect their new prime minister to sit down with his U.S. counterpart on relatively neutral ground in the United Nations headquarters at the far edge of Manhattan.
Their meeting is currently penciled in for Tuesday afternoon, sandwiched between Burnham’s 15-minute address to the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday evening and Trump’s morning speech to the same hall — which given his past form, may drown out other headlines with whatever he says there.
Advertisement
That may prove convenient for Burnham.
“There will be so much going on that it reduces the intensity and scrutiny,” said Claire Ainsley, a former aide to Starmer who is now at the center-left Progressive Policy Institute think tank.
POLITICO spoke to a dozen current and former senior U.K. officials, ministers and MPs, many of them granted anonymity to speak frankly, about Burnham’s likely handling of the visit. Almost all predicted he would opt for a middle road somewhere between Starmer’s initial charm and the more combative approach of Canadian PM Mark Carney: Get in, smile, press the case for Ukraine, and try to leave without a major upset.
Downing Street’s overwhelming priority for the New York visit has been to squeeze in an IRL meeting with Trump, with whom Burnham has now spoken to by phone twice, according to a person familiar with the preparations. It will allow the two men to engage but with far lower stakes than a one-to-one visit in Washington or London, just one of a series of leader meetings that blend into the noise of a multilateral summit.
The hope, one U.K. government official said, is to “get the Trump meeting done and dusted in a relatively safe environment.”
That was then
The shift away from Starmer’s more high-pressure encounters is driven not so much by Burnham’s laid-back style — the new PM said last month he will “say what I feel” to Trump while also trying to “find a connection” — as by a profound change in the balance of risk since 2024.
Advertisement
Burnham has less to prove. Starmer, who took office shortly before Trump’s second election victory, signed deals on tech, trade and pharmaceuticals from scratch. Warming to Trump was the “medicine required at that period,” said a U.K. diplomat.
His successor’s job is to fix the mess of unresolved threads left behind.
Burnham also has the benefit of hindsight, having watched Starmer’s efforts to praise Trump lead to embarrassment when the president lambasted the PM over the Iran conflict, oil drilling and tech taxes. Trump at one point even dissed Starmer as “no Winston Churchill.”
Donald Trump shakes hands with Britain’s former prime minister Keir Starmer at a joint press conference at the White House on February 27, 2025. | Carl Court/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
The new PM won’t “bend the knee in the way Starmer did,” predicted the same U.K. diplomat. He won’t be going to “kiss the ring,” added the first U.K. government official quoted above. “It’s completely different this time. There’s no drama about having to stay in his good books.”
Yet Trump still has two years left in office, and a smooth relationship will be vital for the U.K. leader who has tried to keep his focus on domestic issues — but is watching his promises to ease living costs be buffeted by rising defense pressures and inflation from the Iran war.
The two men will also meet at a point where Britain and its allies are turning their heads away from the U.S.
Advertisement
Two years ago “Trump was at the height of his powers,” said one Starmer Cabinet minister. “The reality is different now.”
While November’s looming midterm elections threaten to dent Trump’s authority at home, abroad his approaches to NATO and the Middle East have led European allies to find solace elsewhere. Britain and its allies are forming groups of so-called middle powers, while Carney pushes closer ties between Canada and the EU that will still be in negotiation long after Trump’s departure. And Burnham has repeatedly talked about strengthening ties with Brussels — seeing through a reset in relations that Starmer initiated.
Olivia O’Sullivan, director of the U.K. in the World Programme at the Chatham House think tank, said the country is now “testing the waters” of loosening its strategic alignment with the U.S. — even as it continues to rely on America’s security and nuclear weapons architecture. (And even as Burnham continues to let the U.S. use Britain’s air bases for limited strikes on Iran.)
Emily Thornberry, the Labour MP who chairs the House of Commons’ foreign affairs committee, said there’s a reason for that: “I think a couple of years ago, the hopes were high that Trump would help with Ukraine, we would have a proper trade deal, and so on. He hasn’t delivered on those things, so we’re getting used to the disappointment. We don’t expect as much.”
One former senior official under Starmer put it more starkly: “The world is just viewing the United States differently. He is doing enormous long-term damage to the U.S.’s relationship with all of its allies. Institutions that have stood for decades can no longer do the jobs that they used to be able to do, because America is proving to be an unreliable ally. This is hugely significant in the long term.”
No list of deliverables
Burnham, whose two calls with Trump since July have both run far over their allotted time, is at least looking to keep things friendly.
Advertisement
The new prime minister is not expected to take a big list of deliverables or policy goals into his meeting, two people familiar with the planning said.
Burnham is expected to press Trump on U.S. support for Ukraine after paying his first overseas trip there last month. British officials hope there is now a more pro-Ukraine atmosphere on Capitol Hill after the House of Representatives passed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill long championed by the late Senator Lindsay Graham.
Thornberry said the PM should urge Trump to speed up supplies of Patriot missiles to Ukraine ahead of the winter. Ukraine’s forces are “winning without the Americans, but they could actually win if the Americans did help,” she added.
Andy Burnham visits the scene of Russian strikes on Lukanivska Market in Kyiv, Ukraine on August 24, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/WPA Pool/Getty Images
Britain’s wider activities at UNGA — which Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband will also attend — could be dominated by a clash over the hardening stance of the U.K., France and Canada against Israel. The three countries issued joint sanctions against West Bank settlements earlier in September, after what one U.K. official described as a “tag team” coordination effort between Miliband, Burnham and the leaders and foreign ministers of allied countries.
The U.K. is hoping to use UNGA to work on the next steps in the humanitarian response for Gaza. British officials are privately hopeful that the U.S. response will continue to be muted; two U.K. government officials said they believed Secretary of State Marco Rubio viewed the intervention as helpful, given it applies pressure to Israel without it coming from the U.S.
Burnham faces a choice about how hard to lean into the issue of the Middle East in his own speech to UNGA. His closest No. 10 aides have kept a “tight hold” on the thinking around his remarks, said the person with knowledge of the planning quoted above.
Advertisement
Whatever he chooses, plenty of dangers lie in wait — not least Trump’s views on oil and gas in the North Sea. Industry figures believe Burnham’s government has delayed a decision on whether to drill at two fields until after an Oct. 8 special election to replace Starmer, where Labour is battling the Green Party. Trump has long been perplexed by the delay.
Burnham’s government has also delayed a key decision on defense spending until 2027, despite pressure from the U.S. to set out a clearer timetable.
And Britain is stuck over how to proceed with its deal giving up sovereignty of the Chagos Islands, a strategically crucial archipelago in the Indian Ocean, after Trump disowned the pact earlier this year. Mauritius — the beneficiary — could agitate at UNGA to unfreeze the deal.
But it’s the issue of artificial intelligence that has lately rocketed up the news agenda. Here, Burnham faces a conundrum.
On the one hand, Britain can sell a “third way” in AI development between Trump’s free-for-all and burdensome regulation in the EU, argued Emily Darlington, a Labour MP and member of the Commons Science and Technology Committee.
“There are things that [U.S. tech firms] need from us, not least some of the really advanced stuff that we’re doing around quantum, and in the future neuromorphic computing,” she said. “We’re a huge market for them. Large language models are desperate to train on British material that goes back centuries. The BBC archive, all of these sorts of things, are what they’re desperate for. There’s a bit of a fight over whether there is a British advantage to allowing them access to that material, and so there is a bit of a negotiation.”
Advertisement
Yet the U.K.’s digital services tax has drawn Trump’s repeated ire, while PoliticsHome reported this week that U.S. officials warned Britain at the London embassy against its online safety restrictions and plans to ban under-16s from social media. One minister said Burnham’s conversation “can’t be on the digital services tax or regulation like the Online Safety Act, because there’s a tangible risk Trump will go ballistic.”
‘Andy has been a lucky general’
The same minister suggested Burnham will want the sort of relationship that Tony Blair had with George Bush — respectful, even if not as equals.
It is a tall order for a president as mercurial as Trump, yet old allies of Starmer insist he paved the way for it. They point to Starmer’s decision to push back against Trump to defend Greenland’s sovereignty, to bring together a “coalition of the willing” for Ukraine and to welcome Kyiv’s leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy after Trump hectored him in the Oval Office.
Volodymyr Zelensky shakes hands with Andy Burnham ahead of their bilateral meeting at Horodetskyi House in Kyiv, Ukraine, on August 24, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/WPA Pool/Getty Images
Starmer was not being nice to Trump because he liked him, argued the Starmer Cabinet minister quoted earlier in this story, but because he had to bring him back from the brink on NATO and Ukraine.
It means Burnham has inherited an established relationship in which he has no need to lavish the president with praise. All he has to do, argue some, is avoid a barrage of abuse on Truth Social.
“Andy has been a lucky general in the calming of Trump,” argued one U.K. official who worked under Starmer. “Keir was dealing with a completely different beast.”
And yet, this person added: “It could all change in the space of two weeks.”

articles.title: How the Air Force Rigged F-15s in the Middle East with Drone-Busting Rockets in a Week
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—As the threat of Iranian-made drones rose in recent conflicts, the Air Force rushed last year to equip F-15E Strike Eagles in the Middle East with a cheap, cost-effective way of defeating them.
The Air Force Test Center was able to field the new capability—laser-guided rockets—in roughly a week, the head of the center revealed at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference here Sept. 16.
It’s not the first time the Air Force has turned to this solution, known as the Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System, to neutralize enemy one-way attack drones and cruise missiles.
APKWS was originally designed as an air-to-ground capability, with a laser-guided kit added to Hydra-70 rockets to turn the system into a precision-guided munition.
The Air Force explored using the rockets in an air-to-air role in 2019, testing the system on the F-16 Fighting Falcon. For a few years, the experiment was considered nothing more than a proof of concept, not a real-world capability.
But as the use of Iranian drones was expanded, the program gained new urgency. The system was rushed first to F-16s in 2024 and then prioritized for F-15Es in 2025. Nine days after testing began in May of last year, the system was being equipped on Strike Eagles in the Middle East, said Brig. Gen. Mark A. Massaro.
“At the end of the first week, we had demonstrated, both in a developmental and an operational sense, that it was a usable capability, and we deployed that capability at the end of the first week,” Massaro said. “We deployed that capability into theater. We deployed some of our maintainers and some of our testers into theater to help the first week.”
The initiative is an example of the Air Force Test Center’s ability to quickly “bridge between raw concept and decisive combat-credible power,” said Massaro. He was involved in tests of APKWS in his previous role as commander of the 96th Test Wing, which conducts developmental testing of weapons for the service, and worked alongside the 53rd Wing, which conducts operational tests.
The need for the system was clear.
