Lee added that South Korea will “carry out the minimum necessary activities” to protect its own merchant ships and oil shipping routes.

articles.title: Russia plans ”accidental” drone strikes on NATO countries, Tusk says
articles.body:
Intelligence assessments indicate that Russian plans include drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told parliament on 17 September. He said Russia could seek to make such attacks appear accidental in order to weaken NATO's resolve.
The warning comes after an escalating pattern of drone incidents and suspected sabotage in Poland, Lithuania and Germany, as European governments face growing security risks linked to Russia's war against Ukraine.
Tusk cites NATO, US and Ukrainian intelligence
Tusk said he was relying on intelligence from NATO, Ukraine, and the United States. He described late autumn and winter as the most critical phase of the war so far and warned of escalating attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure.
"There is a real risk that the territory of one or several NATO countries on the eastern flank may be entered by drones or other types of missiles," Tusk said.
He said the purpose could be to show that Article 5 "exists only in theory" and to weaken NATO's willingness to respond.
Jet-powered drones near the Polish border
The 17 September attack struck near Yahodyn, close to the Dorohusk border crossing. Tusk said Russia had used jet-powered drones that travel at higher speeds and altitudes, making them harder to intercept.
A pattern of incidents near NATO territory
The warning follows several incidents near NATO's eastern border. On 13 September, a drone struck a passenger train at Yahodyn, near the Ukraine-Poland border. Ukraine's state railway company said it was "highly probable" that the Russian drone's intended target was a diplomatic train that had carried former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt. Former CIA Director David Petraeus was on a separate train that remained at the station. No one was injured.
On 15 September, Italian NATO jets shot down a drone in Lithuanian airspace after it apparently entered from Belarus. Lithuanian authorities said the wreckage indicated it had likely been carrying explosives. Poland also recovered a Gerbera-type drone carrying a live warhead from the Baltic coast near Rusinowo.
Germany on 1 September blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack involving explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport on 4–5 August, adding another NATO country to the series of incidents.
From warning to coalition
Tusk visited Ukraine on 18 September for the inaugural Carpathian Eight summit. Zelenskyy said Ukraine and its European partners were building an anti-ballistic coalition, while Polish Deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski said Warsaw was preparing its largest military aid package for Ukraine, potentially including Patriot missiles.
Russia's Foreign Ministry rejected Tusk's accusations as "contrived" and "far-fetched".

articles.title: Russia has ramped up ballistic strikes on Ukraine using repurposed S-400 missiles – Reuters
articles.body:
Russia has ramped up ballistic strikes on Ukraine using repurposed S-400 missiles – Reuters
New data on Russian missile strikes shows that Russia has been increasingly using RM-48U missiles, originally designed as targets for air-defence crews, against Ukraine.
Source: Reuters, citing official Ukrainian data
Quote: "RM48Us made up more than half of the 228 ballistic and hypersonic missiles fired at Ukraine in July and early August, according to the figures compiled by military analysts at the General Prosecutor's Office."
Details: Reuters reported that in July Russia used the highest number of ballistic and hypersonic missiles in a single month since the start of the full-scale invasion.
Quote: "Of those 158 strikes, 87 were from RM48Us, the data showed. The pace of the aerial assault has only intensified; there were 70 Russian ballistic and hypersonic strikes in the first eight days of August, the Ukrainian data showed, with 36 of them from RM48Us."
More details: The mass use of RM-48Us could be intended to deplete Ukraine's stockpiles of interceptor missiles, said Sidharth Kaushal, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a London-based defence think tank.
"Their use allows the Russians to husband the more capable missiles they have, the Iskanders, but also the KN-23s and the Zircons, for winter when they would want to really lean into their ballistic missile campaign," Kaushal said.
Reuters also points to a shift in the ratio of RM-48U missiles to Iskander-system missiles used by Russia.
Quote: "Indeed, as the RM48U attacks surged in July, the number of Iskanders fired fell to 38 from more than 100 the previous month, the Ukrainian data showed."
More details: "RM" stands for "raketa mishen", meaning "missile target" in Russian. RM-48Us are launched from Russian S-400 surface-to-air missile systems. The Ukrainian Prosecutor General's Office and Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) say the missile travels along a high-speed ballistic trajectory. The Prosecutor General's Office noted that the RM-48U is less powerful and accurate than Iskander ballistic missiles.
The Prosecutor General's Office said military experts have also established that RM-48Us deviate from their intended target by an average of around 300 m. Their warheads can also scatter metal fragments over a wide area when they detonate.
DIU reported that Russia plans to produce over 480 RM-48Us this year, more than double the 200-plus missiles it manufactured last year.
Background: DIU recently revealed the structure and component base of the Russian RM-48U missile, as well as the companies involved in its production.
	
Subscribe on Patreon to back our journalism long-term.

articles.title: “What Ukraine needs right now”: Poland to provide Ukraine with scarce F-16 missiles to shoot down jet-powered drones
articles.body:
Poland will provide another aid package to Ukraine, which will include, among other things, “what Ukraine needs right now,” Deputy Minister of National Defense Stanisław Wziątek said, reports Polskie Radio. He said the package would include missiles for F-16 fighter jets, which the Ukrainian military uses to shoot down Russian drones.
Ukraine is critically short of missiles for F-16 fighter jets, which shoot down Russian UAVs. Recently, it was reported that pilots sometimes took off without missiles, using only the aircraft’s built-in M61A1 Vulcan cannon, which is dangerous for civilians. Poland’s newly promised aid will include these missiles for Ukraine.
Among other things, Poland will provide aviation equipment, the report said. Media reports added that the aid package may be worth around €50 million.
Ammunition for F-16s and possible aviation equipment
“Our aid is in the process of being prepared. Everything will happen in a moment. I cannot say what it contains, I can only say that it is what Ukraine needs right now. This includes basic ammunition. These are the ones mounted on F-16s to shoot down Russian drones,” Wziątek said.
AIM-9 and AIM-120 are air-to-air missiles that the Ukrainian Armed Forces use with F-16s to fight Russian aviation, Militarnyi says. The outlet adds that last year Ukrainian F-16s were spotted with APKWS II missiles, which are effective against drones. As for the aforementioned aviation equipment, Poland may provide decommissioned MiG-29 fighter jets or drones, the media outlet suggests.
The MiG-29 does not use the same scarce stocks of AIM-9 and AIM-120 missiles.
Missile shortage is not new
In July 2025, America abruptly suspended arms supplies to Ukraine, affecting some types of weapons. Among them were more than 90 US-made AIM air-to-air missiles that were in Poland and on their way to Ukraine, but were withdrawn by the US, according to a Wall Street Journal article. Since then, Ukraine has received Western aid for air defense systems, but missiles have remained among the items in short supply.
Ukraine faced a severe shortage of F-16 missiles from late November to mid-December, according to Reuters. One source said Ukraine had "nothing to put on its jets for almost a month."
While F-16s likely rank first by number in the Ukrainian Armed Forces, the Soviet-made MiG-29 ranks second, Euromaidan Press. Ukraine had enough R-73 missiles for this fighter, but when the Ukrainian Armed Forces also began using them for ground-based launchers after 9M33 missiles for Soviet Osa air defense systems ran out, the rate of consumption increased sharply.
Ukrainian forces were observed resuming the use of older missiles that had been considered obsolete. There is an alternative: using the fighter’s cannon. However, this practice is dangerous.

articles.title: EU pledges €3.3 billion for Ukraine, von der Leyen says “more is coming” as Russia’s escalating air war makes life in Ukrainian cities increasingly difficult
articles.body:
EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen says Europe will provide Ukraine with another €3.3 billion for missiles and drones as Russia intensifies attacks on Kyiv and seeks to make daily life in Ukraine's cities impossible.
Ukraine has repeatedly appealed to its partners for more air defense as Russia develops increasingly sophisticated ways to attack Ukrainian cities, while Ukraine’s stocks of air-defense interceptors have fallen to critically low levels.
Following a call with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, von der Leyen said the EU would disburse the funds on 18 September. She also said the EU had approved funding for Patriot air defense systems through its Ukraine Support Loan.
Ukraine needs more air defense
Russia has increasingly combined large numbers of attack drones with ballistic and cruise missiles, forcing Ukraine to defend vast areas while facing shortages of high-end interceptors.
The most difficult targets are Russia’s ballistic missiles, which can reach Ukrainian cities within minutes and require specialized systems such as Patriot to intercept. Ukraine has repeatedly called for more Patriot batteries and interceptors as Russia increases missile attacks.
Ukraine also needs additional air defense capabilities to counter Russia’s increasingly sophisticated drone attacks. Russia is deploying faster, more advanced Geran-type drones that are more difficult to intercept, increasing pressure on Ukraine’s already limited air-defense stocks.
Von der Leyen said the EU had approved funding for Patriot systems last week, but acknowledged that “clearly more is needed.”
The new €3.3 billion package will fund the procurement of missiles and drones for Ukraine, strengthening its ability to defend against Russian attacks.
Europe proposes joint air defense development
Von der Leyen also announced that the EU is prepared to use remaining funds from its Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program to launch a new joint EU-Ukraine defense initiative.
The proposed program would focus on developing a European air and missile defense system, building on the jointly developed anti-ballistic Freya system.
The goal is to combine Ukraine’s battlefield experience and defense innovation with European technology and industrial capacity, according to von der Leyen.
The announcement comes as Ukraine is trying to strengthen its air defenses ahead of another winter of Russian attacks, when strikes against energy and other critical infrastructure could have an especially severe impact on civilians.
The EU has billions in unspent defense funds. It wants to use them for projects with Ukraine
Von der Leyen calls for broader support
Von der Leyen said the EU has already mobilized nearly €15 billion for Ukraine in 2026, with additional support planned. She added that “more is coming.”
She also said Ukraine needs to complete reforms in the Verkhovna Rada to unlock further funding and continue its path toward EU membership.
“Europe is stepping up,” von der Leyen said. “Now others must step up their support too.”

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Elite Russian drone unit pulls back from northern Donetsk Oblast amid Ukrainian offensive
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Elite Russian drone unit pulls back from northern Donetsk Oblast amid Ukrainian offensive
Key developments on Sept. 18:
- Russia pulls elite drone unit from northern Donetsk Oblast after losses from Operation Vivaldi, Ukraine's military says
- Russia increasingly using repurposed S-400 training missiles to bombard Ukraine, Reuters reports
- As elections get underway, Russia closes Sochi polling stations over drone threat
- Ukrainian National Guard creates recruitment center for foreign volunteers, Ukrainian Prime Minister announces
- Head of Ukraine's Eastern Operational Command steps down amid military reshuffle
Russia pulled units of its elite unmanned systems formation Rubicon from the front line in northern Donetsk Oblast after suffering heavy losses during Ukraine's ongoing Operation Vivaldi offensive, Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps said on Sept. 18.
"3rd Corps fighters disabled Rubicon's command system: they destroyed its logistics, ammunition depots, drone launch sites, newly formed units, and experienced UAV operators," the unit said in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda.
"The Russians lost the ability to quickly replenish the unit with resources and trained personnel."
The Rubicon Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies is a sprawling Russian drone unit and the core of Russia's recently formed Unmanned Systems branch of the military.
The unit specializes in cutting off logistics, hunting Ukrainian drone teams on the ground, and intercepting high-value reconnaissance and strike drones, and is made up of detachments, each numbering several hundred personnel.
The Rubicon contingent was systematically attrited during both the lead-up to Vivaldi and in its early stages, Oleksandr Borodin, the 3rd Corps spokesperson, said in a comment to the Kyiv Independent.
"Most specialized drone units in the area suffered significant losses among qualified personnel and material and technical resources," Borodin said.
"One of these units was the 'notorious Rubicon,' and it was this unit that was withdrawn from our zone of responsibility in the most difficult hours for the enemy, probably due to the trends of a rapid decline in its combat potential."
read also
Russia increasingly using repurposed S-400 training missiles to bombard Ukraine, Reuters reports
Russia increasingly uses repurposed S-400 training missiles to strike Ukrainian cities, Reuters reports, citing figures compiled by military analysts at Ukraine's General Prosecutor's Office.
Russia fired 87 of the RM48U training missiles at Ukraine in July, compared to 10 in June and 14 in May. The RM48U is significantly less accurate than a purpose-built ballistic missile but still capable of causing significant damage.
Russia uses such repurposed training missiles, originally designed to serve as aerial targets in military training, to keep up pressure on Ukraine and conserve stocks of their more valuable ballistic missiles, an analyst interviewed by Reuters said.
"Their use allows the Russians to husband the more capable missiles they have, the Iskanders, but also the KN-23s and the Zircons, for winter when they would want to really lean into their ballistic missile campaign," Sidharth Kaushal, a senior research fellow at London think tank RUSI, told Reuters.
Ukraine’s sole defense against ballistic missiles is the American-supplied PAC-3 Patriot. Patriot interceptors have been in short supply amid intensified Russian ballistic missile attacks and the U.S. war in the Persian Gulf draining global Patriot interceptor stocks.
read also
As elections get underway, Russia closes Sochi polling stations over drone threat
Voting for Russia's State Duma elections in the Black Sea city of Sochi was put on hold on Sept. 18, with polling stations closed due to the threat of a Ukrainian drone attack, local authorities said.
"Exhaustive security measures have been taken at polling stations in Sochi," said the city's mayor, Andrey Propushin.
"Members of election commissions, observers and voters, who are at the precincts, have been moved to shelters until the 'drone attack' threat is lifted."
Russia on Sept. 18 began its three-day elections for the 450-member State Duma, the lower chamber of Russia's legislature, for the first time since the outbreak of the full-scale war in Ukraine.
Elections in Russia are tightly controlled by the regime but can help the Kremlin gauge the level of public support for the invasion of Ukraine, now ongoing for more than four and a half years.
The ruling United Russia party, backed by Russian President Vladimir Putin, is broadly expected to maintain control over the Russian legislature.
With the exponential expansion of Ukraine's "deep-strike" drone campaign over the past 12 months, Russian cities on the Black Sea coast, usually popular with tourists in the warmer months, have increasingly coming under fire.
read also
Ukrainian National Guard creates recruitment center for foreign volunteers, Ukrainian Prime Minister announces
The Ukrainian National Guard has launched a centralized recruitment center which aims to boost foreign recruitment and aid foreign volunteers that enlist in the Ukrainian National Guard, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced on Sept. 18.
"The Center will coordinate the recruitment of foreign volunteers for contract service and will accompany them at all stages: from interviews and checks to training," Koretskyi said in a statement on social media.
"The candidate's path to service should be as fast as possible. Combat units should receive the necessary reinforcements more quickly," he continued.
The Ukrainian National Guard is under the jurisdiction of Ukraine's Ministry of Internal Affairs, unlike regular military forces, but includes some of Ukraine's most effective military units, such as 1st Azov Corps and 2nd Khartiia Corps.
Ukraine is increasingly turning to the recruitment of foreign volunteers to replace losses and to supplement domestic manpower reserves. "Our goal is to fill up to 30 to 50% of assault and infantry positions with foreigners," former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said in June.
"Recruiting foreign volunteers to the Defense Forces is one of the state's priorities. The task is to scale this work and attract more people to the Ukrainian army who are ready to defend our state together with Ukrainians," Koretskyi said.
read also
Head of Ukraine's Eastern Operational Command steps down amid military reshuffle
Major General Viktor Nikoliuk announced on Sept. 17 that he is leaving his post as commander of Ukraine's Eastern Operational Command.
"I can say with confidence that I am handing over to my successor a fully combat-ready force capable of steadfastly conducting active defensive operations," he wrote.
The general assumed leadership of the Eastern Operational Command — a group of forces defending some of the most embattled regions along Ukraine's front lines, including units in Donetsk, Luhansk, Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kharkiv oblasts — in April 2026. He previously served as the commander of the Donetsk Operational-Strategic Group.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Poland’s Tusk heads to Kyiv after warning of Russian strikes on Ukrainian allies
articles.body:
- 
  Russia is planning hybrid strikes with drones or rockets on European countries supporting Ukraine, among them Poland according to its prime minister, Donald Tusk. Russia will pretend the attacks are “accidental” in order to “paralyse or at least weaken the motivation of Nato countries” to rush to the defence of the member state coming under attack, Tusk said in a speech to the Polish parliament. “There is a real risk that drones or other types of projectiles will enter the territory of one or several countries on the eastern flank and even cause destruction,” Tusk said, vowing that “if anyone dares to attack us, they will face a resolute response from us and our allies”.
- 
  Tusk announced he would travel to Ukraine overnight, arriving on Friday, in what might be seen as an act of defiance against Russia after European leaders were in transit during a drone strike on a train near the Polish-Ukrainian border on Sunday. Officials usually keep their travel plans to Ukraine secret for security reasons. In Kyiv, he said he would discuss with Volodymyr Zelenskyy how to defend against the new types of drones, as well as discuss with partners including Slovakia further sanctions against Russia.
- 
  The Slovak prime minister, Robert Fico, also said he would be in Kyiv as he claimed Europe is closer than ever to a large-scale war erupting from the war in Ukraine and politicians must strive for peace. Fico has kept warm relations with Russia while criticising EU and Nato aid to Ukraine, though Slovakia’s arms industry is simultaneously a producer of artillery shells supplied to Kyiv’s forces. On Friday the European Union will disburse €3.3bn to Ukraine to buy missiles and drones, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, has announced.
- 
  Tusk said Russia was not ready for any peace talks “without the total capitulation of Ukraine”. “They are convinced the winter will be tragically critical for Ukraine.” He said last winter Poland stepped in with deliveries when Ukraine’s energy infrastructure came under attack, but if border crossings are destroyed it will be much harder for Warsaw to offer such help this winter. “Russia’s goal is to destroy as much as possible the economy and logistics of Ukraine,” Tusk said, adding that intelligence indicates continuous attacks of “very high frequency and intensity” on six main Ukrainian cities should be expected in the near future.
- 
  A drone hit a petrol station near Ukraine’s border with Poland on Thursday, Tusk said separately at a press conference in Warsaw. A spokesperson for the Polish military told TVN24 that air defences were activated on Thursday after a jet-powered drone approached Polish airspace before exploding about 4km (2.5 miles) from the Polish border. Poland’s Lublin and Rzeszow airports temporarily suspended operations on Thursday as the air force responded to Russian drone activity, Polish authorities said.
- 
  Russian missiles and drones injured at least 19 people in Ukraine’s capital and the surrounding region, authorities said on Thursday. Kyiv’s military administration said more than 10 locations were hit, while 33 sites were damaged in the wider region. A 10-year-old girl and a 12-year-old boy were among the injured, the administration said.
- 
  Ukraine’s air force said it destroyed or suppressed 131 Russian aerial targets during the overnight attack in the Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia and Odesa regions. The attack involved ballistic and cruise missiles as well as drones and decoys. In Odesa, seven people were injured, including two children, according to Ukraine’s state emergency Service. Apartments on the 14th through 16th floors of a residential building were damaged. A private residential building in Odesa was also destroyed and others damaged.
- 
  Ukrainian forces struck an oil refinery in Yaroslavl and a military airfield in the Rostov region, Zelenskyy said on Thursday. Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s operation against the Yaroslavl oil refinery was conducted jointly by the country’s Security Service, special operations forces, military intelligence and the foreign intelligence service. The security service also struck a military airfield in Rostov, damaging an An-12 aircraft, two An-26s and three helicopters. Reuters said that according to its industry sources, the refinery halted crude processing after the Ukrainian attack. The local Russian governor confirmed the damage.
- 
  A Russian drone struck a civilian vessel flying the flag of Tanzania in the Black Sea on Thursday, killing the ship’s captain and injuring three crew members, according to Oleh Kiper, the regional head in Odesa. Russia damaged the Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi bridge in the Odesa region, significantly limiting Ukraine’s ability to transport grain to its Danube river ports, Ukrainian state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia said on Thursday. According to Ukrzaliznytsia, about 3,000 grain wagons are bound for the Danube ports. Without the bridge, they would need 26 days to reach the ports. “The situation is very difficult. We are working to restore the Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi bridge,” a company official said.

articles.title: U.S. May Have Committed War Crimes in Iran, U.N. Report Says
articles.body:
The U.S. may have committed war crimes when its strikes allegedly hit an elementary school and a sports facility in Iran, according to a United Nations report publicly released on Thursday.
The U.N.’s Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran said it found “reasonable grounds to believe that the United States committed a war crime by launching indiscriminate attacks that killed or injured civilians or damaged civilian objects.”
The U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, triggering a war that has stretched into its seventh month. Among those attacks, the mission identified U.S. Tomahawk missile strikes that hit Tree of Tayyiba Elementary School in Minab, killing more than 150 people, including 120 children, and an alleged U.S. missile strike that dispersed tens of thousands of tungsten pellets over a sports complex and residential area in Lamerd, killing 22 civilians. (The U.S. denied carrying out any strike within the vicinity of Lamerd on Feb. 28.)
Both civilian facilities were “clearly identifiable,” the report said.
“The U.S.’s failure to update information in relation to the school in its targeting databases and to verify that the building was a military objective before launching the attack went beyond mere negligence,” the report said. “Rather, the U.S. directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen.”
The mission is expected to present its findings, which also conclude that Iranian authorities likely committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on protesters in December and January, to the U.N. Human Rights Council on Monday.
“People in Iran are caught between intensified repression and violence by their government and renewed armed conflict and insecurity resulting from the hostilities between Iran and the U.S and Israel,” the report said.
The war has produced a significant civilian toll, with at least 2,100 people killed across the region by late April. In Iran, human rights groups estimate that more than 1,700 civilians were killed by the end of April, including more than 1,000 civilians who were killed in the first five days of the U.S.-Israeli bombing campaign. That includes hundreds of women and children, dozens of health care workers, and at least nine journalists. Iranian authorities reported another 18 deaths from U.S. strikes on Sept. 1, which included several civilians. Israel’s strikes on Lebanon have also killed more than 4,300 people and displaced more than one million since early March, according to Lebanon’s Health Ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants.
U.S. conduct in its war against Iran has come under growing scrutiny. On Sept. 1, an apparent U.S. strike hit a wedding celebration in Kuhestak, killing five people and wounding more than 60. Washington has not accepted responsibility, although it launched an internal probe into the strike. An analysis by Reuters indicated that the damage was likely caused by a direct hit from a U.S. munition.
The U.S. also carried out strikes on bridges and electrical infrastructure in Iran in July, after President Donald Trump repeatedly threatened attacks on Iranian bridges and power plants. In March, Trump threatened to “blow up” Iran’s desalination plants if Tehran did not reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a move that legal experts said could violate international law. He also warned in April that a “whole civilization will die tonight” unless Iran acquiesced to U.S. demands. Israel’s bombing of Iranian fuel depots, which shrouded Tehran in plumes of toxic black smoke, also raised warnings of potentially decades-long harm to public health.
The State Department told the Associated Press that it did not consider the latest U.N. report credible. The Trump Administration withdrew from the Human Rights Council, which comprises 47 countries, in February 2025, over its “anti-American rhetoric and antisemitism,” the department said.
White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told news outlets the Human Rights Council has “accomplished nothing for human rights while spouting unserious nonsense for decades.”
“The only party in this conflict that has committed war crimes is the Iranian regime, which has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region,” Kelly said.
What the U.S. has said about the strikes
In March, the Pentagon launched a formal command investigation into the Minab school strike following a preliminary review. It has not released its preliminary findings, although a U.S. official told the Associated Press that the strike was likely the result of outdated target coordinates supplied by the Defense Intelligence Agency. The school was adjacent to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps complex, but satellite imagery showed the school had been separated from the compound in 2016. It had been publicly listed as a girls’ elementary school for years.
Members of Congress have also questioned whether the Pentagon used artificial intelligence tools to identify the school as a target. No publicly disclosed evidence has established that an AI model independently selected the school as a target.
In June, Trump said the incident was still under investigation. “Nobody did that on purpose,” he told reporters at a press conference in France.
The Pentagon told Reuters on Thursday that the investigation is ongoing.
The U.S. was also accused of carrying out strikes with precision missiles that scattered clouds of tungsten pellets in the city of Lamerd, which the U.N. report also mentioned.
On March 28, BBC Verify reported that weapons experts had identified the type of missile used in Lamerd from video footage as a probable U.S.-made Precision Strike Missile (PrSM). A visual analysis by the New York Times also indicated the same type of missile.
A review by the conflict monitor Airwars last month mapped three apparent missile detonations over a sports complex and two residential neighborhoods in Lamerd. Weapons experts told AP that the missiles appeared to be PrSMs and were unlikely to have been fired by Iran or Israel.
On March 31, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) refuted claims that the U.S. struck Lamerd and said U.S. forces did not launch strikes in Lamerd or within 30 miles of the city on Feb. 28.
CENTCOM said that the missile visible in video footage was too long to be a PrSM, and suggested it was instead an Iranian Hoveyzeh cruise missile.
“U.S. forces do not target civilians, unlike the Iranian regime which has attacked civilian locations in neighboring countries more than 300 times,” CENTCOM said on March 31. No formal investigation into the alleged strike has been announced since.
In May, CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper told Congress that the military was investigating only one case involving possible U.S.-caused civilian deaths: the Minab school strike.
Iran may have committed crimes against humanity in deadly crackdown
The mission also found grounds to believe that the Iranian government committed crimes against humanity during their “violent” crackdown on mass protests beginning late December. Iranian security forces killed 3,038 people and injured 25,000, according to official counts, although the report said the toll is likely higher. At least 221 children, including two two-year-olds, were killed in the crackdown, the report said, citing a human rights organization.
The government arbitrarily detained tens of thousands of people, some of whom were subjected to torture, solitary confinement and denial of legal advice, the report said.
Security forces also attacked health care facilities, arresting wounded protesters and health care workers, the report said.
The mission said at least 29 men were executed, five publicly, in connection with the protests following summary trial. More than 70 people, including five women and three children, are at “imminent risk” of execution, the report said.
Iran has not publicly commented on the report.
In January, Iranian protesters urged Trump to make good on his promise that “help is on its way.” Trump said he was considering military action, although he ultimately declined to launch a strike at the time, and called on demonstrators to continue standing up to the theocratic regime.
In recent weeks, amid renewed U.S.-Iran hostilities, Trump has again urged the Iranian public to resist their government, asking “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?”

articles.title: Poland Warns Russia May Target Ukraine Supporters With "Accidental" Strikes
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Poland Warns Russia May Target Ukraine Supporters With "Accidental" Strikes
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that the most likely scenario for the coming months involves Russian hybrid drone and missile attacks against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland, according to Onet on September 17.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Speaking in Poland’s Sejm , Tusk said recent attacks near the Polish border were a particular cause for concern. He stressed the need to provide the public with detailed information about possible developments based on currently available intelligence.
“I want to present to the public the most likely scenario for the next few months, because this scenario involves serious events and requires focus, seriousness, and the mental readiness to face difficult tests,” Tusk said.
According to the Polish prime minister, there is a risk that drones or missiles could enter the territory of one or more countries on NATO’s eastern flank and potentially cause damage, while such incidents could subsequently be presented as accidental.
“In short: there is a real risk that drones or other types of missiles could enter the territory of one or more countries on the eastern flank, even cause destruction, while the official version would be that it was an accident,” Tusk said.
Tusk emphasized that this was not the only possible scenario, noting that unpredictability has become a defining feature of contemporary politics.
He added that intelligence assessments point to the possibility of Russia carrying out hybrid drone and missile strikes against countries providing support to Ukraine.
“According to intelligence assessments, the Russian plan also includes hybrid drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland. These possibilities have been discussed for a long time, but today this information is very consistent and, unfortunately, convincing,” Tusk said.
According to Tusk, such attacks could be made to appear “accidental” in an effort to weaken NATO countries’ willingness to invoke the Alliance’s provisions in response to aggression against one of its member states.
His remarks come amid heightened concerns over Russian drones near Poland. On September 14, Polish forces recovered a Russian-origin military drone from the Baltic Sea off the country’s northern coast.
Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz reported the discovery the same day, saying troops had located and retrieved the aircraft from the water near the beach in Rusinowo, close to Jarosławiec.
Further details emerged on September 16, when Polish military prosecutors told the Polish Press Agency that the recovered drone had been carrying a live warhead, which was neutralized at the scene. Preliminary findings identified the Russian aircraft as a Gerbera 2 drone.
