articles.title: European leaders prepare public for ‘intensified threat’ from Putin
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — Top European officials are increasingly alarmed that Russia could stage drone or missile attacks against NATO countries as Moscow steps up its hybrid campaign across the continent.
The warnings underscore a growing sense of anxiety in Europe amid fast-proliferating incidents of airspace violations and sabotage attempts in recent months. NATO allies have repeatedly said they see the attacks as pressure from the Kremlin to reduce their support for Ukraine but have muted their response over fears of escalation.
French President Emmanuel Macron summoned party leaders and 2027 presidential candidates for an emergency meeting on Friday to talk about Ukraine, Iran and the growing energy crisis.
He called Tusk’s warnings “sound and well-documented” as he announced a new critical infrastructure protection plan, adding: “In recent weeks … the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and France has intensified.”
Guillaume Lacroix, leader of the Radical Party of the Left, left the meeting saying: “At the age of 50, I have rarely felt such vertigo.”
“It is no coincidence that the Polish prime minister is speaking out so strongly,” Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said Friday. “We need to take that warning very seriously … we must consistently demonstrate that we do not accept this and that we will take action if necessary.”
On Thursday, Finnish President Alexander Stubb told his country it was “worth mentally preparing for something to happen” including sabotage and Russian drones.
Advertisement
Moscow is also ramping up its bellicose rhetoric ahead of Russia's legislative election this weekend that is widely expected to keep President Vladimir Putin's United Russia party in power.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov this week warned Europe it would face a “very short” war if NATO allies attempted to attack the country.
“Russia has stepped up the pace of its activities — we need to remain vigilant,” said one senior European defense official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. “This may be seen as a manifestation of a broader trend ... we have seen similar warnings before, and there may well be more to come.”
So far, the latest incidents haven't prompted any additional multilateral responses, a second senior European defense official said. But “we are monitoring closely,” they added.
U.S. intelligence reports in August warned that Moscow was planning a limited assault on a NATO country in the coming years. CIA Director John Ratcliffe warned Russian officials in Moscow late last month not to escalate conflict with NATO allies, in particular Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, in response to Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Yet it remains unclear whether the latest warnings are based on fresh intelligence.
On Friday, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said Vilnius had “the same intelligence” as Tusk “about a possible foreign-flag operation” but suggested that dated back to July.
“I see the public statements of politicians about this as part of a coordinated campaign to warn Russia not to make stupid decisions and not to try to do something thinking that it will not reach [NATO’s mutual defense clause] Article 5 and will not be washed away,” he said.
Allies have not formally been briefed on any new intelligence inside NATO, according to two alliance diplomats, and NATO has so far not changed its threat assessment.
“At this time, we see no imminent threat of attack,” said a NATO official speaking on behalf of the organization, adding: “But we cannot not be naive or complacent, and we must make sure NATO remains strong in the years ahead.”
Advertisement
Ed Arnold, a former NATO official and adviser at the D Group consultancy, said the warnings could also be designed to raise public awareness of threats and to “pre-bunk” false flag attacks before they take place.
A senior NATO military official said that Russia may be lashing out because of its difficulties in defeating Ukraine. “It therefore may incorrectly perceive the only way out is through increasing its hybrid campaign — that’s a losing proposition, because we are ready to respond.”
Between January and August, there were 100 officially attributed hybrid incidents across Europe compared to 60 during the same period last year, according to the Ukraine-based Sahaidachnyi Security Center think tank — with a particularly sharp rise in airspace violations.
A senior NATO official said the real number was “easily 200 plus” not counting cyberattacks — of which there are “thousands” each month against the military alliance’s Brussels headquarters alone. “Numbers are up, severity is up, [Russia’s] risk appetite is up,” they said.

articles.title: Russians vote in election that Putin sees as barometer of public support for his war in Ukraine
articles.body:
Russians began voting on Friday in a three-day parliamentary election which President Vladimir Putin has said will show that millions of people back his army fighting in Ukraine, even though most anti-war candidates were not allowed to run.
The State Duma election, the first since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, is widely expected to see the ruling pro-Putin United Russia party retain its dominance in Russia's tightly controlled political system.
The result is likely to be held up by the Kremlin as evidence of widespread public support for Putin's policies and, in particular, for his prosecution of Europe's deadliest conflict since World War Two, now in its fifth year.
"Your choice, and your will, will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our soldiers, that we are a united people bound together by shared values, historical memory, and love for our homeland, and that no one will succeed in dividing or intimidating us," Putin said in a televised address before the vote.
An advert on state TV urging people to vote showed Russian military commanders down the ages before cutting to soldiers holding up the national flag after winning a battle in Ukraine with the slogan: "Their voice is the voice of victory. Your vote is the strength of Russia!"
In another move to boost morale and support for fighting on until victory, bone fragments from the sword hand of a medieval Russian prince who won a famous victory over the Mongols were sent to the front in Ukraine in the run-up to the vote.
Voting in Moscow, Anatoliy Simonenko, 76, said he was sanguine about what might happen after the election amid speculation, repeatedly denied by the authorities, that a new wave of mobilization may be announced.
"There are some very grim predictions, and others that are more optimistic. I expect the outcome will likely fall somewhere in the middle. War is war. It entails expenses, defense spending, and cuts to various social benefits. Well, it’s necessary; there’s no getting around it," he told Reuters.
Another voter, who declined to give his name, said he believed the results were easy to rig and raised doubts about an electronic voting system being used in some parts of the country. The electoral commission has rejected such suggestions as false.
State media showed Putin casting his own vote electronically from his Kremlin office.
Candidates against Ukraine-Russia War have been excluded from Moscow's Duma election ballot
Most anti-war candidates were excluded from the ballot before voting across Russia's 11 time zones got underway, after the Supreme Court ruled last month that the liberal Yabloko party, which wants a ceasefire in Ukraine, had breached electoral rules, something it denied.
Some candidates from Yabloko, which has traditionally only got single-digit support in opinion polls, are still running in individual constituencies that account for half the 450 seats in the lower house of parliament.
In the run-up to the vote, Lev Shlosberg, a senior figure in the Yabloko party, was jailed for 11 years for comments about the war. Its deputy leader, Maxim Kruglov, was jailed for seven years on similar charges in June.
Discrediting the army or spreading what authorities regard as fake news is punishable with long jail terms.
Some opinion polls show public support for peace talks has risen to over 60%, and the Kremlin has repeatedly said that it is ready to resume such talks.
However, it has also made clear, as its troops push to take control of the rest of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine, that any settlement must leave it in full control of all of that territory and that it only wants a long-term deal, not a ceasefire.
Voting is taking place at a time when opinion polls show some Russians have become more anxious about how the conflict affects them.
The economy is also under strain, and the authorities are expected to use the vote to gauge the depth of society's war weariness as fuel shortages caused by Ukrainian drone strikes on oil refineries roil some parts of the country, and businesses grapple with drone attacks on their warehouses, high interest rates, a labor crunch and Western sanctions.
National unity vital amid Ukraine attempting to stir unrest, Kremlin claims
The Kremlin says national unity is vital because of what it says are increasingly dangerous efforts by Ukraine's intelligence services and other enemies to stir unrest inside Russia.
Initial and partial results are expected to begin trickling out on Sunday evening, and near-complete results to be available on Monday.

articles.title: Russia slams Japan over US missile deployment
articles.body:
Russia slams Japan over US missile deployment
Russia has demanded that Japan remove US mid-range Typhon missile systems from its territory, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has said, describing the deployment as unacceptable and a threat to national security and regional stability.
In a statement published by the Foreign Ministry on Friday, Zakharova said Moscow sent Tokyo a formal protest note on September 3 after the US deployed the launchers to the southwestern island of Kyushu, 1,300 km from the city of Vladivostok.
“The Japanese side was told to stop this practice and remove the above-mentioned systems from its territory,” she said, adding that Moscow opposes these deployments regardless of the duration.
The US Army brought Typhon systems to Japan’s Kanoya Air Base in Kagoshima Prefecture in June for the Valiant Shield exercise and kept them there for another drill being held this month. The launchers are slated to leave Kanoya in mid-October but are expected to be stored at US military facilities elsewhere in Japan. No live firing is planned during the deployment.
The Typhon is capable of launching SM-6 missiles, as well as Tomahawk land-attack cruise missiles, which have a range of around 1,600 km. The US developed the Typhon after withdrawing from the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty, which prohibited US and Soviet ground-launched and cruise missiles with ranges of 500 to 5,500 km.
Zakharova noted that China recently delivered a similar protest to Japan over its “remilitarization.”
The dispute comes amid another spike in tensions between Russia and Japan over the four southernmost Kuril Islands, which were incorporated into the Soviet Union after Tokyo’s defeat in World War II. Japan still claims the islands of Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan, and the Habomai Islands, which they refer to as the Northern Territories.
Last month, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi protested President Vladimir Putin’s first visit to Iturup, calling the trip “absolutely unacceptable.”
Days later, Russia conducted missile drills near the southern Kurils involving the cruiser Varyag, the nuclear-powered submarine Omsk, and a Bastion coastal missile system, prompting another protest from Tokyo.
The dispute over the Kuril Islands has been a stumbling block to Russia and Japan signing a peace treaty. Moscow suspended the negotiations in March 2022 after Tokyo took part in the Western sanctions imposed on Russia over the Ukraine conflict.

articles.title: Russia votes in parliamentary election as war in Ukraine drags on
articles.body:
Russia votes in parliamentary election as war in Ukraine drags on
Polls opened in Russia's Far East on Friday as the country began three days of voting for its parliamentary election, the first since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Kremlin's main party, United Russia, is poised to keep its grip on power alongside other parties aligned with President Vladimir Putin, as the only party that criticised the war was removed from the ballot.
It's a challenging time for Russia to hold a parliamentary election, even one whose outcome is all but assured.
The economic and political climate has been seriously affected by 4 and a half years of full-fledged war with Ukraine. Swarms of enemy drones have inflicted massive damage on Russian oil refineries and logistical facilities. The public, which no longer sees the fighting as something distant, is increasingly nervous.
Read moreAt least five injured in Russian drone strikes in Kyiv region
United Russia, the main Kremlin party, is poised to keep its overwhelming grip on the State Duma alongside a few other parties aligned with President Vladimir Putin. Still, authorities have tightened control over the first wartime balloting for the lower chamber of parliament since the 2022 full-scale invasion.
The Kremlin stifled even the slightest signs of dissent before three days of voting that began Friday in Russia's Far East. The only party that dared to criticise the war was unceremoniously removed from the ballot, and a few anti-war politicians have been imprisoned or forced to flee abroad.
For the first time, the election includes residents of four Ukrainian regions that Moscow illegally annexed after the invasion. Ukraine has called the vote illegal.
With the result predetermined and Putin’s political dominance under no immediate threat, analysts say the Kremlin sees the election as a key effort to mobilise public support for the war and legitimise its action.
“Your choice and resolve will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our fighters, that we are a united people, bound by shared values, historical memory, and love for the Motherland,” Putin said in an address before the vote.
Read morePutin urges Russians to vote in parliamentary election as show of support for Ukraine war
A summer marked by Ukraine's long-range drone strikes brought the war home for millions of Russians.
The attacks exacerbated problems for the economy, which has plunged into stagnation after an initial boost from massive military spending. The government raised taxes and increased domestic borrowing to keep the growing budget deficit under control.
Strikes on Russian oil refineries sparked a severe fuel crisis that peaked in June, eased for a few weeks and then returned in August.
Adding to the pain was a series of attacks on warehouses of online retailers Wildberries and Ozon. Hundreds of thousands of individual sellers lost their merchandise, sending a shock wave through the economy.
All this dampened the public mood. Polls recorded a dip in Putin’s approval ratings, even though they remained high, with the independent Levada Center showing it at 76 percent in August, down from 87 percent in September 2025.
Even some senior members of Russia’s elite openly expressed discontent.
Andrei Klepach, chief economist of the state VEB.RF bank, warned of possible internal turmoil.
“We won’t win the competition in this war of attrition,” he said at a seminar. “Our costs are mounting. I’m almost sure that we will come to face a social crisis.”
Klepach was dismissed the day after his comments were published.
Putin acknowledged the attacks inflicted significant damage but insisted the economy can weather it. He said Ukraine had opened a “Pandora's box,” inviting massive retaliation.
Russia intensified attacks on Kyiv and other cities with missiles and new jet-powered drones, exploiting Ukraine’s shortage of defensive interceptors. Moscow also dramatically stepped up its barrage on Black Sea ports, disrupting Ukrainian exports of grain and other agricultural products, a key source of revenue.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Amid the escalation, fears mounted that the Kremlin was mulling a massive mobilisation.
A partial mobilisation of 300,000 reservists in 2022 prompted hundreds of thousands of Russians to flee abroad, undermining domestic stability. Since then, the Kremlin has relied on volunteers to fight, offering comparatively high wages and other benefits. Military experts warned, however, that the flow of volunteers has ebbed while massive losses have continued.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy repeatedly claims the Kremlin is considering a postelection mobilisation, which Putin dismissed as “nonsense.”
At a September 5 Kremlin meeting with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and a subsequent call with President Donald Trump, Putin said Russia holds the upper hand on the battlefield, signalling he will keep his maximalist demands for striking a peace deal.
In July, the Central Election Commission cleared 11 parties for the parliamentary ballot, including Yabloko, the only one to openly criticise the war.
Weeks later, however, the country’s Supreme Court removed Yabloko from the ballot. It was acting on an appeal from the nationalist Motherland party that called liberal Yabloko’s anti-war stance akin to seeking the violation of Russia’s territorial integrity.
Kremlin-watchers described the move as an apparent sign of infighting between elements of the government who wanted a semblance of competition to increase voter turnout, and those who feared Yabloko's presence could bring open criticism of the war and political instability.
“The risks that the campaign would turn into a struggle for and against peace – that is, a dispute about the war – were quite high, and this clearly was not part of the plan,” said Tatyana Stanovaya of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center.
Maxim Kruglov, a deputy chairman of Yabloko and former member of Moscow's city council, was convicted in June of spreading false information about the military and sentenced to seven years in prison.
Last month, a court in the Pskov region convicted Yabloko member Lev Shlosberg of speaking out against the war and sentenced him to over 11 years.
Half of the Duma's 450 seats are filled by approved parties and the other half by the winners of races in single-constituency races. Yabloko was banished from the party list voting.
Then, authorities methodically barred individual Yabloko members from running in most of its single-constituency races for the Duma and regional legislatures.
Liberal politician and war critic Boris Nadezhdin, who tried to challenge Putin in the 2024 presidential election, left Russia last month, fearing imprisonment after he was designated as a “foreign agent” and barred from seeking office.
Read moreUS announces charges against five alleged agents for Russia over assassination plots
United Russia, which controls over two-thirds of the Duma's seats, is set to maintain its dominance of the lower house despite public fatigue with the war and the worsening economy. Some Russian reports indicate the Kremlin has slightly lowered its target for United Russia but expects it to retain full control of parliament.
“United Russia may be allowed to slip a little … to bring its actual sort of declared results more in line with probably its real results,” said analyst Mark Galeotti, who heads the Mayak Intelligence consultancy, adding that the Kremlin will ensure it “is still absolutely dominant within the Duma".
One aim of the elections is showing they are “legitimating rituals to give the impression that mass consensus is behind the Kremlin", he said.
Other members of the “systemic opposition” – the Communist Party, the Liberal-Democratic Party and A Just Russia Party, which all follow Putin’s course and strongly support the war – are expected to retain their parliamentary presence.
While Ukraine's attacks have fueled broad anxiety, they also could bring a demand for a tougher response against Kyiv, “as long as they don't have to be involved in it", Galeotti said in a podcast.
Chris Weafer, CEO of the Macro-Advisory Ltd., said that while Ukraine's attacks have affected public morale, there's no immediate threat to the Kremlin’s political domination.
“There has been a ‘rally around the flag’ anyway since the start of conflict and the opinion polls consistently show the very high level of support,” he said.
While the results are predetermined, “the public narrative and particularly the turnout” is what's important to the Kremlin to claim broad public support for its action, Weafer added.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

articles.title: Pentagon, Lockheed to Expand Production of Secretive New Joint Advanced Tactical Missile
articles.body:
The Pentagon announced a deal with Lockheed Martin on Sept. 17 to expand production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, an advanced new Air Force and Navy air-to-air missile meant to equip fifth- and sixth-generation fighters.
The “framework” agreement aims to give Lockheed a “long-term demand” signal, part of a push by President Donald Trump’s administration to build and sustain a more robust munitions manufacturing industrial base.
The announcement “establishes the framework for future multiyear procurement of JATM,” according to the Pentagon release.
“We will deliver JATM at the speed our nation and allies demand while providing value for taxpayers and our shareholders,” Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed Missiles and Fire Control, said in a company release.
A Lockheed spokesperson declined to answer further questions from Air & Space Forces Magazine, deferring to the Department of Defense. A Pentagon press officer also declined any further comment about the announcement.
The announcement should signal to Lockheed and other munitions-makers that a stable market is taking shape, said Mark Gunzinger, director of future concepts and capability assessments at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies.
“It is difficult for industry to justify expenditures needed to accelerate and scale up production,” the retired Air Force colonel said. “This is a key reason why this is an important framework.”
Next-Gen Option
The JATM is the successor to the AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, which has been in service since 1991.
The radar-guided, medium-range, supersonic AMRAAM has undergone major upgrades since its inception, most recently in 2020. The F-22 Raptor, F-35 Lightning II, F-15 Eagle variants, and the F-16 Fighting Falcon can all carry it, and the Air Force isn’t looking to stop buying the missile even as it looks to the JATM.
The service is seeking $953 million for 618 AMRAAMs in its fiscal 2027 budget request, while the Navy is asking for $673 million to buy 388 AMRAAMs.
The JATM seeks to overmatch the Chinese military’s PL-15 and PL-17 missiles and will reportedly double the AMRAAM’s range and hit targets in excess of 120 miles away, though much of its capabilities have been shrouded in secrecy for years.
In its fiscal 2026 budget request, the Air Force revealed it had bought 144 JATMs in 2024-2025 and planned to buy at least another 112 missiles. The fiscal 2027 request, still pending before Congress, has $1.5 billion in procurement to scale up production, but budget documents don’t list any quantities.
While upgraded AMRAAMs provide an improved strike option for fighter aircraft, the JATM is necessary for advanced aircraft already fielded and those in the pipeline, such as the F-47 and Collaborative Combat Aircraft variants, the FQ-42 Vengeance and FQ-44 Fury.
“It doesn’t make sense to invest in highly survivable and incredibly capable fifth- and sixth-gen fighters and bombers just to saddle them with payloads of weapons that will not survive to reach their targets in a fight with a peer adversary,” Gunzinger said.
Mix for the Future Fight
Though reports on the current conflict with Iran don’t indicate the U.S. is using large numbers of air-to-air missiles, a future conflict with a peer adversary such as the Chinese military is likely to look much different.
“Multiple Mitchell Institute wargames have spotlighted the need to rapidly grow the U.S. Air Force’s inventory of advanced air-to-air weapons, which could be nearly depleted within a couple of weeks of high-intensity combat with a peer adversary,” Gunzinger said.
This isn’t the first time the Pentagon has announced plans for multiyear procurement of key missiles.
In July, the Pentagon announced a similar framework for a USAF program known as the Family of Affordable Mass Munitions, which will produce lower-cost cruise missiles that experts believe will be needed in future conflicts for higher strike volumes.
That deal anticipates 8,000 missiles annually once production is at full strength. Work is expected to ramp up by 2028 with 5,300 missiles produced, increasing to the 8,000-missile mark by 2031.
While the FAMM deal will bulk up low-cost options for the Air Force, work on more expensive but more capable munitions are an important part of the equation.
“Our air forces will have a future high-low mix of counter-air weapons, but it’s far more important to focus on the cost to achieve an effect in the battlespace like countering an enemy air threat than the unit cost of a weapon,” Gunzinger said. “The key is to determine the right high-low mix based on optimizing cost per effect instead of simply chasing lower unit costs.”
Allies and Partner Purchases
The U.S. isn’t the only country interested in JATM—Australia announced $736 million in spending to equip its Royal Australian Air Force with the weapon.
That move, along with potential deals with other allies and partners, could also help reduce missile costs for the U.S.
“I believe sharing production with key allies as soon as possible is critical to improving their interoperability with U.S. air forces and lead to cost-sharing agreements that can accelerate weapon development and acquisition,” Gunzinger said.
Beyond cost savings, having allies buy the next-generation missile for their fleets also gives the U.S. ways to standardize weapons loaders across a coalition and share munitions when needed, he said.

articles.title: Russia demands removal of of U.S. Typhon missile systems from Japan, but launchers set to remain in the country after Orient Shield exercise
articles.body:
Russia has demanded that Japan remove U.S. Typhon missile systems that are currently deployed on the island of Kyushu as part of the ongoing multinational Orient Shield military exercises. After the exercises end later this month, the launchers are expected to leave Japan’s Kanoya Air Base but to remain in the country. Beginning around mid-October, they are due to be moved for storage to a U.S. military facility in Japan, according to a statement by the Chief of Staff of Japan’s Joint Staff.
On Sept. 3, Moscow sent Tokyo a formal note of protest over the deployment, Russia’s Foreign Ministry announced earlier today. The ministry called the deployment of the systems in Japan “unacceptable under any pretext” and demanded their removal from the country regardless of how long they are stationed there or the terms of their deployment.
The Typhon systems have been at the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force’s Kanoya Air Base in Kagoshima Prefecture since June, when the U.S. military deployed them there in advance of the Valiant Shield 2026 exercises which ran from June 22 to July 1. The systems are also being used in the Orient Shield 26 exercises running from Sept. 8 to 24, which involve ground forces from Japan, the United States, and Australia. Japanese military officials have described this year’s Orient Shield as the largest in the exercise’s history.
This is the first time Typhon has been deployed directly at a facility of the Japanese Self-Defense Forces. The system was temporarily stationed in Japan in September 2025, but at that time it was deployed at the U.S. Marine Corps Air Station Iwakuni. This year also marks the first deployment of Typhon to Kyushu.
The ground-based Typhon system can launch Tomahawk cruise missiles and SM-6 multipurpose missiles. Tomahawks have a range of about 1,600 kilometers, which would allow them to strike targets along a large portion of China’s eastern coast if fired from southern Japan. The U.S. and Japanese militaries have not disclosed how many launchers were moved to Kanoya Air Base.
Japan has stressed that the deployment is temporary. The country’s defense minister said in June that after the September exercises wrap up, the launchers are expected to leave Kanoya for storage at a U.S. military facility elsewhere in Japan. He said the United States had assured Tokyo that Typhon was not being permanently deployed in the country.
Moscow had objected to the deployment even before the system arrived. In May, Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said the presence of Typhon in Japan posed a “direct threat” to Russia’s Far Eastern borders.
In late August, a week before Orient Shield began, Russia’s Foreign Ministry protested the exercises once again. Relations between Moscow and Tokyo deteriorated further in August after Vladimir Putin visited Iturup, one of the disputed southern Kuril Islands.
Japan lodged a protest with Russia, calling the trip to the island “utterly unacceptable.” Tokyo considers the southern Kuril Islands (which it calls the Northern Territories) to be Japanese territory. Russia controls the islands and disputes Japan’s claim to sovereignty.
The Insider previously reported that in August 2025, Russia formally abandoned a voluntary moratorium on the deployment of ground-based intermediate- and shorter-range missiles. Russia’s Foreign Ministry cited the appearance of U.S. Typhon systems in the Asia-Pacific region among the reasons for the decision.

articles.title: Apex Europe targets defence’s biggest challenges
articles.body:
Apex Europe will bring defence leaders, industry and experts together in London this October to tackle some of the most urgent operational challenges facing allied forces, from autonomous warfare and deep strike to air defence and protecting critical undersea infrastructure.
Allied defence forces across the globe now operate in an era where advantage is dependent on the ability to innovate at pace. Conventional conflicts as we’ve seen with Ukraine are increasingly being shaped by autonomy, mass, speed and connectivity. Armed forces across land, sea, air and cyber domains face the recurring challenge of how to adapt to a constantly shifting technological landscape.
An upcoming defence trade show attended by industry leaders and experts across the globe seeks to bring these pressing questions into sharp focus this autumn. Apex Europe, held in parallel with Apex Defense, is set to have its inaugural show on 7-8 October at the Magazine London, one of the city’s premier event spaces near The O2 area. At its core, the programme centres around identifying, assessing and solving the most pressing challenges facing the defence sector and collective allied armed forces in an increasingly complex geopolitical landscape.
The Mission Sets have been curated around the leading problems facing the sector, each inviting select industry, government, military, and academia to address them.
Operational Problem A: Interoperability and Integration of Uncrewed Systems Across European and NATO
The first problem brings into focus the large-scale challenge of integrating crewed and uncrewed forces across domains. Countries across the globe have highlighted this enormous challenge, particularly with regards to optimising the balance between high-end and low-cost capabilities, coordinating cross-domain command and control as well as building resilience against cyber and EW threats. In the UK we’ve seen great emphasis in the Defence Investment Plan on the Carrier’s Hybrid Air Wing, or equally the loyal wingman of the RAF. For this potential to be maximised, autonomous systems must be interoperable.
Operational Problem B: Delivering Warfare Advantage Through Autonomous Mass
Similarly, the event aims to invite discussion on how to utilise autonomy to gain decisive operational advantage. Autonomy changes the economics of warfare. The central question is moving from what a single exquisite platform can achieve to what a force can generate when hundreds or thousands of autonomous systems can be produced, deployed, replenished and replaced at speed. Mass, however, is not simply a matter of acquiring more platforms. It requires resilient supply chains, common architectures, software that can be updated rapidly, distributed command and control, and an industrial base capable of absorbing wartime demand. This will factor in sustaining autonomous operations under contested conditions as well as the adaptation and iteration at the speed of the frontline.
Operational Problem C: Generating Combat Power Through Deep Precision Effects
Long-range precision strike is becoming less about individual weapons and more about the ability to build a persistent, responsive system for generating effects at depth. Precision depends on the resilience of the wider architecture: radar, intelligence, communications, targeting and battle management must continue to function when the adversary is actively trying to disrupt them. The strategic opportunity is to think beyond inventories of missiles and strike platforms and towards an integrated deep-effects enterprise – one capable of creating dilemmas across an adversary’s system rather than simply hitting individual targets.
Operational Problem D: Countering Undersea Threats and Protecting Critical Infrastructure
Another mission set central to Apex Europe this year is countering undersea threats. As the seabed becomes a frontline, protecting energy pipelines, communications cables and other critical subsea infrastructure requires far greater awareness of what is happening below the waterline. The event will explore how to detect, track and neutralise undersea and hybrid threats, maintain persistent surveillance and deny access to critical infrastructure, and deploy layered sensing, precision effects and resilient architectures to sustain advantage in contested maritime environments.
Crucially, this challenge extends beyond traditional anti-submarine warfare, requiring closer integration between navies, governments, infrastructure owners, industry and autonomous systems. Later this year, Undersea Defence Technology (UDT) Australia is due to have its inaugural event in Adelaide, further reinforcing the importance of the subsea environment.
Operational Problem E: Countering Low-Cost, Rapidly Proliferating UxS Threats
Apex Europe will also address the growing challenge of low-cost, rapidly proliferating threats from uncrewed systems. The focus will be on detecting and discriminating small, low-signature threats, while balancing layered and cost-effective defeat mechanisms. Discussions will explore the role of attritable and mobile C-UxS capabilities, alongside greater integration of cross-domain and allied counter-UxS operations to deliver a scalable and sustainable defence against increasingly accessible autonomous threats.
Operational Problem F: Enhancing Layered and Integrated Air and Mission Defence Across Domains
Modern air and missile defence is increasingly a problem of integration rather than individual systems. The focus will be on 360-degree surveillance and real-time threat identification, cross-domain integration and adaptable, scalable engagement mechanisms across the threat spectrum. At the heart of this is resilient command and control – connecting sensors, effectors and decision-makers into a coherent architecture that can respond to complex, saturated attacks while preserving high-end capabilities for the threats that demand them.
Operational Problem G: Fighting in Denied, Degraded and Contested Battlespace
The final mission set addresses the growing reality of fighting in a denied, degraded and contested battlespace, where connectivity and access to information can no longer be taken for granted. The focus will be on spectrum management in an increasingly congested and contested electromagnetic environment, accelerating tactical EW adaptation, and building cyber and EW effects at scale. Alongside this, forces must be able to exploit and sustain access to space for command, control and targeting – maintaining decision advantage even when networks, data and communications are under constant pressure.
What this is all about
These Mission Sets represent Europe’s most pressing operational priorities and point to a broader shift in the character of warfare that must urgently be addressed. The issue is not simply acquiring more autonomous platforms, longer-range weapons or additional air-defence systems; it is building a force that can connect those capabilities, generate them at scale and continue operating when an adversary attacks the underlying architecture. Technological advances are key, but technology alone will not determine outcomes. Industrial capacity, interoperability, software, doctrine, data and operational experimentation are becoming inseparable parts of combat power and will be central to the discussions at Apex Europe’s inaugural event this October. The advantage will go to those able not only to field better systems, but to adapt, integrate and regenerate them faster than their adversaries.
Apex Europe forms part of a dynamic technology event series that puts near-term operational needs at the heart of the programme and exhibition; held in parallel with Apex Defense (January in Washington, D.C.)
Brought to you by the organisers of major international military and industry events such as DSEI Germany, DSEI Japan, and DSEI UK.

articles.title: Tusk warns of ‘accidental’ Russian strikes against Ukraine’s allies in fall and winter
articles.body:
Donald Tusk looks on during a joint press conference with the Austrian Chancellor in Warsaw on September 17, 2026. | ROLAND Schlager/AFP via Getty Images
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned Thursday that Russia could launch drone or missile strikes in the coming months against countries supporting Ukraine and play them off as accidents.
Speaking in the country’s parliament, Tusk said intelligence assessments from NATO, Ukraine and Poland indicated that “the most likely scenario for the next few months” is that Russia will step up attacks against Ukraine and its allies, including Poland.
Tusk said Russia’s aim was to “weaken NATO’s integrity” and convince its members that “Article 5 is more theoretical than practical.”
“There is a real risk that drones or other types of missiles could enter the territory of one or several NATO countries on the eastern flank and cause damage. And the official narrative will be that it was an accident and that there is no reason for anyone to consider any kind of NATO response,” Tusk said.
He also said that “not all politicians in the West, in the United States or Europe are thinking about how to defend Poland, Lithuania, Latvia or Estonia, dreaming of immediately proving that they are ironclad allies and will come to Poland’s aid under Article 5.”
“You know that yourselves,” Tusk added.
U.S. President Donald Trump has on numerous occasions cast doubt on the principle of collective defense.
The prime minister also said that some politicians and political groups in Europe were “just waiting for an excuse” to declare, in the event of a conflict, that “we are not going to die for Poland, we are not going to die for Latvia or Lithuania.”
The warning came as Tusk said the coming fall and winter months could prove “tragically critical” for Ukraine, with Russia expected to carry out continuous, high-intensity strikes on major Ukrainian cities while targeting warehouses, rail infrastructure and other logistics essential to the country’s defense.
Such attacks have intensified in recent weeks, also covering western Ukraine close to the Polish border, as Russia has increased its use of jet-powered drones that Ukraine has struggled to intercept.

articles.title: Ukraine Drones Make Orchestrating Russia’s Elections Tougher
articles.body:
Kremlin-orchestrated voting in the Russian Black Sea resort city of Sochi on Friday was halted, and voters and officials were ordered to head underground or into concrete bunkers following a regional alert warning of possible Ukrainian drone strikes.
Sochi Mayor Andrey Proshunin, in a statement published on his official Telegram channel, ordered election commission members, observers, and voters present at the polling stations to move to shelters and stay there until an all-clear, before ballot-casting might continue.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Please observe safety precautions; the threat is currently being countered. Polling stations will resume operations as soon as it is safe to do so,” Proshunin said.
Air defenses were tracking and attempting to engage Ukrainian drones operating in regional airspace, and all citizens should remain calm, he said.
According to unconfirmed reports in local media, on Friday at least one Ukrainian drone struck and damaged a Sochi voting site, blowing out windows and breaking up fixtures and furniture inside a public building.
Authorities moved the polling station “to a reserve site,” and ballot-casting would continue once polling sites re-opened, Ella Pamfilova, Chairperson of the Central Election Commission, said in a briefing as reported by the news platform BFM.RU.
Russian national elections taking place between Sept. 18-20 will select representatives for all 450 seats in the State Duma, the lower house of parliament. Regional governors and legislature members will also be determined by around 111 million eligible voters.
Slovakia’s Fico Pours Cold Water on Fulfilling NATO’s Article 5 Mutual Defense
On Wednesday, on the eve of polls’ opening, a Ukrainian drone struck and killed Elena Astanina, a Ukrainian citizen collaborating with Russian occupation authorities in the Ukrainian city of Tokmak in southern Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, pro-Russia news sites reported.
Astanina had served as a Russian election council member since 2022 and was attacked by a drone while helping prepare a voting site, the news magazine Zhivaya Kuban reported.
The independent Russian news agency SOTA, and later Kremlin state media TASS, confirmed the strike and Astanina’s death. A statement from Zaporizhzhia region occupation authority chief Sergei Obertas praised Astanina as a Russian patriot and said the state would assist her family.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova on Thursday said that Ukraine was launching drone strikes with the intent of undermining “democratic elections” in her country, and spun the Ukrainian strike on Astanina as a terrorist attack against a peaceful Russian citizen.
In occupied districts of Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, voting was proceeding as planned on Friday, according to Ukrainian news agencies, but officials were using paper records to conduct voting and track ballots after Ukrainian drone strikes targeting electric transformers in the region cut off power.
A statement from the Russia-run local power utility Khersonenergo confirmed the loss of electricity deliveries to some 150,000 customers, but blamed the outage on “a technical problem.”
Russia’s defense ministry on Friday morning claimed its forces had shot down 629 Ukrainian drones in Russian airspace, making the night’s raids by shootdown claims one of the four or five most massive drone attacks of the entire Russo-Ukrainian War.
Ukrainian military sources and independent media said that the night’s attacks targeted port facilities in the city of Taganrog on the Azov Sea, and a nearby military airfield in Rostov-on-Don. Both air raids were follow-up attacks, with dozens of Ukrainian aircraft having hit and damaged a Taganrog aerospace factory and megawarehouse on Tuesday, and a power substation and military airfield near Rostov on Thursday.
Some Ukrainian drone sorties have reached 3,000 km (1,250 miles) deep into Russia, with massed drone attacks usually targeting Russian Federation military- or energy-linked infrastructure. Although initially scoffed at by authorities as pinpricks mighty Russia might ignore, actual or threatened Ukrainian drone attacks are now taken more seriously by local officials.
On the first day of national elections, which the Kremlin traditionally has used to pump up patriotism and state-manage an image of a stable and prosperous Russia under President Vladimir Putin’s leadership, Russia’s Central Election Commission published instructions to election officials about what to do if Ukrainian kamikaze aircraft seemed en route and potentially able to disrupt the voting process, a major Russian daily reported.
Officials at a voting site forced to shut down because of a potential or actual Ukrainian drone attack should turn over voter registers, voting boxes, and ballots to the election site boss for storage in a safe, while police and emergency response officials would supervise the orderly evacuation of the voting site, official step-by-step procedures at a voting site in the Volga region city of Kazan mandated, according to a Friday BiznesOnline report.
A policeman stationed by the safe until an all-clear was called would ensure a fair poll without fraud, the article says.
Although more than 1,200 km (750 miles) from probable Ukrainian launch sites, industrial sites in Kazan have been regularly hit by Ukrainian drones for more than a year. Probably the most frequently attacked facility has been the Nizhnekamsk oil refinery, which Ukrainian drones have hit at least seven times since November 2025, Kyiv Post’s records show.
United Russia, the ruling party backed by Putin, is widely expected to retain its dominant position and supermajority thanks to state-controlled media and state repression of opposition parties.
Sochi, with a permanent population of over 500,000 that rises to more than 3 million during the high season, is Russia’s wealthiest and most exclusive beach resort. Putin’s luxurious 40-hectare Bocharov Ruchei summer home, with a helipad, yacht mooring, tennis courts, orchards and fresh and seawater swimming pools, sits in Sochi’s elite northern district.
Ukraine, since launching a long-range drone bombardment of Russia in mid-2025, has hit port, oil refining and fuel storage structures around greater Sochi at least 10 times, but never attacked Putin’s residence, Kyiv Post’s strike records show.
The most recent confirmed Ukrainian attack in Sochi’s vicinity took place on Sept. 14, with at least four drones destroying an advanced Russian S-400 air defense system deployed to protect the city and Bocharev Ruchei from Ukrainian air strikes, those records show.

articles.title: US attack submarine operates in Norway’s High North
articles.body:
The Virginia-class fast attack submarine USS Delaware has completed a port visit to Grøtsund, Norway, as the US Navy continues to expand undersea operations in the High North, according to US Sixth Fleet.
The submarine concluded the visit on 7 September after hosting senior US Sixth Fleet personnel and Norwegian officials, with the deployment forming part of wider American activity across the Norwegian Sea and Arctic approaches.
Rear Admiral John W. Stafford, commander of Task Force 169, said operating submarines through the region was important both for European security and for the defence of the United States. He said: “Operations in the strategic gateways of the High North and Norwegian Sea are of paramount importance to maritime security, both for the defence of Europe and the defence of the U.S. homeland.”
Stafford added that routinely deploying US undersea forces alongside other capabilities was intended to improve interoperability with allies and strengthen the ability to deter and defend across the theatre. The US Navy said the presence of Delaware in the region forms part of broader efforts to maintain freedom of manoeuvre and navigation, with American submarines routinely operating between the Arctic and Atlantic.
Those deployments are used for maritime domain awareness, surveillance and wider security tasks across the European region. Virginia-class submarines are designed for a broad range of missions, including anti-submarine and anti-ship warfare, land attack, intelligence gathering, surveillance and reconnaissance, special operations and support for uncrewed systems. They can also employ Tomahawk cruise missiles for strike missions and support special operations forces from beneath the surface.
The visit to Grøtsund comes as Norway continues to play an increasingly important role in allied activity in the High North, where NATO forces regularly train and operate across the North Atlantic, Norwegian Sea and Arctic approaches. US Sixth Fleet, headquartered in Naples, oversees American naval operations across Europe and Africa and regularly works alongside NATO allies and other partner forces.

articles.title: Russia planning “accidental” strikes on eastern NATO states, warns Poland
articles.body:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental.
Addressing parliament on Thursday, the prime minister said that “citizens absolutely have the right to know what scenario can be expected based on the information available today”. Intelligence from allies, including the United States and Ukraine, indicates that various scenarios are possible, but one is most likely, said Tusk.
Over the next few months, Russia’s recent tactic of using jet-powered drones to strike targets in Ukraine near the Polish border will likely continue, said Tusk, as well as attacks on Ukrainian economic and logistics infrastructure, such as railways.
“Russia’s plan, according to intelligence, also includes hybrid drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland,” continued Tusk. “These possibilities have been discussed for some time. This information is now very consistent and, unfortunately, convincing.”
💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️
Istnieje realne ryzyko, że na teren któregoś z państw NATO mogą wlatywać drony, dokonywać zniszczeń. I te „przypadkowe” według Rosji uderzenia mogą się powtarzać. pic.twitter.com/bScJBjQQF1
— Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 17, 2026
The aim, said Tusk, would be to “weaken NATO member states’ motivation to apply appropriate NATO regulations in the event of aggression against any member state”. Russia’s “official narrative will be that this is an accident and there’s no reason for anyone to consider any kind of NATO response”.
The prime minister said that the incidents could be similar in nature to the night one year ago when around 20 Russian drones entered Polish airspace across its eastern border.
“These ‘random’ attacks could repeat themselves, becoming an increasingly glaring illustration of NATO’s helplessness, as conceived by the Russians,” said Tusk.
In response to last year’s drone incursions, Polish and allied NATO jets shot down some of the drones. Poland then invoked article 4 of the NATO treaty and received increased air-defence support from a number of NATO allies.
Russia has recently stepped up its attacks on western Ukraine, including a number of strikes close to the Polish border. Tusk noted that, in response, Poland has begun reinforcing security at border crossings, including installing 28 new bomb shelters and expanding air-defence systems
The prime minister also confirmed that he would be travelling to Kyiv later on Thursday. He planned, among other things, to discuss with President Volodymy Zelensky how they would cooperate on air defence and utilise Ukraine’s experience and capabilities in this area.
On the night of Thursday to Friday, the latest round of Russia attacks on Ukraine prompted Poland to scramble aircraft, activate air-defence systems, and close parts of its eastern airspace – actions that have recently become increasingly common.
A drone has struck a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw, around 2 km from the Polish border, amid the latest mass Russian attacks on Ukraine.
Separately, a truck around 800 metres from a border crossing with Poland was also hit last night https://t.co/ZbfE2iDLOk
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 13, 2026
In his remarks to parliament, Tusk also noted that “announcements by some global leaders that Russia is ready for a kind of ceasefire…have not come true”. He then mentioned President Donald Trump directly.
“Since the president of the United States announced that Russia had assured him it was ready to honour such a partial ceasefire with Ukraine, numerous attacks have occurred, including on energy infrastructure in Ukraine,” said Tusk.
“The information we have received regarding the course of consultations and talks at various levels between the US and Russia is quite clear: Russia is not ready for any serious talks on a ceasefire, let alone peace, without Ukraine’s de facto surrender.”

articles.title: End of the ‘unipolar order’: Sino-Russian vetoes deal a blow to US Iran sanctions push
articles.body:
End of the ‘unipolar order’: Sino-Russian vetoes deal a blow to US Iran sanctions push
TEHRAN – The United Nations Security Council on Thursday failed to adopt a US-drafted resolution that would have extended the mandate of a panel of experts monitoring sanctions on Iran, after China and Russia vetoed the measure.
The draft received 11 votes in favor, with China and Russia voting against and two members abstaining. It sought to extend the mandate of the Panel of Experts supporting the 1737 Iran Sanctions Committee until September 2027.
The committee and its expert panel had been suspended under Security Council Resolution 2231, adopted in 2015 to endorse the Iran nuclear deal. The UK, France and Germany last year triggered a “snapback” mechanism, arguing that the move restored previous UN sanctions and revived the committee and its expert panel.
China and Russia dispute the validity of the snapback and said that Resolution 2231 expired in October 2025, meaning the previous sanctions regime and its subsidiary bodies were not restored.
“Security Council Resolution 2231 expired on Oct 18, 2025, and the Security Council has ended its consideration of the Iranian nuclear issue,” Fu Cong, China’s permanent representative to the UN, told the Council.
“Disregarding these facts, forcing through the restoration of sanctions against Iran in the Security Council, and putting forward an obviously controversial draft resolution will only undermine the unity and credibility of the Council and create obstacles to diplomatic effort,” Fu said, adding that China firmly opposed the move.
Fu said that as the situation in the Middle East and negotiations on the Iranian nuclear issue “remain deeply deadlocked”, the Security Council should “play a constructive role in promoting negotiations and easing tensions, rather than becoming a platform for individual members to engage in political confrontation and exert pressure”.
Fu said China calls on the countries concerned to fully implement the measures related to the “Termination Day” under Resolution 2231, “uphold the authority of the Security Council and the credibility of multilateral diplomacy, and create the necessary conditions for a political solution to the Iranian nuclear issue”.
The dispute over the snapback has effectively paralyzed the committee since its purported restoration last year. The Council has been unable to agree on a chair for the committee, preventing it from convening and conducting substantive work.
France, which holds the rotating Security Council presidency for September, convened a briefing last week on the work of the 1737 Iran Sanctions Committee. China and Russia opposed holding the meeting, but the Council adopted the provisional agenda by 11 votes in favor to two against, with two abstentions.
“The president of the Security Council should also respect the concerns of all parties, promote greater unity and cooperation within the Council and enable it to play its proper role, while avoiding actions that could further aggravate differences and divisions,” Fu said.
Fu said the immediate priority amid the conflict in the Middle East is to urge the parties concerned to remain calm and exercise restraint, cease the use or threat of force, ease tensions, and create the necessary conditions for the parties to restore and implement a ceasefire, return to negotiations and reach a peace agreement, “thereby safeguarding peace and stability in the Middle East and beyond”.
Russia also weighed in, with Vassily Nebenzia, Russia’s UN Ambassador, telling the Council after the vote: “We strongly urge western colleagues to stop their very dangerous actions on the Iran front, which threaten further complication of settling the crisis in the Persian Gulf.”
Iran’s mission to the UN thanked Russia and China for opposing what it called a “politically motivated” US draft resolution.
“Iran deeply appreciates Russia and China for their consistent and principled positions and decisive actions today,” it said in a post on X, adding that they “prevented yet another cynical attempt by the United States and its allies to abuse the Security Council for their political purposes”.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf declared that the “unipolar order” has ended after Russia and China rejected the resolution.
“The unipolar order in which one side extracts concessions through force and coercion has ended. China and Russia’s vetoes rejected the political abuse of the Security Council and reaffirmed the rule of law. We must defend multilateralism; unilateralism serves no one’s interests,” Ghalibaf said on X.
The vote occurred against the backdrop of a coordinated US-Israeli campaign to revive illegal sanctions pressure on Iran, following a move by the Board of Governors of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) last Thursday to refer Tehran to the UNSC over fabricated safeguards allegations.
Iran has categorically rejected the move as politically motivated, emphasizing that its nuclear activities remain exclusively peaceful. Tehran has further highlighted that the US and its European allies are weaponizing the Agency to advance their political and military objectives in the aftermath of Washington’s unlawful withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement and its subsequent policy of “maximum pressure” against the Islamic Republic.
Tehran has consistently maintained that the Agency’s stated inability to verify certain activities stems from the precarious security environment created by US-Israeli sabotage and threats against Iran’s peaceful nuclear facilities. Russia and China have repeatedly questioned the legal basis of the IAEA’s referrals, warning that the nuclear issue must be resolved through genuine diplomacy rather than coercive pressure, illegal sanctions, or the misuse of the Security Council.
The failure of this resolution marks a significant diplomatic setback for the United States, illustrating the growing international resistance to the instrumentalization of UN bodies for narrow political agendas. Iran reiterated its longstanding position that Security Council Resolution 2231 expired definitively on October 18, 2025.
The Islamic Republic of Iran views the principled stances taken by China and Russia as a defense of the rule of law, the integrity of international law, and the legitimate status of the Security Council. The United States continues to insist on exploiting every tool at its disposal, including its seat on the Security Council, in a desperate attempt to transform the body into an arena for political confrontation and pressure. By seeking to impose its unilateral positions upon the international community, Washington undermines the Council’s fundamental role in maintaining international peace and security.
The message of Thursday’s vote is unequivocal: there is a profound legal disagreement regarding the foundations of the claims surrounding the “snapback” mechanism. Repeating a false claim does not transform it into a legal reality.

articles.title: Ukraine’s NATO envoy calls for more air defense donations
articles.body:
A Ukrainian military member sitting next to Sting drone interceptors used to target Russian drones, during the monitoring of the sky for drone threats, at an undisclosed location in teh Dnipropetrovsk region on April 15, 2026. | Roman Pilipey/AFP via Getty Images
KYIV — Ukraine needs more air defenses, but allies are starting to doubt if they can help Kyiv withstand the growing scale of Russian attacks, Alyona Getmanchuk, Ukraine’s ambassador to NATO, told POLITICO on Friday.
“Their logic is straightforward: can we truly be effective against this level of terror when Ukraine’s most pressing need is Patriot interceptors, and we do not have enough of them, as stockpiles have been depleted and production rates remain insufficient?” Getmanchuk said in a written statement.
She said Kyiv’s allies should see that helping Ukraine is also in their interest.
Advertisement
“We need to stop viewing assistance that enables Ukraine to defend itself as purely a matter of supporting Ukraine. It is also in NATO’s own interest … the more drones and missiles Ukraine can destroy in its own airspace, the fewer will cross the borders of neighboring NATO countries,” the envoy added.
Getmanchuk underlined that Western countries still have stocks of interceptor missiles to donate, including missiles close to the end of their service lives.
“There is hardly a better way to decommission them than by using them in the Ukrainian sky,” Getmanchuk said.
Kyiv is proposing a workaround: allies hand over interceptors from their existing stocks now, and Ukraine replaces them later with missiles it has already ordered.
“It’s a swap — not a donation. What we need is to get through this winter,” Getmanchuk said.
Ukraine is placing substantial orders, using both partner funding and the EU’s €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan. These contracts cover not only hundreds of Patriot interceptors — both PAC-2s and PAC-3s — but also European systems, including SAMP/T and Aster 30 missiles, IRIS-T and others.
Advertisement
Growing numbers of Russian ballistic missiles are passing through due to Ukraine’s shortage of interceptors. Kyiv also needs other air defenses to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones.
“Our short list of urgent air-defense needs therefore consists of three major categories, not one: Patriot interceptors, air-to-air missiles, and all types of MANPADS and missiles for them,” she said.
In addition to direct donations, Getmanchuk called on countries to boost their funding to the NATO-led PURL program, in which allies buy U.S. weapons to give to Ukraine. NATO says PURL now supplies 90% of Ukraine’s Patriot interceptors.
The ambassador underlined that helping Ukraine now will also save allies money once the war is over.
“The more we can protect today, the less we will have to rebuild tomorrow,” she said.

articles.title: India’s homegrown air defense system finds new buyers
articles.body:
- Former DRDO Chairman Samir Kamat said India has exported its Akash air defense missile system to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.
- Armenia remains the only other confirmed foreign Akash buyer, having signed for the Mk 1S variant with deliveries starting in late 2024.
Former DRDO Chairman Samir Kamat said India has exported its Akash surface-to-air missile system to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, extending New Delhi’s defense export reach into Central Asia for the first time.
The Akash is a medium-range air defense system built to intercept aircraft, helicopters, drones and cruise missiles. Bharat Dynamics Limited manufactures the missile, using radar and command-and-control systems developed by India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation. Kamat did not specify how many systems were delivered, their configuration, or the value of the deals.
His statement follows earlier reporting in August that said Turkmenistan and Tajikistan were negotiating purchases of the newer Akash Mk 1S variant but had not yet signed formal contracts. It is not clear whether the exports Kamat described represent those same deals reaching completion, or a separate delivery. Neither Indian officials nor the two Central Asian governments have released further detail.
Armenia was the first, and until now the only confirmed, foreign buyer of the Akash system, signing a deal for the Mk 1S variant and beginning deliveries in late 2024. That sale gave India a track record it has pointed to since in pitching the system elsewhere in the former Soviet space.
The Mk 1S upgrade adds an Indian-developed active radio-frequency seeker for terminal homing, on top of the command guidance the missile uses during its mid-course flight. That combination is meant to improve accuracy against maneuvering targets and make the missile harder to defeat with electronic jamming than the original, purely command-guided Akash. The system uses India’s Rajendra phased-array radar to track and engage multiple targets at once, a capability suited to defending fixed sites and stretches of border rather than a single point target.
Tajikistan and Turkmenistan currently rely mainly on older Soviet and Russian-made air defense equipment, including S-125, Kub, Buk and S-300 systems. Aging stockpiles and changing aerial threats have pushed both countries to look at diversifying their suppliers, a dynamic Armenia’s earlier purchase is seen as having encouraged elsewhere in the region. As with Armenia, where the initial missile sale was followed by additional purchases of Indian radar, artillery, rocket systems and vehicles, further Indian defense sales to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan could follow if the Akash purchases are confirmed.
The moves would add to a broader shift in Central Asia’s arms market, a region long dominated by Russian suppliers, toward a wider set of options that now includes India’s defense industry.

articles.title: Ukrainian air defense shoot down 69 of 93 enemy UAVs; hits recorded at 13 locations
articles.body:
Ukrainian defense forces shot down 69 out of 93 enemy drones overnight into Friday, though enemy aerial weapons struck 13 locations, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense systems shot down or suppressed 69 enemy UAVs—including Shahed and Gerbera types, other drone types, and three Banderol/Dan-T units," the message reads.
In total, overnight into September 18 (starting at 18:00 on September 17), the enemy launched an attack using 93 strike UAVs—including Shahed types (46 of which were jet-powered), Gerberas, Parodiya decoy drones, and Banderol/Dan-T units—from the following directions: Orel and Millerovo (Russian Federation), temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardeyske (temporarily occupied Autonomous Republic of Crimea), and the Sea of Azov.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian defense forces.
Meanwhile, attacks from enemy aerial weapons were recorded at 13 locations, and debris from downed objects fell at three locations. Additionally, some enemy munitions failed to reach their targets; information regarding them is being clarified.
The attack is ongoing, and enemy UAVs remain in the airspace, the command added.

articles.title: Russia increasingly using repurposed S-400 training missiles to bombard Ukraine, Reuters reports
articles.body:
Russia increasingly using repurposed S-400 training missiles to bombard Ukraine, Reuters reports
Russia increasingly uses repurposed S-400 training missiles to strike Ukrainian cities, Reuters reports, citing figures compiled by military analysts at Ukraine's General Prosecutor's Office.
Russia fired 87 of the RM48U training missiles at Ukraine in July, compared to 10 in June and 14 in May, Reuters said. The RM48U is significantly less accurate than a purpose-built ballistic missile but still capable of causing significant damage.
Russia uses such repurposed training missiles, originally designed to serve as aerial targets in military training, to keep up pressure on Ukraine and conserve stocks of their more valuable ballistic missiles, an analyst interviewed by Reuters said.
"Their use allows the Russians to husband the more capable missiles they have, the Iskanders, but also the KN-23s and the Zircons, for winter when they would want to really lean into their ballistic missile campaign," Sidharth Kaushal, a senior research fellow at London think tank RUSI, told Reuters.
RM48Us accounted for more than half of the 228 ballistic and hypersonic missiles fired at Ukraine in July and early August, according to data collected by military analysts at the General Prosecutor's Office, cited by Reuters.
The S-400, for which the training missiles were originally built, is an air defense system that entered service in August 2007. Like its predecessor, the S-300, it can also strike targets in ground-attack mode.
Ukraine’s sole defense against ballistic missiles is the American-supplied PAC-3 Patriot. Patriot interceptors have been in short supply amid intensified Russian ballistic missile attacks and the U.S. war in the Persian Gulf draining global Patriot interceptor stocks.

articles.title: Russia has been losing more than 10,000 military personnel in Ukraine for the third consecutive week, according to Estonian intelligence
articles.body:
Russia has been losing more than 10,000 military personnel in Ukraine for the third consecutive week, according to Estonian intelligence
Kyiv • UNN
Estonian intelligence reported more than 10,000 Russian casualties in a week. Ukrainian strikes have reduced Russia’s oil-refining capacity by 30%.
The losses of the Russian armed forces in the war of aggression against Ukraine have remained at more than 10,000 servicemen for the third consecutive week, exceeding the pace of mobilization. ERR reports this, citing a statement by Colonel Ants Kiviselg, head of the Intelligence Centre of the Estonian Defence Forces, UNN writes.
For the third consecutive week, Russia has lost more than 10,000 servicemen, including the wounded and dead. The average daily losses this week amounted to approximately 1,600 troops, meaning that slightly more than 11,000 servicemen were lost over the course of the week. Thus, the trend continues: Russia is losing more troops on the battlefield than it is able to recruit
The head of the Intelligence Centre of the Estonian Defence Forces also noted that Ukraine had for the first time released data on its counteroffensive in the direction of Lyman, Donetsk region, during which approximately 85 square kilometres were liberated and cleared.
Ukrainian operations in Donetsk region are currently continuing
Speaking about Ukraine's other successes, Kiviselg noted that strikes on Russian oil facilities in Krasnodar Krai, Saratov and Samara regions, as well as in the Republic of Tatarstan, are continuing; there was also a strike on the port of Makhachkala on the Caspian Sea, attacks on chemical plants in Perm Krai and Volgograd, and a strike on a drone manufacturing plant in Rostov region.
Kiviselg also referred to a report by the International Energy Agency (IEA), according to which the condition of Russia's oil refineries has deteriorated as a result of Ukraine's long-range strikes, while sanctions are making it more difficult to repair the damage caused by airstrikes.
According to IEA estimates, Russia's oil-refining capacity will remain 30% below its pre-war level over the next 18 months.

articles.title: “Possible casualties” – Sārts warns of escalation of Russia’s hybrid war in Europe
articles.body:
As Russia intensifies its hybrid war in Europe, more serious attacks could be expected, according to Jānis Sārts, Director of the NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence.
The expert said on X that reports of planned Russian attacks against European countries have once again appeared in foreign media in recent days.
The reports refer to hybrid attacks, something Latvian officials have also warned about. Sārts, however, believes that “hybrid attacks” is not the best description of what is happening.
In his view, the growing number of such reports most likely indicates that new intelligence has become available.
“As the hybrid war in Europe is already underway, this signals Russia’s decision to intensify it –
more serious attacks, possible casualties and less caution in carrying out attacks,”
he said.
According to Sārts, intelligence and security services apparently believe that efforts in recent months to deter Russia from such an escalation have been unsuccessful. Therefore, Europe must be prepared for such a development, he stressed.
Sārts said that if a larger attack takes place, the key factor determining what happens next will be how strong the collective response is and how painful it proves for Russia.
As previously reported, the number of Russian hybrid attacks against NATO member states has increased significantly, a senior Alliance official revealed in September.
More than 200 such incidents were recorded last year alone,
the official said, adding that this figure does not include routine cyberattacks. NATO headquarters itself faces thousands of cyberattacks every month.
The official said Russia is seeking to undermine political and practical support for Ukraine while preparing for possible further escalation. This includes spying on critical infrastructure and logistics chains, as well as pre-positioning malware in key industrial control systems.
NATO is particularly concerned about changes in the nature of the attacks, the official said, explaining that their “number is increasing, their severity is increasing, and the appetite for risk is increasing”.
NATO is seeking to strengthen deterrence through military measures and better protection of critical infrastructure.
The Alliance also plans to establish a critical energy infrastructure network to exchange security information with operators and support joint emergency exercises, counter-drone measures and cyber defence.
In particularly serious cases, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander could ask member states to use offensive cyber capabilities, the official said.
Latvia’s Constitution Protection Bureau (SAB) told LETA in August that Russia currently does not pose a direct military threat to Latvia, although a number of indicators point to potential longer-term plans.
National Armed Forces (NBS) Commander Kaspars Pudāns has also said that Latvia currently faces no direct military threat. At the same time, the NBS is preparing for possible hybrid provocations by Russia.

articles.title: Macron orders France to prepare its critical infrastructure for drone and cyberattacks amid a growing ‘Russian hybrid threat’
articles.body:
Macron orders France to prepare its critical infrastructure for drone and cyberattacks amid a growing ‘Russian hybrid threat’
French President Emmanuel Macron said he has ordered his government to draw up a plan to protect critical infrastructure — including defense industry sites — from drone attacks and cyberattacks as Russia’s hybrid threat grows.
“In recent weeks, the threat — particularly the Russian hybrid threat — facing Europeans and France has intensified,” Macron told reporters at the Élysée Palace after meeting with the leaders of France’s political parties.
Such attacks would not go unanswered, he said. Macron also accused Russia of trying to intimidate European countries and weaken support for Ukraine.
A day earlier, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told parliament that Russia is planning “hybrid” strikes with missiles and drones against countries that support Ukraine. “These potential strikes would be quote-unquote ‘accidental’ in nature, intended to paralyze or at least weaken the resolve of NATO states to invoke the relevant NATO provisions in the event of aggression against a member country,” he said.

articles.title: Poland’s prime minister says Russia is preparing ‘accidental’ drone and missile strikes on NATO countries that support Ukraine
articles.body:
Poland’s prime minister says Russia is preparing ‘accidental’ drone and missile strikes on NATO countries that support Ukraine
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told parliament that Russia is planning “hybrid” strikes using missiles and drones against countries that support Ukraine.
Tusk cited intelligence assessments, the Reuters news agency reports. “There is a real risk that drones or other types of missiles may fly into the territory of one or more NATO countries on the eastern flank, even cause destruction,” he said.
“These potential strikes would be quote-unquote ‘accidental’ in nature, intended to paralyze or at least weaken the resolve of NATO states to invoke the relevant NATO provisions in the event of aggression against a member country,” Tusk said.
According to Tusk, these Russian attacks could coincide with “political changes in certain European countries granting power […] to those who, increasingly invoking noble slogans of peace, pacifism and needless casualties, will call for peace,” but which in fact call for ”the total capitulation of Ukraine.”
Drones have repeatedly entered the airspace of Estonia, Lithuania, and Latvia in recent months. Authorities in those countries said the drones were Ukrainian and had strayed into their airspace because of Russian electronic warfare.
NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace overnight on September 15, the first time a drone has been destroyed in the country’s history. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda later said the drone was Russian.
Russian forces also used drones to attack a gas station near the Yahodyn border crossing on the Polish–Ukrainian border and a passenger train on the Kyiv–Warsaw railway line overnight on September 13. Another train carrying Western politicians returning from Ukraine was traveling nearby when the drone struck. Tusk said the incident showed that “escalation by the Russian Federation is becoming a fact, and examples of it are getting closer and closer to our border.”
