articles.title: Scores killed as Houthis, Yemen govt, Saudi Arabia trade attacks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Scores killed as Houthis, Yemen govt, Saudi Arabia trade attacks
Fresh fighting left scores of combattants dead in Yemen on Thursday, as Saudi Arabia reported its first death since hostilities flared anew and its Yemeni government allies sought to roll back the group's recent gains.
The sides have been locked in increasingly violent exchanges since Yemen's civil war roared back to life, with the Iran-backed Houthis launching a new offensive that saw them capture all of the country's Red Sea coast.
At least 23 government soldiers were killed over the previous 24 hours in missile and drone attacks by the group in two southwestern provinces, a government military official told AFP on Thursday.
Houthi military sources reported 40 fighters killed in Saudi airstrikes and fighting on the ground during the same period.
Earlier in the day, Saudi Arabia's civil defence agency reported the country's first fatality since the Houthis began targeting their territory as part of their revived campaign.
"The fall of shrapnel from a downed drone in Taif governorate resulted in one death, two injuries, and material damage to several buildings and vehicles," the agency said, in a statement posted on social media, adding that the person killed was a Yemeni national.
Images posted by Saudi state media showed windows in cars and shop fronts shattered by the shrapnel, with nearby buildings also damaged.
The incident came a day after Riyadh accused the Houthis of launching a "cowardly" thwarted drone attack targeting Islam's holy city of Mecca, a claim the group denied.
The EU voiced its "full solidarity" with Saudi Arabia as it condemned the recent Houthi strikes.
"We urge the Houthis to cease all military action," said a statement from EU foreign affairs spokesman Anouar El Anouni, adding "the targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructure is unacceptable".
Earlier in the day, the Houthis said "Saudi enemy warplanes targeted three telecommunications towers" in Taiz province, with one civilian killed and another injured in strikes on the town of Abs, Almasirah television said.
The Houthi-backed outlet later reported that "three children were killed and several Yemeni nationals were injured in strikes by the Saudi-backed mercenaries", a reference to the country's internationally-recognised government.
The Houthis have been reporting dozens of daily Saudi strikes since they launched their new offensive and seized control of strategic areas overlooking the Red Sea's Bab al-Mandab Strait from government forces.
With Iran already throttling the Strait of Hormuz since the outbreak of the wider Middle East war, their Yemeni allies' latest gains cement their hold on the other main shipping corridor for Gulf oil and gas.
The route had been especially important to Saudi Arabia, the world's top crude exporter, which had used a pipeline to bypass the Hormuz and send oil to the Red Sea, which links Europe and Asia via the Suez Canal.
In July, a fragile 2022 truce between the Houthis and the government fell apart after the group allowed an Iranian plane to land in the capital Sanaa in defiance of Riyadh's control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
They also announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began striking its ships and territory.
The conflict in the Arabian Peninsula's poorest country has forced more than 100,000 people to flee their homes, according to the United Nations.

articles.title: Ukrainian Neptune Missile Strike Destroys Three Buildings at Russia’s Atlant Aero Drone Factory
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukrainian Neptune Missile Strike Destroys Three Buildings at Russia’s Atlant Aero Drone Factory
Three production buildings at the Atlant Aero drone manufacturing facility in Taganrog, Russia, were completely destroyed in a Ukrainian Neptune missile strike, according to an assessment by the OSINT project Exilenova+ on September 17.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The facility specializes in the production of unmanned aerial vehicles and components for drones, Exilenova+ said.
According to the assessment, one warehouse used for military purposes sustained significant damage in the strike, with its roof collapsing over an area measuring approximately 60 by 40 meters.
Another production building was almost completely penetrated by the strike, with damage covering an estimated area of 70 by 40 meters.
According to Militarnyi, the strike occurred on September 15, when NASA’s FIRMS system, which monitors thermal anomalies on the Earth’s surface, detected a large fire at the site.
The company supplies unmanned systems to the Russian Armed Forces and specializes in manufacturing the Molniya family of drones. Its products include the Molniya-1 and Molniya-2 strike drones, as well as the Molniya-2R reconnaissance variant.
Atlant Aero has been sanctioned by Ukraine, Canada, and the European Unionm Militarnyi reported.
The strike came days after reports of fires near another aviation-related facility in Taganrog. On September 12, Exilenova+ reported that satellite fire-detection data and videos posted by local residents indicated multiple fires across the city, including near the Beriev Taganrog Aviation Scientific and Technical Complex.
The Beriev facility is involved in maintaining and modernizing several types of Russian military aircraft, including A-50 airborne early warning and control aircraft, Be-series amphibious aircraft operated by the Russian Navy, and Tu-95MS/MSM strategic bombers. Russian forces use Tu-95 bombers to launch Kh-101 air-launched cruise missiles against Ukraine.

articles.title: ‘You’re Eroding Trust’: What Trump Shifting Tens of Millions in Military Aid Means for U.S. Alliances
articles.body:
The Trump Administration announced this week that it plans to shift tens of millions in military aid from countries in Europe and the Middle East to nations in Latin America with right-leaning governments.
A State Department official confirms to TIME that the department notified Congress that $52 million in foreign military funding for Iraq, North Macedonia, Slovakia, and Tunisia will be diverted to Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, and Peru, and that the funds will be used to “combat narcoterrorism in our own backyard and help continue to secure the Panama Canal.” The department did not specify how much military funding the U.S. will continue to provide those Middle Eastern and European nations following the shift.
“The proposed reprogramming in the Western Hemisphere will reduce opportunities for adversaries to establish or sustain strategic footholds in our hemisphere,” the State Department official says.
The reallocation of military funding reflects a broader shift in the U.S.’s priorities when it comes to foreign policy. Since Trump’s return to office last year, his Administration has worked to buttress the U.S.'s presence in the Western Hemisphere in the name of curbing drug trafficking from Central and South America and squashing the influence of other nations, such as China, in the region.
The Trump Administration has also sought to recalibrate its foreign policy regarding the Middle East and Europe. A national security strategy laid out by the White House at the end of last year stated that the Administration intended to take a more hands-off approach to armed conflict in those regions and allow them to become more militarily self-reliant. The diversion of foreign military aid marks the latest in several moves Trump has made to cut U.S. troops and funding in Europe during his second term—though in the Middle East, his war in Iran has engaged the U.S. in months of conflict.
Experts warn that the shift in military funding—and the broader plans of realigning U.S. foreign policy it fits into—threatens to weaken the country’s alliances around the world over the long term.
“You're eroding silently, quietly, bit by bit, this trust in the United States,” Jim Townsend, who served as Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for European and NATO Policy for eight years in the Obama Administration, tells TIME of the Administration diverting military funding from European and Middle Eastern countries. “And then when we need them to do something … well, you're turning to a weaker country because you have been pulling their assistance and all of these tools that we have to make them a stronger ally.”
And the Trump Administration’s increasing support for conservative-led nations in the Americas carries its own risks, contends Rebecca Bill Chavez, who served as the Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Western Hemisphere Affairs in the Obama Administration.
“U.S. security relations, these are some things you build over time, and if they start to become relationships only with particular governments rather than with countries, that's risky,” she says. “We have to show the region that we are a reliable partner. And one of the best ways to do this is to be consistent.”
How—and why—the Trump Administration is ramping up U.S. military involvement in the Western Hemisphere
During Trump’s second term his Administration has increased military funding to Latin American countries, as well as boosting the U.S.’s own military presence in the region.
The U.S. has also conducted a number of military operations in the region since Trump returned to the White House, including a series of lethal attacks on what federal officials claimed were vessels transporting narcotics to the U.S. from the Caribbean that have drawn blowback from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle in Washington. The Trump Administration has also partnered with Ecuador for a joint military operation targeting “narco-terrorists” in the South American country, while announcing plans for further campaigns of the same kind in other nations in the region.
And in January, the U.S. launched a military operation in Venezuela that resulted in the capture of the country’s then-leader Nicolas Maduro, who had previously been indicted in the U.S. on charges of drug trafficking and corruption. After the operation, Trump pledged that “American dominance in the Western Hemisphere will never be questioned again.”
These moves reflect what the President has referred to as the “Trump Corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine or, later, as the “Donroe Doctrine,” a revival of a 19th century foreign policy framework first articulated by former President James Monroe that was used to justify assertions of U.S. military and economic control in Latin America.
“Reinvigorated by my Trump Corollary, the Monroe Doctrine is alive and well—and American leadership is coming roaring back stronger than ever before,” Trump said in a December proclamation.
A national security strategy released by the White House in November detailed that “Trump Corollary” in effect as an assertion that the U.S. must be “preeminent in the Western Hemisphere … a condition that allows us to assert ourselves confidently where and when we need to in the region.”
“We want to ensure that the Western Hemisphere remains reasonably stable and well-governed enough to prevent and discourage mass migration to the United States; we want a Hemisphere whose governments cooperate with us against narco-terrorists, cartels, and other transnational criminal organizations; we want a Hemisphere that remains free of hostile foreign incursion or ownership of key assets, and that supports critical supply chains; and we want to ensure our continued access to key strategic locations,” the strategy document reads.
The strategy described the Administration’s plans to back like-minded leaders in the Western Hemisphere as well, stating that it would “reward and encourage the region’s governments, political parties, and movements broadly aligned with our principles and strategy.”
Experts warn about the potential consequences of shifting military aid
Townsend warns that reducing military funding for European and Middle Eastern countries will weaken their ability to collaborate with and support the U.S.
“It creates allies who are not as strong as they could have been,” Townsend says. “It creates allies who are not as helpful as they could have been, and they're creating allies that are not as integrated and as pro-U.S. as they could have been.”
This is especially true, he asserts, for members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), which include North Macedonia and Slovakia. Trump has repeatedly clashed with the U.S.’s NATO allies during his second term, going so far as to threaten to pull out of the military pact after several other member countries declined to help the U.S. in its ongoing war against Iran.
Foreign military financing (FMF) allows other governments to purchase U.S. military equipment and carry out military trainings in tandem with the U.S. Without it, countries may be left unable to purchase key defensive equipment, such as drones or aircrafts, Townsend explains, which in turn weakens U.S. military alliances in the region.
Chavez meanwhile tells TIME that many Latin America nations could benefit greatly from U.S. military support, but argues that selecting who receives that support based on political ideology isn’t sustainable for U.S. relations in the region.
“All of this raises the question whether U.S. security assistance is increasingly being tied to the political orientation of a president rather than to long-term relationships with countries and institutions, and there's a risk there,” Chavez says.
Townsend contends that there is also risk in supplying military equipment to Latin American governments which could use it for ill.
“In the past, the trouble has come when we've been feeding money to a regime that ends up killing the opposition,” he says. “It's been a very spotty record in terms of assistance that we give to countries in the Caribbean or in Central America, Latin America, where this money ends up going to the wrong people.”

articles.title: Blast hits military site in NATO state
articles.body:
Blast hits military site in NATO state
Seven people have been injured in an explosion at a military shooting range in western Sweden, with five suffering serious injuries, according to local media reports. The incident near Karlsborg sparked alarm among parents, who feared that young conscripts may have been among the victims, before officials clarified that those injured were armed forces employees.
In a statement on Thursday, the Swedish Armed Forces said an explosion occurred at the Kraks shooting range shortly after 4:00 PM, injuring several people, some seriously, adding that the incident is being investigated.
National public broadcaster SVT reported that seven men in their 20s and 30s were taken to the hospital, including one by helicopter. Five were being treated for serious but non-life-threatening injuries, reportedly in intensive care, while the other two sustained minor injuries.
While the authorities would not say what caused the incident, Aftonbladet reported that an explosion occurred in connection with clearing old, unexploded ammunition.
The incident sparked alarm among parents before officials stressed that no conscripts were involved. “We have had some worried mothers and fathers calling, but it is not conscripts who were injured,” Armed Forces spokesman Mikael Agren told SVT.
An emergency department employee at a local hospital described the situation as “chaos,” with reports suggesting that the facility reinforced its emergency and operating departments but did not formally enter emergency mode.
Kroks range is administered by the local Skaraborg Regiment but is used by units from across Sweden.
The Karlsborg military hub hosts the Unmanned Aircraft System Center, which was opened last year to allow Sweden to catch up in drone warfare, which has become a staple of the Ukraine conflict.
This year, Ukrainian drone operators with frontline experience took part in the NATO-led Aurora 26 exercise in the wider Karlsborg area. However, there is no indication that drones or Ukrainian personnel were involved in the blast on Thursday.
The incident comes as Sweden, like many other NATO members, continues its military buildup; its defense budget has grown by 18% in 2026 alone. In 2017, Stockholm reactivated the draft, citing a deteriorating security environment and difficulties recruiting enough personnel voluntarily; in 2024, it joined NATO, citing the Ukraine conflict.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has criticized Sweden for taking steps to host NATO military infrastructure on its soil, stressing that Stockholm’s policies do not improve geopolitical stability. He also said Russia has no major disputes with Sweden.
Sweden has seen similar training accidents in the past. In March 2024, two conscripts and two instructors suffered shrapnel wounds after a hand grenade exploded near them during an exercise at the Mastocka range in the southwestern part of the country. The Work Environment Authority later found safety deficiencies in the training.

articles.title: South Korea rebuffs Trump: No troops for US war on Iran
articles.body:
South Korea rebuffs Trump: No troops for US war on Iran
TEHRAN — In a decisive stance reflecting growing domestic anti-war sentiment and strategic prudent realism, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung announced on Friday that Seoul will not deploy its armed forces to join the US war against Iran, effectively rejecting escalating demands from Washington to entangle the East Asian nation in its Middle Eastern conflict.
Speaking at a news conference in Seoul, President Lee stated in unambiguous terms that South Korea will not participate in combat operations or allow its military assets to be dragged into Washington’s military campaign.
“There won’t be deployment that would involve or enter war. I can tell you that very clearly,” Lee told reporters. “We won’t deploy military assets in any form to that end.”
However, the South Korean leader noted that his administration is currently reviewing potential non-combat measures limited strictly to safeguarding commercial navigation and energy supply lines in the region. Seoul currently maintains a naval footprint off the coast of Somalia dedicated to anti-piracy missions, a model some officials have suggested could be adapted to protect South Korean flag-ships.
“[It] is also clear that we must do the minimum as other countries do to protect our commercial shipping and crude shipments, and also the safety of our people,” Lee added, attempting to balance domestic political pressure against Washington’s persistent arm-twisting.
The official refusal from Seoul comes amidst heightened friction between the long-standing military allies. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticized South Korea for what he characterized as insufficient support for Washington’s war effort against Tehran. In an apparent retributive move that has alarmed defense analysts in Seoul, the Trump administration recently scaled back major joint military exercises between US and South Korean forces.
Despite Washington’s economic and military leverage, Seoul’s refusal underscores the severe domestic and geopolitical constraints facing South Korean policymakers as they navigate the fallout from the US-Israeli war of aggression in West Asia.
Widespread domestic opposition in Seoul
President Lee’s firm statement follows weeks of intense domestic backlash and mounting public outrage across South Korea. Defense authorities in Seoul had previously disclosed that a specialized fact-finding mission had been dispatched to assess maritime conditions around the strategic Strait of Hormuz—a move that triggered immediate alarm among civil society groups and anti-war activists.
Earlier this month, dozens of South Korean anti-war activists, civil society leaders, and ordinary citizens gathered directly across from the massive United States embassy compound in central Seoul. Demonstrators fiercely condemned Washington’s pressure on their government, framing the US campaign against Iran as an “illegal war” of aggression.
Unfurling banners and holding signs reading “Do not join a war of aggression,” the protesters voiced deep indignation over indications that political and military leaders in Seoul were contemplating a military “contribution” to the waterway’s security at the behest of the White House.
Directing their chants toward the presidential office, the crowd echoed a resounding plea reflecting broad public sentiment against foreign military entanglements: “We cannot send our young people into a sea of death!”
While defense spokespersons in Seoul attempted to cool public anger by maintaining that no final deployment decision had been made, the public outcry highlighted the immense political cost any military compliance with Washington would entail for the South Korean government.
Tehran’s firm warnings against coercion
The prospect of South Korean military involvement in the Persian Gulf had drawn strong and explicit warnings from diplomatic authorities in Tehran, who made it clear that any foreign intervention alongside hostile American forces would carry severe economic and diplomatic consequences.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei repeatedly emphasized that any operational involvement by third countries in the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz would be viewed as direct participation in US aggression.
In a detailed statement published in the Korean language on his official X account on September 7, Baghaei highlighted the historic depth of bilateral relations between Tehran and Seoul. He noted that Iran and South Korea have maintained diplomatic and economic ties for more than 64 years, built upon a solid foundation of mutual respect and constructive cooperation. Tehran, he reiterated, has consistently attached high value to its friendly bonds with the South Korean people.
However, the Iranian spokesman clearly delineated the boundaries of peaceful engagement amid Washington’s blatant violations of international law. Baghaei stressed that the Iranian nation is exercising its inherent right to self-defense against acts of aggression and responding decisively to US war crimes targeting civilians.
Under such fraught circumstances, Baghaei warned, any operational participation or military presence by foreign forces in the Persian Gulf and the strategic Strait of Hormuz would constitute direct support for the aggressor.
Urging South Korean policymakers to maintain an independent foreign policy aligned with international law and long-term national interests rather than American adventurism, the spokesman emphasized that responsible nations must resist foreign coercion.
“No sovereign and responsible country will submit to US pressure and blackmail to collude in committing acts of aggression and heinous crimes against the great Iranian nation,” Baghaei pointed out.
Washington’s fracturing alliances
Seoul’s reluctance to be drawn into the conflict exposes the growing isolation of the United States as it attempts to construct an international coalition to bolster its campaign in West Asia. Allies in both Europe and East Asia have shown marked reluctance to sacrifice their own strategic security and commercial stability for a war widely viewed as illegal and strategically disastrous. Yet, South Korea’s explicit refusal to send combat forces illustrates that even Washington’s closest treaty allies are unwilling to blindly follow American directives into the Persian Gulf.
Quagmire of war
The current regional crisis traces its origins back to the unlawful military campaign launched on February 28, when the United States and Israel embarked on a coordinated, unprovoked assault against Iran’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Conceived in Washington and Tel Aviv with the illusion of achieving a rapid and decisive breakthrough, the war of aggression has instead evolved over the past seven months into a crushing geopolitical and military quagmire for the aggressors.
Far from coercing the region into submission or forcing sovereign nations to fall in line, the US-Israeli campaign has fractured Washington’s global alliance system, severely disrupted international maritime trade, and driven global energy markets into turmoil. By threatening allies like South Korea with military and economic retaliation while attempting to force participation in an unlawful war, the United States has succeeded only in exposing the limits of its global influence and the catastrophic miscalculations that have characterized its regional doctrine from the outset.

articles.title: Lithuania's foreign minister confirms Polish intel on Russia preparing hybrid attacks against Ukraine's allies
articles.body:
Lithuania's foreign minister confirms Polish intel on Russia preparing hybrid attacks against Ukraine's allies
Kęstutis Budrys, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Lithuania, has confirmed that his country also possesses intelligence about Russia preparing hybrid attacks against Ukraine's allies after a similar warning from Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
Source: European Pravda, citing Baltic states news website Delfi
Details: Budrys' comment concerned a recent statement by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who warned of Russian "plans for hybrid attacks using drones and missiles against countries supporting Ukraine, particularly Poland".
As the minister noted, public warnings from politicians regarding the threat are part of coordinated campaigns aimed at discouraging Moscow from staging provocations.
Quote: "I want to assure everyone that Lithuania has the same intelligence information as other countries in the region and countries that have deployed their troops here. There is no other information."
Details: According to the minister, he discussed this topic with the NATO secretary general, his deputy, and commanders of the armed forces of European countries. "I wanted to make sure we were talking about the same thing. The news is this – yes, we are talking about the exact same thing. Lithuania has the same information; we discussed this as a potential false-flag operation by Russia," Budrys stressed.
Background:
- Prior to this, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk claimed that intelligence data indicates Russian "plans for hybrid attacks" against countries supporting Ukraine.
- European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has announced plans for a new security strategy for European countries to complement NATO's Article 4.

articles.title: German prosecutors open new investigation after drone wreckage found near military base, echoing Leipzig incident
articles.body:
Germany’s Federal Prosecutor’s Office has opened an investigation after parts of a drone were found near the Wunstorf Air Base in Lower Saxony, Bild reports. German media outlet NDR, citing law enforcement sources, has reported that the drone found near Wunstorf is the same model as the UAV that was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 5. The outlet notes that this kind of design cannot be bought in a store, and that one of the drone’s components was 3D-printed — just as in the Leipzig case.
According to Bild, Germany’s Federal Prosecutor’s Office has taken over the investigation into the incident around Wunstorf due to the possible link to the Leipzig incident. On Sept. 1, the German government officially accused Russia of a hybrid attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport. At a press conference, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that, in response to Russia’s actions, Germany is closing the Russian House in Berlin and the Russian Consulate General in Bonn.
Russia, for its part, withdrew its consent for the operation of Germany’s Consulate General in St. Petersburg and demanded that the German Goethe-Institut cultural centers in the country cease operations.
German investigators later identified two suspects in the Leipzig/Halle Airport sabotage: Russian national Oleg L. and Belarusian national Andrei K. According to Welt am Sonntag, Oleg L., who was responsible for planning and logistics, is linked to Russia’s Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU).
A day earlier, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk asserted that Russia is planning “hybrid” drone and missile strikes on countries that support Ukraine — including NATO member Poland itself. The war, he said, is entering its most critical phase.

articles.title: Russia launched 93 drones at Ukraine, 72 of which were neutralized by air defense
articles.body:
Russia launched 93 drones at Ukraine, 72 of which were neutralized by air defense
Kyiv • UNN
On the night of September 18, Russia launched 93 drones and munitions at Ukraine. Air defense shot down and jammed 72 targets; 13 hits were recorded.
Air defense neutralized 72 drones and "Banderol"/"Dan-T" loitering munitions used by the Russian army to attack Ukraine on the night of September 18. This was reported by the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, UNN writes.
Details
According to the report, starting at 6:00 p.m. on Thursday, September 17, Russian invaders launched 93 Shahed-, Gerbera-type attack drones, Parodiya-type decoy drones, as well as Banderol/Dan-T-type loitering munitions at Ukraine. Of the Shahed-type drones, 46 were jet-powered.
The Russians launched the attack weapons from the directions of their settlements of Orel and Millerovo, as well as from the waters of the Sea of Azov and the temporarily occupied territories—Hvardiiske (the Autonomous Republic of Crimea) and Donetsk
The enemy attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 8:00 a.m. Friday, air defense had shot down/jammed 69 Russian drones of various types, including Shahed and Gerbera drones, as well as three Banderol/Dan-T munitions.
Enemy impacts were recorded at 13 locations, and the fall of downed targets (debris) was recorded at three others.
Some of the enemy's attack weapons did not reach their targets. Information about them is still being clarified.
The Air Force emphasizes that Russian UAVs are still being detected moving in the skies over Ukraine. Citizens are urged to follow safety rules.
Russia's losses in the war have reached 1.515 million troops18.09.26, 07:44 • 1790 views

articles.title: EU to disburse $3.8B for missiles and drones to Ukraine: Von der Leyen
articles.body:
Ayhan Şimşek
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
The European Union will disburse €3.3 billion ($3.8 billion) to Ukraine for missiles and drones, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Thursday after a phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
“Tomorrow, we will disburse another €3.3 billion to Ukraine,” von der Leyen said in an official readout of the call.
She said the payment comes as Russian strikes continue to hit the Ukrainian capital.
“Russia is relentlessly targeting Kyiv, trying to make daily life impossible for its inhabitants,” she said. “We stand with them. And with all Ukrainians.”
The funds are part of the €28.3 billion set aside for Ukraine’s defense this year under the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan.
Von der Leyen said the bloc last week approved EU funding for Patriot systems through the same loan, a step that also opened the way for Ukraine to buy US-made Patriot interceptors used against ballistic missiles.
“But clearly more is needed,” she said.
She said Brussels was ready to use remaining funds from SAFE — Security Action for Europe, the EU’s defense financing instrument for member-state investment and joint purchases — to start a new program for joint EU-Ukraine defense projects.
“We want to develop together a European air and missile defense system, building on our joint anti-ballistic Freya system,” said von der Leyen, “so that we can combine Ukraine’s battlefield experience and innovation with Europe’s technology and industrial strength.”

articles.title: US clears way for $24.3 billion fighter jet sale to Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
US clears way for $30.9 billion fighter jet sale to Saudi Arabia
WASHINGTON - The US Department of State said on Sept 17 it has approved the potential sale of Lockheed Martin’s F-35 Lightning II fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, as the kingdom is drawn deeper into war in the Middle East.
A sale would mark a significant policy shift from the US, potentially altering the balance of military power in the Middle East and testing Washington’s definition of maintaining its ally Israel’s “qualitative military edge.”
Saudi Arabia made a direct appeal for the jets in early 2025 to US President Donald Trump and has long been interested in Lockheed Martin’s fighter.
The estimated US$24.3 billion (S$30.9 billion) sale would include 48 of the military aircraft and 49 Pratt & Whitney engines along with communications equipment, spare parts and other support items, the State Department said.
Washington weighs weapons sales to the Middle East in a way that ensures Israel maintains a “qualitative military edge”, effectively guaranteeing that Israel gets more advanced US weapons than regional Arab states.
The Saudi embassy in Washington welcomed the proposed sale, describing it as a further step in defence cooperation between the two countries.
“The proposed F-35 sale reflects the strength and enduring nature of the Saudi-US strategic partnership and the continued advancement of our defence cooperation,” the embassy said on X.
The F-35, built with stealth technology that allows it to evade enemy detection, is considered the world’s most advanced fighter jet.
Israel has operated the aircraft for a decade, building multiple squadrons, and remains the only Middle Eastern country to possess the weapons system.
Saudi Arabia, the largest customer for US arms, has sought the fighter for years as it looks to modernise its air force and counter regional threats, particularly from Iran.
The kingdom’s renewed push for what would constitute two squadrons comes as the Trump administration has signalled openness to deepening defence cooperation with Riyadh.
The Saudi Air Force flies a mix of fighter aircraft including Boeing F-15s, European Tornados and Typhoons.
The F-35 issue has also been intertwined with broader diplomatic efforts.
The administration of former US President Joe Biden previously explored providing F-35s to Saudi Arabia as part of a comprehensive deal that would have included Riyadh normalising relations with Israel, though those efforts ultimately stalled.
Trump has made arms sales to Saudi Arabia a priority since returning to office.
In 2025, the United States agreed to sell the kingdom an arms package worth nearly US$142 billion, which the White House called “the largest defence cooperation agreement” Washington has ever done.
Congressional scrutiny could pose challenges to any F-35 sale.
Lawmakers previously questioned arms deals with Riyadh following the 2018 murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, and some members of Congress remain wary of deepening military cooperation with the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia is pursuing ambitious economic and military modernisation plans under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030 agenda.
The kingdom has sought to diversify its defence partnerships in recent years while maintaining its decades-long security relationship with Washington. REUTERS

articles.title: Ukrainian Neptune missiles destroy three drone factory buildings in Russia's Taganrog – OSINT
articles.body:
Ukrainian Neptune missiles destroy three drone factory buildings in Russia's Taganrog – OSINT
Three production buildings at the Atlant Aero plant in Russia's Taganrog have been completely destroyed in a strike by Ukrainian Neptune missiles.
Source: Ukrainian OSINT community Exilenova+, which tracks the results of strikes using open-source data
Details: Exilenova+ notes that the plant specialises in the production of unmanned aerial vehicles and components for them.
Quote: "One of the warehouses, which was used for military purposes, has suffered a roof collapse as a result of the missile strike. The affected area is approximately 60×40 m."
Details: Exilenova+ said another production building has suffered significant damage: its structures were almost completely penetrated across an area of approximately 70×40 m.
A satellite image posted by the community shows the destroyed and damaged facilities at the plant.
Exilenova+ has not specified the date of the strike that caused the damage visible in the satellite image. However, in a 15 September post, the OSINT community reported a missile strike on Taganrog and a large fire on the premises of the Beriev Aircraft Company and the former Taganrog Automobile Plant (TagAZ), which was detected by NASA's FIRMS satellite monitoring system. The TagAZ site houses production and warehouse facilities belonging to Atlant Aero.
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine says Atlant Aero produces the Molniya-1 and Molniya-2 fixed-wing attack drones and the Molniya-2R reconnaissance UAV.
Background: In April, Ukrainian forces also attacked Atlant Aero with Neptune missiles, destroying two production facilities and damaging four others.

articles.title: NATO drills new layered air defence over Romania
articles.body:
NATO has carried out a multinational air and missile defence exercise over Romania as the Alliance shifts from traditional air policing towards a broader system designed to counter aircraft, drones and cruise and ballistic missiles, according to Allied Air Command.
The Flexible Deterrent Option training on 9 September brought together fighter and tanker aircraft from France, Greece, Romania, Spain and Türkiye, alongside NATO Airborne Warning and Control System aircraft and a tanker from the Multinational MRTT Unit.
The main focus was Integrated Air and Missile Defence, with the participating forces also conducting Close Air Support training with Romanian ground forces. Aircraft taking part included French Rafales, Romanian and Greek F-16 Fighting Falcons, Spanish F/A-18 Hornets and Turkish F-16s. Spain also deployed an A400M Atlas tanker, while Turkey contributed a KC-135 Stratotanker.
NATO said the activity formed part of a wider move away from an Air Policing framework primarily concerned with safeguarding Alliance airspace against aircraft and uncrewed systems, towards a multi-layered air defence posture capable of dealing with a wider range of threats.
The new framework is intended to cover threats including conventional aircraft, uncrewed aerial systems, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles, using sensors, command-and-control systems, fighters and other capabilities as parts of a single integrated network.
Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Alberto B. Calvo López, commander of the Spanish detachment conducting NATO Air Defence duties at Mihail Kogălniceanu Air Base, said: “The evolving threat also reminds us of the importance of collective, layered air defence, in which sensors, command and control systems, fighters and other Allied capabilities must be able to operate as a single, integrated system.”
The exercise used a “Red” versus “Blue” scenario focused on Integrated Air and Missile Defence.
NATO AWACS aircraft acted as the principal command-and-control element for the “Red” force, directing tanker aircraft and coordinating with Romanian forces on the ground. The training was designed to test how airborne and ground-based systems could be brought together in real time, with information shared between participants and command procedures rehearsed against a simulated air threat.
NATO’s Combined Air Operations Centre at Torrejón in Spain oversaw the activity, providing operational-level command and control while coordinating aircraft and supporting capabilities across the exercise. AIRCOM said the new Air Defence framework brings the Alliance’s air and missile defence activities under common rules, guidelines and command procedures regardless of the type of threat being faced.
The intention is to give NATO commanders greater flexibility to move and combine forces supplied by different member states, synchronising sensors, aircraft and other assets across several domains. The Romanian exercise was also intended to test how quickly allied forces could be assembled and integrated under a Flexible Deterrent Option, with those activities used to rehearse collective defence arrangements before they might be required during a crisis.

articles.title: Moscow summons British envoy over weapons supplies to Ukraine
articles.body:
The Russian Foreign Ministry summoned Britain's chargé d'affaires in Moscow, Danae Dholakia, on Friday to issue a formal protest about what it called London's "further increase" in weapons supplies to Ukraine.
In a statement, the ministry said that by sending more arms to Kyiv, "London is placing itself in the position of an accomplice to the bloody atrocities committed by the Kyiv regime, which can only be characterized as terrorism and war crimes."
A spokesperson for Britain's Foreign Office called the summoning "yet another attempt to deflect attention from Russia's barbaric full-scale invasion of Ukraine and discredit the UK on the world stage."
Russia currently has no ambassador in London, and relations are dire.
The departure of the previous Russian ambassador, Andrei Kelin, in July prompted British media speculation - denied by Russia - that Moscow was downgrading diplomatic relations because of London's role as one of Ukraine's biggest supporters.
Poland joins anti-ballistic missile coalition with Ukraine
Also on Friday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that Poland has joined an anti-ballistic missile coalition with Ukraine and other allies.
"From today, Poland is part of this major project... we agreed on the forms and frameworks of this cooperation," Tusk said in a video posted on X/Twitter.
Tusk attended a summit on Friday of a new regional grouping of eight Carpathian countries, held in western Ukraine and launched by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Ukraine and nine European countries announced in July an air-defense coalition that would jointly develop a new anti-ballistic missile system as an alternative, cheaper solution to the US Patriot system.
Tusk told a press conference at the summit that Poland has prepared a new "significant" donation package for Ukraine, without giving further detail.
"I will be very consistent here. No one will change my opinion that Poland has to support Ukraine in its war against Russian aggression... History cannot divide us vis-à-vis Russia today," Tusk said.
After his bilateral meeting with Tusk at the summit, Zelensky thanked Poland for the new aid package.
"Ukraine and Poland are strong neighbors, friends, and partners, and we have one common enemy," he said on the Telegram app.

articles.title: Military Airfield Repeatedly Targeted in Rostov as 50+ Drone Swarm Hits Region Again
articles.body:
Ukraine launched a large-scale drone attack on Russia’s Rostov Oblast overnight on Sept. 18, with more than 50 drones reportedly intercepted over Rostov-on-Don, Taganrog, Bataysk and five other districts, Oblast Governor Yuri Slyusar said.
Slyusar said no one was injured, but falling drone debris damaged homes, cars, gas infrastructure and power lines.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In the city of Azov, five private houses and four vehicles were damaged, while several gas pipelines were hit, disrupting supplies to some homes, according to the governor.
Local residents reported loud explosions beginning around 12:30 a.m. Rostov-on-Don Mayor Alexander Skryabin warned residents that air defenses were operating and urged them to remain indoors.
The precise target of the attack has not been confirmed.
A Ukrainian monitoring channel, Supernova, claimed that an airbase in Rostov may have been targeted. Ukrainian channels also circulated footage purportedly showing air-defense fire and explosions over the city. The Crimean Wind channel reported a fire “in the area of the airfield.”
The reports could not be independently verified.
The overnight attack came a day after Ukraine said it had struck the Rostov-Central military airfield.
Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) said the Sept. 17 strike damaged three military aircraft and three helicopters, including an An-12 military transport plane and two An-26 aircraft. The SBU said a fire broke out at the aircraft parking area and was followed by explosions.

Ukraine has previously reported strikes on the same airfield. On Sept. 6, the Ukrainian General Staff said it had hit the facility, while also claiming that a Podlet radar system and two Pantsir-S1 air-defense systems were destroyed. No visual evidence was provided to substantiate those claims.
Russia’s Defense Ministry has not provided details about the reported overnight attack beyond the regional authorities’ statements.

articles.title: US-Israel arms transfers: 2,000 pound bombs, destruction in Gaza
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US-Israel arms transfers: 2,000 pound bombs, destruction in Gaza
The United States' approval of a $2.8bn arms deal with Israel has renewed criticism of US policy towards Tel Aviv, with the package set to include 2,000-pound bombs that have frequently been used in both Gaza and Lebanon to devastating effect.
The approval, which could bypass Congress, is set to replenish the stockpile of heavy munitions, according to reporting from the New York Times.
What are these munitions, where have they been used, and why have they spurred controversy? The New Arab takes a look.
Heavy munitions
The arms package consists of 40,000 heavy bombs developed and made by the US, including 20,000 MK-84 bombs and 20,000 BLU-117 bombs.
The bombs are nearly identical, weighing 2,000 pounds (907kg), creating up to 50 feet (15 metres) deep craters in use, as well as being programmed to detonate above ground as well as underground.
Detonation above ground can send shrapnel 1,000 feet (300 metres) in any direction.
Alongside the bombs, the US will also be supplying 20,000 I-2000 Penetrator warheads. These bombs are also 2,000 pounds but are reinforced and explode on delay, allowing them to punch through surfaces before exploding underground.
Where have they been used?
These bombs have been extensively used by Israel in its wars on Gaza and Lebanon, to deadly effect.
Israel’s war on Gaza has killed over 73,000 Palestinians in a dense urban environment that saw Israeli strikes sometimes killing hundreds at a time in built-up areas, particularly during the first months of the war.
Their repeated use in Gaza, and Israel’s other wars, has seen the US resupply Israeli stockpiles several times in the last three years. In 2024, the Biden administration blocked the transfer of 2,000-pound bombs amid public pressure urging Washington to stop Israel’s invasion of Rafah, which occurred anyway.
US President Donald Trump later unblocked the transfer of the weapons, just a few days into his administration.
According to the New York Times, it has identified 208 craters at least 40 feet across in an area of southern Gaza where Israel told civilians to move to safety.
One such incident in the Jabaliya Refugee Camp at the start of the war killed around 195 Palestinians and wounded a further 777, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.
Israel’s bombardment of Gaza, which has since seen the systematic destruction of infrastructure in Israeli-occupied areas of the enclave, has destroyed most of Gaza’s housing and other infrastructure, including schools, hospitals, roads, water and sewage.
Though Israel has launched campaigns against seven Middle Eastern countries since the outbreak of its war on Gaza -- including Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, Iran, Iraq and Qatar – MK-84 bombs are not deep-strike munitions, meaning they have a minimum range that’s limited to the aircraft's operational range, limiting their usage to areas where Israeli aircraft can directly fly over.
Where is the backlash?
The sale has generated backlash from parts of the US political scene, which has seen figures from both sides of the aisle become increasingly wary of the partnership with Israel.
The most vocal critic of the deal among the Democrats has been Representative Gregory W. Meeks, Ranking Member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and supporter of Israel, who said he would not clear Trump’s proposal.
In a press release published on Wednesday, Meeks said that though he is committed to Israel’s security, “the Trump administration’s proposed sale of 40,000 2,000-pound bombs, some of the most destructive munitions in our arsenal, raises grave, unresolved concerns about how these munitions could be used in densely populated areas of Gaza and Lebanon".
“The Trump administration has not provided sufficient assurances that these weapons will be used by the Netanyahu government in accordance with U.S. law and with appropriate protections for civilians. I therefore will not clear this sale at this time,” he added.
Democrat Senator Chris Van Hollen also weighed in on X, saying he would work to stop the transfer.
Within the Republican political commentariat, Tucker Carlson, who in recent years has distinguished himself as a staunch critic of Israel’s wars in the region, also hit out against the decision.
“By definition, what the Netanyahu government has done in Gaza is genocide. The 40,000 new bombs the Trump administration is sending will be used to do the same in Lebanon, and likely in other countries in the region.
“If you wanted to extend the Iran war into the indefinite future, this is exactly what you’d do,” he added.
It is unlikely that Congress will be able to stop the transfer, as it would require a resolution of disapproval with a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate, which has never happened before, according to the New York Times.
Both the Trump and Biden administrations have also bypassed congressional reviews when selling and transferring arms to Israel since the start of Israel’s war on Gaza by invoking emergency authority.

articles.title: Czech Gripen jets flew to Poland amid Russian drone attack on Ukraine
articles.body:
Czech Gripen jets flew to Poland amid Russian drone attack on Ukraine
NATO airspace near Poland's eastern border after drones were spotted flying over Ukraine's west.
Source: Czech news agency České Noviny, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The Czech jets ultimately did not have to intervene. After being relieved by Polish fighter jets, the Gripens safely returned to Pardubice.
"The Gripen jets have taken off on the orders of the alliance headquarters as part of NATO's integrated air and missile defence system. If necessary, we are willing to defend the airspace of our allies," the Czech military said.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on 17 September that intelligence services believe Russia is planning hybrid attacks using drones and missiles against countries supporting Ukraine. He noted that late autumn and winter will be the most critical period in Russia's war against Ukraine.
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš responded by telling Czech news portal TN.cz that Russia is waging hybrid warfare against Czechia. "That is why our intelligence services are paying maximum attention to all risks related to the activities of Russian secret services directed against our country," he said.
Background:
- On the morning of 18 September, Poland scrambled its fighter jets as Russia carried out another attack on Ukraine.
- Rzeszów and Lublin airports suspended operations amid Russian attacks on Ukraine.

articles.title: Russian weekly losses top 10,000 troops killed and wounded for third week running – Estonian intelligence chief
articles.body:
Russian weekly losses top 10,000 troops killed and wounded for third week running – Estonian intelligence chief
Estonian intelligence has noted that Russian losses in the war against Ukraine have remained above 10,000 troops killed and wounded for a third consecutive week, exceeding the number Russia can recruit.
Source: Estonian public broadcasting network ERR, citing Colonel Ants Kiviselg, Head of the Intelligence Centre of the Estonian Defence Forces, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Kiviselg said Russia's average losses this week are around 1,600 personnel per day, meaning total losses for the week amount to just over 11,000 troops killed and wounded.
Quote: "The trend therefore continues, with Russia losing more troops on the battlefield than it is able to recruit."
More details: Kiviselg also said that Ukraine has for the first time released data on its counteroffensive towards Lyman in Donetsk Oblast, where around 85 sq km of territory has been liberated and mopped up in the course of the operation.
Quote: "Ukrainian operations in Donetsk Oblast are currently continuing."
More details: Among other Ukrainian successes, Kiviselg listed airstrikes on Russian oil facilities in Krasnodar Krai, Saratov Oblast, Samara Oblast and the Republic of Tatarstan, a strike on the Caspian Sea port of Makhachkala, attacks on chemical plants in Perm Krai and Volgograd, and a strike on a drone manufacturing plant in Rostov Oblast.
Quote: "Among military targets, there have been attacks on airfields in Rostov Oblast, as well as air defence systems and launch sites used to store long-range drones in Rostov and Oryol oblasts. The damage is still being assessed, but the Ukrainians have probably managed to either put some aircraft out of action or damage them and the same applies to helicopters."
Background:
- Estonian intelligence noted earlier that Ukraine had reached Russian plants located nearly 3,000 km from the border for the first time.
- Estonian intelligence has also suggested that the problems that are beginning to affect ordinary Russians could have an impact on September's elections to the State Duma, the lower house of the Russian parliament.

articles.title: Sybiha: ICAO conveys Ukraine's position on risks of flights to Russia to all member states
articles.body:
The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) has officially responded to Ukraine's letter and conveyed to all member states a clear position regarding the risks associated with continued flights in Russian airspace, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha announced.
“We are grateful for receiving our call and conveying to all member states a clear position on the risks of continuing operations in the Russian sky,” Sybiha said on X Friday.
According to him, Ukraine, as a member state, reaffirms its commitment to the protection of civil aviation: “What is more, since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, this is exactly what our Defense Forces have been doing by intercepting Russian drones and missiles. This deadly metal threatens lives of our people as well as airspace of neighboring countries, now reaching far beyond Ukraine’s borders and regularly disrupting air traffic of the NATO countries.”
Sybiha emphasized that Ukraine is determined to maintain peace, both in the air and in all other spheres. At the same time, according to him, Russia is not inclined to do so.
“It deliberately terrorizes the airspace and civilians of Ukraine and other countries with regular missile barrages and drone incidents,” he said.
The Minister also emphasized that the protection of civil aviation and ensuring the security of airspace must remain a shared responsibility: “International airlines, insurers, and other aviation companies should take the threats seriously and act accordingly by ceasing operations in Russia.”
As previously reported, in early September, Ukraine officially notified ICAO that Russian airspace poses danger to civil aviation due to intensified military activity.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had previously stated that Ukraine was warning every airline using Russian airspace—as well as anyone utilizing key Russian airports—that Russian skies were becoming extremely dangerous, while emphasizing that Ukraine itself poses no threat to civil aviation.
He stressed that the consequences of the Russian escalation would be felt in Russian airspace, "which is already—and will increasingly become—an operating zone for our drones and missiles, which are actively and rightfully striking back in response to Russia's war."
Subsequently, ICAO urged member states to strengthen measures protecting civil aircraft against risks arising in conflict zones, amid growing threats to civil aviation posed by modern military technologies.

articles.title: Poland joins European Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition
articles.body:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk has announced during a visit to Ukraine that Poland has joined the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, a group of European countries that are jointly developing an integrated air defence system for the continent.
“Yes, Poland is now part of this great project,” said Tusk, “a group of countries and companies that will work together to protect against ballistic missiles…mean[ing] much safer European, and therefore also Polish, skies.”
He added that he had “established the form and framework for this cooperation” during talks today with President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was hosting a summit of eight countries from around the Carpathian Mountains: Ukraine, Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria and Hungary.
Speaking at a press conference alongside Tusk, Zelensky also confirmed that “we will be partners” in the missile coalition and Poland “is welcome there”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).
Jesteśmy w Koalicji Antybalistycznej. pic.twitter.com/prtqKznHnB
— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 18, 2026
The Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition was established in mid-July this year during a meeting in Paris of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of countries that are supporting Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression.
Alongside Ukraine, the coalition also included Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden and the United Kingdom.
In late July, Kyiv announced that it wants a prototype anti-ballistic system, which has been codenamed Freyja, ready in the first half of next year. Ukrainian arms manufacturer Fire Point is the lead industrial partner in the project.
At the time, there was some confusion and criticism in Poland regarding the fact that the country had not been included in the coalition. Speaking today, Tusk admitted that there had been “a certain misunderstanding” at the time, but it is “now clear that Poland is also part of this initiative”.
The alliance is hoping to develop a cheaper complement to the US-made Patriot air-defence systems, which Ukraine and many other European countries use but which rely on American supplies.
Zelensky has recently called on Ukraine’s allies to provide it with Patriot missiles. However, that issue caused political controversy in Poland earlier this year, when the right-wing opposition criticised the government for handing over some of its missiles to Kyiv, arguing that it would weaken Poland’s own defences.
Speaking today alongside Tusk, Zelensky said that the new missile coalition would bring Poland and Ukraine “even closer to each other” and provide benefits to both countries, reports PAP.
“Ukraine possesses unique technologies developed during the war, and we are ready to share them with Donald [Tusk] and our Polish partners,” said Zelensky.
The Polish government has confirmed that it has transferred Patriot missiles to Ukraine following opposition criticism
It also released a list of all military donations to Ukraine since 2022, showing that the former PiS government gave much more equipment https://t.co/8BmDy5BjiB
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026
Both leaders made reference to recent tensions between their countries, in particular over the Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians.
“We may sometimes speak very directly, but if we are friends, we must openly discuss topics that are sensitive to both sides,” said Zelensky, quoted by PAP. “We are friends, and Russia is the enemy. If we begin a dialogue based on common understanding, we will manage everything.”
Tusk, meanwhile, thanked Zelensky “for your willingness to at least try to understand our Polish sensitivities” regarding “difficult, painful issues from the past”. He pledged to “always support Ukraine in your fight against aggression”, regardless of “adversities and negative trends”.
Meanwhile, Tusk expressed hope that the newly formed Carpathian Eight group of countries, which met today in that format for the first time, would help provide further impetus for Ukraine on its path towards European Union membership.
Today, for the first time, here in Ukraine, in our part of the Carpathians, we hold a Summit that brings together all the Carpathian states, the regions and communities of our countries. We are launching a new format – “C8,” the Carpathian Eight – bringing together us and our… pic.twitter.com/tcIupMsBBK
— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) September 18, 2026
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Main image credit: KPRM/Flickr (under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)
Daniel Tilles is editor-in-chief of Notes from Poland. He has written on Polish affairs for a wide range of publications, including Foreign Policy, POLITICO Europe, EUobserver and Dziennik Gazeta Prawna.

articles.title: Russia was sure the terrain made this village impossible to take—Ukraine walked in anyway
articles.body:
Ukrainian troops pushed into a front-line village Russian forces were sure they could never reach, an officer from the assault force told Army TV. He described a methodical, house-by-house clearing—then a Russian response that, once the village fell, called the footage an AI fake.
Through 2026 Russia has pressed on this stretch of the eastern front, creeping toward the fortress belt, the chain of fortified cities anchoring Donetsk Oblast. Retaking Serednie is one move in a quiet Ukrainian counteroffensive that has clawed back ground on this axis—which is why this village changing hands lands harder than the map suggests.
The terrain Russia trusted
Serednie sits on the Lyman direction in eastern Ukraine, an axis where Russian forces have been pressing toward Ukrainian-held Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Troops from Ukraine's 66th Separate Mechanized Brigade entered the village during Operation Vivaldi, said the deputy commander of its first mechanized battalion, Kassta, callsign Timokha.
Ukraine’s Vivaldi counteroffensive disrupts Russia’s plan to encircle Donetsk Fortress Belt – ISW
Sitting on their own gains there, the Russians assumed no counterattack could follow and were certain the terrain itself ruled out any move into the village.
"The enemy, having success in this direction, did not expect that any counterattack or offensive could come in response," Timokha said.
Preparing for the operation took more than a day or two, he added, because the village was full of basements and buildings that each had to be checked. Reconnaissance came first, then fire from drones, heavy bomber drones, and artillery to grind down a garrison he put at at least a platoon, before assault groups moved in with friendly units alongside.
Operation Vivaldi as a whole, run under an information blackout, has cleared 75 km² of enemy infiltration pockets and de-occupied another 10.
Then the Russians called it AI
Small Russian attempts to retake the village broke apart on the approaches, Timokha said. The louder reaction came online: Russians claimed the Ukrainian liberation videos were made with artificial intelligence.
He likened it to Sviatohirsk, where Vladimir Putin announced the town's capture before the commander of Ukraine's Third Army Corps, Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, publicly denied it, Timokha said.

articles.title: Germany gets its first F-35 as Europe’s fighter plans fall apart
articles.body:
Boris Pistorius speaks to the media while standing in front of a Bundeswehr Airbus A400M transport plane at the 2026 ILA Berlin Air Show on June 12, 2026 in Schoenefeld, Germany. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
FORT WORTH, Texas — Germany received its first F-35 jet on Friday but the collapse of Europe's flagship next-generation fighter project is forcing Berlin to rethink what will follow the U.S.-built jet.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius was in Texas at the Lockheed Martin factory for the ceremony. The delivery of the fighter jet was long-planned, but the death of the Franco-German-Spanish Future Combat Air System fighter jet development program earlier this year is fueling calls in Berlin to expand the initial €10 billion order of 35 American jets.
The Lockheed Martin F-35A Lightning II is supposed to solve Germany's immediate problem: replacing its aging Tornado fighter-bombers and preserving its role in NATO nuclear sharing while Europe developed its own next-generation fighter.
Advertisement
But without the FCAS, Berlin is left without an obvious European successor.
“We want and need to maintain nuclear sharing,” Pistorius said ahead of the handover. The F-35, he argued, is currently “the only aircraft in the world” capable of fulfilling that mission.
Under the NATO nuclear-sharing program, Germany and other select allies have aircraft that can carry U.S. nuclear bombs, although the decision to use them remains with Washington.
The first F-35s will remain in the United States for training, with German pilots and technicians preparing for operations before more jets are sent to Büchel in late 2027. Full operational capability is expected by 2030.
Berlin currently operates around 80 Tornados, and some missions will migrate to the Eurofighter Typhoon. But the collapse of FCAS has opened a longer-term gap in Germany's plans for its combat-air fleet.
During June's Berlin Air Show, Pistorius said Berlin is weighing whether to acquire additional F-35s as a “bridge” option after the FCAS failure, to join an existing international sixth-generation program or to develop a national effort headed by Airbus.
Advertisement
German Air Force Chief Lt. Gen. Holger Neumann said at the show that he has asked the defense ministry to procure “fifth-gen-plus platforms beyond 2035,” adding: “I’m not saying the new system has to be ready [in 2035], but we have to pick up there.”
“The F-35 has a clear mission in nuclear sharing,” said Marie-Christine von Hahn, managing director of Germany’s aerospace and defense industry association BDLI. But she warned that the procurement should not distract policymakers from a larger challenge.
“Europe’s air forces need their own wings,” she said. “In Germany in particular, we must continue to be capable of developing, building, maintaining and upgrading combat aircraft ourselves.”
FCAS troubles
The fighter component of FCAS collapsed due to fights over control between the leading French and German companies involved in the project. Paris and Berlin also clashed over the role of the fighter, with France pushing for a lighter jet able to land on its aircraft carrier while Germany wanted a heavier one for air-superiority roles.
Germany is also looking at the U.K.-Italian-Japanese Global Combat Air Programme, although the current members are not keen on expanding the number of partners.
Advertisement
Then there's the future sixth-generation U.S. F-47 under development by Boeing, which could go into service by the end of the decade. However, U.S. President Donald Trump has said the U.S. will sell less capable versions to its allies, undercutting their attractiveness.
While a sixth-generation aircraft remains a long-term goal, for German industry the crucial question is how deeply domestic companies will be integrated into the maintenance and future support structure of the F-35.
Lockheed Martin says that about a quarter of the jet's components are made in Europe. Germany's Rheinmetall is making fuselage parts to be supplied to foreign customers.
That makes the F-35 a product of the close defense-industrial ties linking Europe, Canada and the U.S. — ties now being tested by doubts over Washington's commitment to European defense under Trump.
Pistorius underlined that those links still matter to German defense.
“Whenever we talk about independence,” he said, “we must also recognize that there are mutual dependencies that keep allies close and allow them to benefit from one another.”

articles.title: Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps says it has crippled Russia's elite Rubicon drone unit
articles.body:
Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps says it has crippled Russia's elite Rubicon drone unit
Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps has said that in the course of the Operation Vivaldi offensive in northern Donetsk Oblast, it has inflicted losses on Russia's elite Rubicon drone unit that have forced the Russian command to withdraw it from the Lyman-Borova front.
Source: 3rd Army Corps in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda
Quote: "Fighters from the 3rd Army Corps have inflicted losses on the elite Russian drone unit in the course of the Operation Vivaldi offensive. The enemy command has been forced to withdraw Rubicon from the Lyman-Borova front.
Soldiers from the 3rd Army Corps have disabled Rubicon's command-and-control system, destroying its logistics, ammunition depots, drone launch sites and newly formed units and killing their experienced drone operators. The Russians are now no longer able to quickly replenish the unit with equipment and trained personnel.
Losing personnel and equipment and being unable to deploy because of Ukrainian electronic warfare and air defence systems, the enemy began to abandon its positions, leaving equipment behind. To preserve what remained of the unit, the Russian command has decided to redeploy Rubicon to another sector."
Details: The 3rd Army Corps said the Russians had initially deployed Rubicon to the Lyman-Borova front as a priority area.
For reference: Rubicon is a Russian military centre for advanced unmanned systems within the Russian armed forces, specialising in the use of attack drones, FPV drones and reconnaissance UAVs.
Background:
- In spring, Ukrainska Pravda reported that the expansion of Russia's Rubicon military unit would be one of the main challenges facing frontline Ukrainian troops during the summer.
- On 15 September, the 3rd Army Corps reported mopping up 75 sq km and liberating a further 10 sq km as part of counteroffensive operations in northern Donetsk Oblast.

articles.title: Ukrspecsystems equips the RAM-2X drone with terminal guidance system with target lock up to 3 km – photo
articles.body:
Ukrspecsystems equips the RAM-2X drone with terminal guidance system with target lock up to 3 km – photo
The Ukrainian RAM-2X drone by Ukrspecsystems has been equipped with a terminal guidance system that allows it to complete an attack independently after locking onto a target.
Source: Andrii Rymaruk, Deputy Director of Ukrspecsystems, in an interview with Defender Media.
Quote: "If the pilot locks onto a target at a distance of up to 3 km, presses the 'Attack' button and then loses communications, the system will automatically engage the target. Once it has locked onto a target, it will not let go, even if the target is moving."
Details: Furthermore, visual navigation was implemented in the RAM-2X, allowing the drone to navigate through space without a GNSS satellite signal. According to Rymaruk, this makes it less dependent on the impact of electronic warfare assets.
"The system positions itself in space, making the operator's job easier," he noted.
Ukrspecsystems is also working on a fully autonomous version of the RAM-2X, which they plan to release by the end of 2026.
Quote: "The crew will no longer have to be involved in every second of the flight: reconnaissance identifies a target, passes on its coordinates, and the aircraft sets off on an autonomous hunt."
Details: It is noted that the RAM-2X has been used by the defence forces of Ukraine since 2024.
According to Rymaruk, around a hundred units of the defence forces currently use the RAM-2X. With the help of these drones, an average of 50 to 60 units of Russian equipment are struck per month.
Background:
- Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that Ukrspecsystems had publicly presented the RAM-2X at the MSPO 2026 defence exhibition in Poland. The drone is designed to strike high-value targets at distances of up to 180 km, can remain airborne for over two hours, and carry a warhead weighing 2.7 or 3.5 kg.
- The RAM-2X can also work in conjunction with the SHARK-M reconnaissance drone, which provides target designation and acts as a relay. According to the manufacturer, RAM loitering munitions have already struck over 450 targets.
- The 429th Achilles Separate Unmanned Systems Brigade also demonstrated how it used a RAM-2X drone together with the 43rd Separate Artillery Brigade to strike a Russian Nebo-M radar system near the Millerovo military airfield.
