articles.title: West's toying with nuclear weapons causes particular concern — Russian MFA
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 18. /TASS/. The Western countries' toying with nuclear weapons is a matter of particular concern, and the situation holds grim prospects, Vladislav Maslennikov, Director of the Russian Foreign Ministry's Department of European Cooperation and Russia's Senior Arctic Official, has told a news briefing.
"For decades, the Baltic Sea was a very stable, peaceful region. As soon as NATO decided to venture there – or rather, its member states decided they needed to strengthen their defense (in their view) in the Baltic (though it is, in fact, more of an offensive posture) – the Baltic ceased to be the peaceful and stable region it once was. Now, generally speaking, we are witnessing the beginning of that same process in the Arctic region," he noted.
"Against this backdrop, the attempts of our Western Arctic neighbors to toy with nuclear weaponry is a source of particular concern. A recent development adding to this picture – which is, let us say, grim rather than promising – was Finland joining the French nuclear deterrence initiative. This follows Helsinki's decision this summer to lift restrictions on the importation of nuclear weapons into the country, at least during peacetime," Maslennikov emphasized.
The senior diplomat added that Russia is the only country in the Arctic Council that is not a member of the NATO alliance.
"Such erosion of the non-proliferation policy and deliberate actions to further undermine it can only be described as utterly reckless and extremely dangerous. The European Union is creating additional obstacles to the development of the Russian Arctic and international cooperation in the North by adopting successive packages of sanctions that are illegitimate under international law," he noted.

articles.title: Israel will seek to purchase new weapons systems from US as compensation for Saudi F-35 sale
articles.body:
The United States informed the Prime Minister's Office that it intends to sell F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia in a $25 billion deal, an Israeli official confirmed to Walla on Friday.
Israel is expected to seek "compensation" from Washington in the form of weapons systems that the US has so far declined to sell to Israel.
A source familiar with the details told Walla that the IDF would prefer that no other country in the Middle East receive the stealth fighter, in order to preserve Israel's qualitative operational advantage. However, the source stressed that even if the deal is signed soon, Saudi Arabia would receive its first aircraft only in five years.
Walla was also told that Israel continues to hold a clear operational advantage over other countries that have purchased the aircraft from the United States. That advantage stems not only from the extensive operational experience accumulated by the Israel Air Force and its pilots over the past three years, but also from Israeli-made weapons systems that Israel has received approval to integrate into its Adir aircraft, the Israeli version of the F-35.
Israel also operates an Adir test aircraft used to develop advanced capabilities for the fighter. The United States, for example, does not operate an aircraft of this type.
Another defense official sought to play down concerns, saying the Israel Air Force's advantage lies "not just in the machine, but mainly in the people."
Following the Saudi-US deal and the wider arms race in the Middle East, Israeli officials are already planning to approach negotiations with the US administration differently over future procurement deals.
Israel seeking to participate in production of classified weapons systems
Israeli officials will also seek participation in the development and production of classified weapons systems.
The IDF's focus is not limited to advanced fighter jets and the next generation of stealth aircraft. It also includes the development of space-based weapons and US participation in the development and production of interceptors for the Arrow 4 and Arrow 5 systems, which are intended to address future threats.
There are also advanced munitions that the United States has declined to sell to Israel. These include systems in the field of bunker-busting weapons, systems designed to operate underground deep inside rocky mountains, autonomous strike systems, and swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles.
Israel is currently struggling to finance a third F-15 squadron and additional F-35 squadrons.

articles.title: Russia kills captain of Tanzanian-flagged ship in latest attack on civilian shipping in Black Sea
articles.body:
Russia killed the captain of a Tanzanian-flagged civilian vessel and wounded three crew members in a drone strike in the Black Sea on 17 September, Ukraine’s Ministry for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport said.
The ministry said Russia is “systematically attacking Ukrainian ports, port infrastructure and civilian commercial vessels,” threatening both people and international shipping in the Black Sea.
The vessel was heading toward one of Ukraine’s ports when it was attacked. The condition of the ship is still being assessed.
Foreign vessels repeatedly targeted
The latest attack follows a series of Russian strikes on foreign-flagged vessels serving Ukrainian ports.
In July, Russia struck the Turkish-owned bulk carrier GOLDEN LEO with cruise missiles as it left Odesa carrying grain, killing 10 people.
Russia also attacked two foreign-flagged cargo ships with drones in June, killing one sailor and injuring five others as the vessels were leaving Ukrainian ports.
In August, a Russian strike on port infrastructure in Odesa damaged a Togo-flagged civilian vessel and injured four people.
Attacks threaten Ukraine’s maritime trade
The repeated attacks have also disrupted Ukraine’s maritime trade route.
In July, Russian strikes on civilian cargo ships brought traffic through the Black Sea corridor close to a standstill at the height of the harvest, with shipowners temporarily stopping vessels from entering Ukrainian ports.
The Ukrainian ministry called for an international response and coordinated action to strengthen the protection of civilian shipping and the security of international logistics routes.

articles.title: Russia’s exiled opposition wants voters at polling stations at noon on the main day of the Duma elections. Its new video borrows from a 1971 American ad against the Vietnam War.
articles.body:
Russia’s exiled opposition wants voters at polling stations at noon on the main day of the Duma elections. Its new video borrows from a 1971 American ad against the Vietnam War.
Actor Nikita Kukushkin, who condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and left the country, has recorded a video supporting the “Noon for a Peaceful Russia” campaign, which Ilya Yashin and several other Russian opposition figures in exile are promoting. They are urging Russians to turn out at polling stations at noon on September 20 — the third and main day of voting in the State Duma elections — as a legal way to register their opposition to the war.
Yashin and Kukushkin posted the video, titled “Ya voyna” (“I Am War”), on their social media accounts on September 18, the first day of the Duma elections. In it, Kukushkin says:
I am war. Help me kill. All you have to do is nothing. Don’t protest. Don’t talk about me. Don’t follow the news. Don’t help the people who have lost their homes. Don’t support the people defending themselves. Say everyone’s to blame. Everyone except the czar. Have a latte at Patriarch’s Ponds. Go to VK Fest. Keep living as though buildings aren’t burning, people aren’t dying, lives aren’t being destroyed around you. Do me a favor: Don’t even think about me. I am war. Help me kill.
He is dressed entirely in black. At the end of the video, a tear runs down his cheek as his face twists into a sinister smile.
The video is an homage to a 1971 American public service ad opposing the Vietnam War. It featured actor Henry Fonda, speaking directly to the camera: “I am war. Help me kill. You don’t have to do anything. Don’t protest. Don’t write your congressman. In fact, do me a favor: Don’t even think about me. I am war. Help me kill.”
The ad was part of the antiwar campaign “Help Unsell the War.” Its name refers to stripping war of its appealing image. Ira Nerken, a 20-year-old Yale student, came up with the campaign after watching a CBS documentary about how the Pentagon used public relations to push its own views on war and peace.
Nerken decided the same methods could make war unpopular. He contacted the head of a New York advertising agency, who recruited hundreds of other advertising professionals to work on the campaign for free. The result was 125 posters and more than 60 antiwar ads, which ran on local U.S. television and radio stations. The major broadcast networks refused to air them.
Time magazine called the “Help Unsell the War” campaign a new and inventive form of antiwar protest, but a somewhat belated one — by 1971, most Americans already opposed the Vietnam War. In 1973, eight years after entering the war, the United States withdrew its troops from Vietnam.
The «Help Unsell the War» campaign has recently drawn renewed attention on social media. Meduza posted about it on its Instagram account.

articles.title: West seeking ‘pretext’ for major Russia-NATO war – Fico
articles.body:
NATO member warns bloc seeking pretext for war with Russia
Europe is moving dangerously close to a direct clash between NATO and Russia, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has warned, accusing the West of seeking a “pretext” for a major conflict between the two sides.
Fico made the comment in a Facebook post on Thursday, which accompanied the remarks he delivered before traveling to Ukraine for a meeting with Vladimir Zelensky and several European leaders.
“I am deeply concerned that they are merely looking for a pretext for a major conflict between NATO and Russia,” he wrote.
Reflecting on the Ukraine conflict, Fico said that the hostilities had “gotten out of control,” while accusing European nations of engaging in increasingly bellicose rhetoric which he said risked dragging the continent into a broader war. “The situation has never been as serious and tense regarding the possibility of a pan-European war conflict as it is now,” he said.
Fico also warned that Bratislava could face pressure from NATO to commit troops if the bloc’s Article 5 – a collective defense clause applied if a member state is attacked – is invoked. “Can anyone imagine being told to prepare 5,000 soldiers, 10,000 soldiers, and that they would go somewhere to fight? We don’t know with whom, why, or for what reason,” Fico said.
“I don’t want Slovakia to be part of any military conflict because of some Article 5,” he stressed, adding that, though his country still “cares about collaboration and fulfilling obligations”. “As prime minister, I will do everything to ensure that Slovakia is never drawn into a war,” Fico stressed.
Fico has consistently opposed military support for Ukraine since returning to office in 2023 while halting government weapons shipments to Kiev. He has also opposed Kiev’s accession to NATO, and insisted that Ukraine’s EU membership is only possible if it meets all the requirements.
He has also argued that the West’s strategy to “bring Russia to its knees” had “completely failed.” “The European Union does not need more weapons and Russophobia. The European Union needs more diplomacy and concrete plans to help the economy,” Fico said last month.
Russia has accused the EU of rapid militarization, with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying the bloc is directing increasing military capabilities against Moscow while portraying it as an enemy.
President Vladimir Putin has consistently rejected claims that Moscow intends to attack NATO countries, but warned last week that deploying European forces to Ukraine “would mean war with Russia.” Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov also stressed that Russia has no intention of attacking the West but warned that if Europe attacked first, the resulting conflict would be “very short.”

articles.title: Ukrainian drones damage homes in Russia’s Rostov region. Moscow mayor says 350 drones were headed for the capital.
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones damage homes in Russia’s Rostov region. Moscow mayor says 350 drones were headed for the capital.
More than 50 Ukrainian drones were shot down overnight over Russia’s Rostov region during an attack on September 18, Rostov Governor Yuri Slyusar said.
According to Slyusar, no one was injured. In Azov, the attack damaged five private homes and several vehicles. In the Neklinovsky district, it damaged the roofs and windows of eight apartment buildings.
The Ukrainian Telegram channel Supernova+ reported that an air base in Rostov-on-Don was also attacked, a claim Russian authorities have not confirmed.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said more than 350 drones headed toward the Moscow region starting on the evening of September 17, and most were destroyed “at long range.” Air defenses shot down 64 more as they approached the Russian capital. Sobyanin did not disclose the aftermath of the attack.
On September 17, Rostov-on-Don came under a massive attack by Ukrainian drones. Part of the city was left without electricity. Telegram channels reported a fire at the “Rostov-on-Don — Tsentralny” military airfield, in the area where helicopters and planes are stationed. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky claimed that an An-12 plane, two An-26 planes, and three helicopters were damaged. Russian authorities did not confirm this.

articles.title: Russia confirms rocket launch behind viral sky “jellyfish”
articles.body:
- Russia's Ministry of Defense confirmed on Sept. 18 that a Soyuz-2.1b rocket launched a classified satellite from Plesetsk the previous evening.
- The glowing shape that fueled online missile-launch claims was a documented "space jellyfish" effect caused by sunlight hitting the rocket's exhaust plume.
Social media users shared widespread footage Thursday evening of a glowing, tentacled shape in the night sky, with some posts claiming it showed a missile launched toward Ukraine. Within hours, astrophysicist and satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell offered a more mundane explanation, and Russia’s Ministry of Defense confirmed it the next day.
“Russia appears to have launched a Soyuz from Plesetsk at around 1650 UTC Sep 17, probably with another Glonass navigation satellite, but no official confirmation yet,” McDowell wrote on X on Thursday.
By Friday, Sept. 18, Russia’s Ministry of Defense released video of the launch, identifying the rocket as a Soyuz-2.1b lifting off from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome carrying a satellite for the ministry’s own use. The ministry did not name the satellite or describe its mission, following its usual practice of keeping military payload details classified.
The glowing shape that alarmed observers is a well-documented optical effect known as a “space jellyfish.” It happens when a rocket climbs high enough into the atmosphere to catch direct sunlight during evening or morning twilight, while observers on the ground remain in darkness. The rocket’s exhaust plume expands rapidly in the thin upper atmosphere, and the illuminated, billowing gas cloud can resemble a glowing jellyfish trailing tentacles across the sky. The same phenomenon has accompanied SpaceX Falcon 9 launches over Florida and California this year, as well as previous Soyuz launches from Russian and Kazakh spaceports.
Plesetsk, located in Russia’s Arkhangelsk region roughly 800 km (500 miles) north of Moscow, is the country’s primary military launch site and has hosted a steady stream of Soyuz-2.1b missions carrying Defense Ministry satellites throughout 2026, including launches in February and April. Those earlier missions were also witnessed and photographed across Finland and Scandinavia, consistent with the rocket’s typical flight path toward high-inclination orbits to the north. That trajectory runs opposite the direction claims about a strike on Ukraine would require, since Ukraine lies south of Plesetsk rather than along the rocket’s ascent path.
McDowell’s guess that the payload was another Glonass navigation satellite has not been confirmed by Russian officials, who described the cargo only in general terms as serving the Ministry of Defense’s interests. Russia has not disclosed the satellite’s orbit, designation, or intended function.

articles.title: Ukraine destroys Russian S-400 launcher in Bryansk region
articles.body:
- Ukraine's Defense Forces destroyed a Russian S-400 launcher near Poroshino, Bryansk Oblast, on Sept. 17 using Fire Point's FP-1 drones.
- Fire Point said the launcher had been modified to strike ground targets, including Kyiv, and Ukraine's General Staff separately reported striking two S-400 launchers in the same region.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces destroyed a Russian S-400 air defense launcher in Russia’s Bryansk Oblast on Sept. 17, using FP-1 drones, according to Fire Point, the Ukrainian company that builds the drone.
Fire Point said the launcher had been modified by Russian forces to strike ground targets and had previously been used against Kyiv. The company said the strike hit the launcher near the village of Poroshino, along highway 15K-303. The open-source monitoring group CyberBoroshno said it geolocated the destroyed vehicle from photos of the wreckage, pinning the site at coordinates 53.134224, 33.944510.
Ukraine’s General Staff separately reported that its forces struck two S-400 launchers overnight into Sept. 17 in the Vygonychi area of Bryansk Oblast, a location close to Poroshino, though it is not clear whether that report describes the same launcher Fire Point identified or a separate one. Russia has not confirmed any S-400 losses. Bryansk’s acting governor, Alexander Bogomaz’s successor Yegor Kovalchuk, said Russian air defenses shot down 82 drones over the region in 24 hours but made no mention of losses among the region’s own air defense systems.
The S-400 Triumf is Russia’s long- and medium-range surface-to-air missile system, built to shoot down aircraft, drones and cruise missiles, and Russia has claimed it can also intercept some ballistic targets. Since 2024, Russia has adapted some of the system’s interceptor missiles for a secondary role, firing them at ground targets in Ukraine on a quasi-ballistic trajectory. That dual use is why destroying individual launchers has become a specific target set for Ukraine, since a single system removed from service can eliminate both an air-defense asset and a launcher capable of hitting cities like Kyiv.
Fire Point introduced the FP-1 in late 2024 as a long-range, one-way attack drone built for deep strikes into Russian territory, with a payload of 60 to 120 kilograms (130 to 265 pounds) and a publicly stated range that has grown over time, from roughly 1,600 km (994 miles) at introduction to as much as 3,400 km (2,110 miles) in extended-range configurations the company began advertising in mid-2026.
The drone has previously been used against Russian refineries and other high-value sites well beyond the front line, including a strike on the Omsk refinery in July and a facility in the Yamalo-Nenets region on Sept. 9.

articles.title: Russians vote in elections with no party opposing Putin or war in Ukraine
articles.body:
The three-day vote will fill 450 Duma seats and 11 regional governorships, with only parties backing Putin and Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine on the ballot. Despite official denials of a new draft, fears of mobilisation are overshadowing the vote.
Russians began voting Friday in a tightly controlled three-day election that will likely see President Vladimir Putin tighten his grip on power after 26 years at the helm, as Russia's all-out war in Ukraine continues well into its fifth year.
Only parties backing Putin and his war in Ukraine are on the ballot: the ruling United Russia, the Communist Party, A Just Russia, the nationalist LDPR and New People.
Yabloko, Russia's only publicly anti-war party still operating inside the country, was barred from participating. The party saw a surge in social media support, particularly among young people, after it was initially allowed to stand.
An unnamed European diplomat said the elections were "pretty much a sham" but described them as "a ritual the Kremlin considers necessary," adding that it would seek to ensure a high turnout.
Independent observers have previously documented the use of state resources to influence results, including bussing voters to polling stations, pressuring employees of state institutions to vote for the ruling party, and pushing online voting as it is easier to monitor and control.
"As in the Soviet era, elections must demonstrate the loyalty of citizens," Russian political scientist and Head of Analysis of Transformation Processes at the NEST Centre Nikolai Petrov said.
The election will fill 450 State Duma seats and the governorships of 11 federal regions, with the country's only remaining anti-war party excluded from the ballot and fears of mobilisation overshadowing the vote.
Running from 18 to 20 September, the election will also choose deputies to regional legislatures in 39 federal subjects.
Voters will choose eight of the 11 regional heads directly, while regional parliaments will elect the remaining three. Polling stations have been opened at Russian border crossings with Poland and the three Baltic states.
Half of the 450 Duma seats will be allocated through nationwide party lists and the other half through single-member constituencies.
Voting in Russian elections is also taking place in parts of Ukraine occupied by Moscow's troops, a move that neither Kyiv nor the West recognises as legitimate.
Kremlin pushes pro-army narrative
Almost 200 candidates in these elections have taken part in Russia's war in Ukraine, according to electoral commissions.
The Kremlin has promoted them as part of Russia's "true elite," but the initiative is primarily a recruitment tool to boost Moscow's troops on the front lines, with few standing any real chance of being elected.
Ahead of the vote, Putin urged Russians to vote to show troops that "behind our fighters stand millions of people" and to deliver an "answer to those who want to weaken Russia".
Meanwhile, Russians fear another wave of military mobilisation, despite Putin personally denying plans for a call-up twice in three days in September alone.
Independent Russian media have counted 17 official denials of an imminent mobilisation. Russia called up 300,000 reservists in the autumn of 2022 in a move that triggered significant public alarm and a mass departure of men of fighting age from the country.
Tatiana Stanovaya of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Centre, which is banned in Russia, said she considered a new draft unlikely.
"They have put so much effort into persuading Russians not to worry about this," she said. "I would be very, very surprised if it happened."
In the streets of Moscow today, few visible signs indicate an election is even under way.
Fears of mobilisation have been further compounded by Ukrainian long-range drone strikes on Russian infrastructure in a bid to defund its war machine, causing fuel shortages and economic losses running into billions of euros.
Many Russians feel the attacks break what Stanovaya described as the Kremlin's tacit bargain with the population over the war.
In prison, in exile, dead
All of Putin's main political opponents are in prison, in exile or dead. Alexei Navalny, his most prominent challenger, died in a Russian penal colony in 2024.
Putin's political opponents have mostly been driven into exile and his main opponent Alexei Navalny died in an Arctic prison in 2024.
Russia's exiled opposition has urged anti-Kremlin Russians not to boycott the elections but instead vote "against Putin's party".
Navalny's widow Yulia Navalnaya also called on anti-war Russians to cast their ballots at noon on Sunday.
Yabloko — which critics say outlived its usefulness after the Kremlin allowed it to exist for many years to create a pretence of political plurality as a catch-all for liberal and discontented voters — disagreed, arguing that it was better not to vote.
"You are suggesting that we once again go, like sheep, dancing to their tune, and vote for those who have caused the deaths of people in Russia and Ukraine?" party chairman Nikolay Rybakov said this week.
'Mad printer'
Parliamentary elections were previously a source of significant political tension: in 2011, mass fraud during the Duma vote and Putin's return to the presidency from the post of prime minister triggered the largest street protests in Russia since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Putin has ruled Russia since 1999 and his United Russia party has dominated politics since the early 2000s.
Under Putin, the Duma's powers have been substantially curtailed, reducing it largely to approving legislation initiated by the Kremlin — a role that has earned it the popular nickname "the mad printer" to mock the speed at which it rubber-stamped highly restrictive and controversial laws.
Any criticism of the war is treated under Russian law as "discrediting the army" and can carry a prison sentence.
Older voters remain among Putin's strongest supporters, although many still complain about living standards.

articles.title: 313,000  “Janfada” for Iran
articles.body:
313,000 “Janfada” for Iran
Tehran stages a defiant display of sacrifice and unity
TEHRAN — From Imam Hussein Square to Enghelab Square, Tehran’s streets on Friday became the setting for one of the largest public mobilizations seen in Iran since the war began in February. Hundreds of thousands of people took part in the “Janfada-ye Iran” — Devoted to Iran — campaign, with women, young people, veterans and other sections of society joining a 313,000-strong parade, according to Iranian organizers.
The scale of the gathering was matched by the symbolism surrounding it. Participants marched under Iranian flags, military banners and images associated with the country’s wartime resistance. Iranian drones and other military equipment were displayed along the route, while veterans of the Sacred Defense and volunteers in military-style formations took part in the parade. Some participants wore white burial shrouds — a stark traditional symbol of readiness to give one's life for the country.
The photographs from Tehran captured the atmosphere from different angles. In one image, a woman in camouflage and a green headband is seen positioned beside a vehicle, looking through the sight of a rifle. In another, a woman with her face partially covered by a patterned scarf holds an assault rifle while other women stand behind her amid Iranian and other flags. The images offer a striking visual of the campaign's central message: that the call to defend the country is being presented not solely through conventional military formations, but also through the participation of civilians, including women.
313,000: A number loaded with history
The choice of 313,000 is not simply a numerical designation.
In Islamic tradition, 313 is associated with the companions of the Prophet Muhammad at the Battle of Badr in 624 CE and, in Shiite tradition, with the number of devoted companions associated with the Imam of the Age. For the organizers of Friday's event, the number therefore carries a religious and historical meaning of steadfastness, loyalty and readiness to stand with a cause at a moment of crisis.
That symbolism was visible throughout the rally. The parade was not presented merely as a military exercise but as a public declaration of readiness, with participants repeatedly invoking the ideas of homeland, independence, national unity and sacrifice.
According to Gen. Hassan Hassanzadeh, commander of the Greater Tehran Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC), around 500,000 people had registered in Tehran for the initiative. Iranian organizers have separately said that more than 31 million people have registered nationwide, while other Iranian reports put the cumulative figure above 32 million.
A rally born in wartime
What gives the Janfada campaign its particular character is the circumstances in which it has developed.
The campaign began on March 29, following the US-Israeli attack on Iran on February 28, and has since evolved from a registration drive into a nationwide mobilization involving public gatherings, volunteer organization and preparations for training. Iranian officials say the volunteers are being organized into formations capable of contributing to national defense and other emergency tasks.
Friday's rally therefore came against the backdrop not of a distant or concluded war, but of an ongoing conflict, economic pressure and severe restrictions on Iran's trade and access to international markets. Recent reporting has also documented the effects of the US blockade and sanctions on Iran's economy and commercial routes.
This is an important distinction when placing the gathering in historical perspective. Across history, societies have mobilized around the idea of sacrifice when confronted by an existential military threat — from the Greek defenders at Thermopylae and the Soviet defense of Stalingrad to the French Resistance during World War II and Iran's own mass mobilization during the 1980–88 Iran-Iraq War.
But Janfada is being organized under a different set of circumstances. It combines a modern state-wide registration campaign, social-media mobilization, religious symbolism, and military-style public exercises while the conflict itself is still unfolding and while the country is simultaneously confronting economic pressure.
It is this combination that has given the campaign much of its political and social significance inside Iran.
Women, youth and veterans in the same formation
The Friday parade also sought to project an image of participation across generations.
Women appeared prominently in the event, including women in military-style uniforms and others carrying rifles. Young people took part alongside veterans of the Sacred Defense. Newly engaged couples were also reported among the participants, while a Jewish rabbi and a Yemeni delegation wearing traditional clothing were present, according to Iranian media reports.
President Masoud Pezeshkian, who attended the gathering, emphasized this diversity in his remarks. He described the turnout as a manifestation of the bond between the Iranian people and their homeland and stressed that “Iran belongs to all Iranians.” He called for unity and broad public participation in preserving 'the country's dignity, independence and territorial integrity.'
The message was significant: the campaign was being presented not simply as a gathering of members of Iran's military or paramilitary organizations, but as a national mobilization cutting across different sections of society.
From the 'Sacred Defense' to a new generation
Iran's modern experience of mass mobilization is inseparable from the Iran-Iraq War, known in Iran as the Sacred Defense.
During that eight-year conflict, Iran mobilized large numbers of volunteers through the Basij and other wartime structures. For an entire generation, the experience created a cultural vocabulary in which sacrifice, martyrdom, national defense and civilian participation became closely intertwined.
The Janfada campaign draws on that historical memory while speaking to a new generation.
The images from Tehran are particularly revealing in this respect. The rifles, uniforms and military vehicles evoke the visual language of wartime mobilization, while the presence of young people and women gives the event a distinctly contemporary character. The burial shrouds worn by some participants add another layer: rather than presenting sacrifice as an abstract concept, the participants were visually associating themselves with the possibility of death in defense of their country.
A message beyond Tehran
The significance of Friday's gathering also extends beyond the capital.
Iranian officials have said that Janfada gatherings are taking place in cities across the country and that the campaign is moving toward the organization and training of volunteer units. Basij chief Hossein Taeb said the volunteers were being prepared for “full-fledged defense,” while Iranian reports said training programs were being developed across ground, air and naval domains.
The campaign has consequently become both a domestic mobilization and an international signal.
For Tehran, the message is that the country's capacity to organize people around national defense has not disappeared under the weight of war, sanctions and economic pressure. The government is presenting the turnout as evidence of national resilience and social cohesion.
When a nation says it is ready
The most powerful element of Friday's scenes may not have been the military hardware displayed along Tehran's streets. It was the human presence surrounding it.
A woman holding a rifle. A veteran marches beside younger volunteers. Families moving through the crowd. Participants wearing burial shrouds. Flags rising above a sea of people stretching through one of Tehran's historic arteries.
For Iran, the language of Janfada reaches deep into a historical memory in which the survival of the homeland has repeatedly been associated with endurance and sacrifice.
Yet this time the setting is different. The pledge is being made while war is still being fought, while economic pressure is intensifying.
That is what makes the September 18 rally more than a single day's parade. It is the latest chapter in a campaign that seeks to transform the idea of sacrifice into an organized form of public participation — and to demonstrate, in the heart of Tehran, that the war has not removed the country's ability to mobilize large numbers of people around the defense of Iran.

articles.title: US to sell fighter jets to Saudi Arabia – why is the plan controversial?
articles.body:
The administration of US President Donald Trump has announced the approval of the sale of nearly 50 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, a policy shift that has raised concerns among some members of Congress, the BBC reports.
For years, Saudi Arabia has sought to acquire the world’s most advanced fighter jets, which are equipped with stealth technology to evade detection. Washington had long been reluctant, primarily because it supplies F-35 jets to its ally, Israel. US law mandates that Israel is guaranteed access to top-tier American weaponry. Congress now has 30 days to review or block the potential 24 billion dollars deal with Riyadh.
On the 17th of September, Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi (Democrat from Illinois) spoke out against the sale of fighter jets to Saudi Arabia. He warned that the move could place the “crown jewels” of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party. Other Democratic politicians and some US defense officials have expressed similar concerns. They believe that Riyadh, based on security cooperation between the two nations, could share sensitive information with China.
In announcing the agreement, the US State Department stated that it would support US foreign policy and national security objectives. The deal with Riyadh is expected to strengthen the security of a major non-NATO ally—a force for political stability and economic progress in the Persian Gulf region.
The proposed sale of military equipment would not alter the military balance in the region.
Trump shares a close relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman; bin Salman visited the White House last November. The two also met in Riyadh last May, where an agreement was concluded for the sale of 142 billion dollar worth of arms to Saudi Arabia.
The latest deal will include 48 F-35 fighter jets manufactured by Lockheed Martin. This would place Saudi Arabia on par with Israel, which possesses 50 such jets. Israel’s Foreign Ministry announced in May that it plans to purchase additional F-35s, bringing the country’s total to 100. A single F-35 costs approximately 82.5 million dollars. Congress had previously questioned deals with Riyadh following the 2018 killing of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi. The administration of U.S. President Joe Biden considered selling F-35s to Saudi Arabia if it normalized relations with Israel, but diplomatic efforts failed.
The proposal to sell the fighter jets comes as Saudi Arabia is engaged in a conflict with Houthi rebels in Yemen. The Houthis have seized control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
Read also: Gulf states cancel meeting with Iran; Houthis attack Saudi Arabia

articles.title: Fire Point drones, missiles strike at least 50 Russian targets over 2 weeks in Sept – company
articles.body:
At least 50 Russian targets were struck by drones and missiles manufactured by Fire Point during the first two weeks of September, the company's press service said.
"During the first two weeks of September, Fire Point drones and missiles struck at least 50 Russian targets," Fire Point said on Telegram on Friday evening.
It is reported that the FP-1 and FP-2 aircraft-type strike unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) struck the following targets: logistics centers – one; oil refineries and oil depots – six; industrial facilities – four; military-industrial complex facilities – two; ships – 16; radar stations – five; air defense systems – four; energy facilities – 11.

articles.title: Lublin and Rzeszów airports suspend flight operations for third consecutive day due to Russian strikes on Ukraine
articles.body:
Amidst fresh Russian strikes on Ukraine, the airports in Lublin and Rzeszów have suspended flight operations for the third day in a row, the Polish Air Navigation Services Agency (PANSA) reported on the social network X.
PANSA noted: "Airports in Lublin and Rzeszów have suspended flight operations."
Specifically, the agency reported operational restrictions at the airports starting September 16 due to Russian attacks on Ukrainian territory.
The Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces had announced the commencement of military aviation operations in Polish airspace in response to renewed Russian air attacks on Ukraine.
"In accordance with established procedures, the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces—through the Air Operations Center-Air Component Command—deployed the necessary forces and assets at its disposal. Ground-based air defense and radar surveillance systems were placed on alert," the message reads.
The command emphasized that these measures were precautionary, aimed at ensuring the safety and protection of airspace, particularly in areas adjacent to the zones under threat.
Subsequently, the Operational Command announced the conclusion of the military aviation operations in Polish airspace, which had been conducted to ensure safety during the Russian strikes on targets in Ukraine.
"Ground-based air defense and radar surveillance systems have returned to standard operating mode," the command noted.
It also reported that no violations of the Republic of Poland's airspace were recorded.

articles.title: Drones hit Rostov-on-Don for the second straight night—OSINT monitors say the military airbase was likely the target again
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones struck Rostov-on-Don for the second consecutive night, with OSINT channels reporting the military airbase was likely targeted again, Militarnyi reported on 18 September. The previous night's strike hit the same installation, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported the destruction of three military aircraft and three helicopters there.
Second consecutive overnight strike
The attack began around midnight, Russian news Telegram channel Astra reported. Rostov-on-Don city mayor Aleksandr Skryabin stated around 02:00 that air defenses were active and urged people to take cover indoors.
Rostov Oblast governor Yurii Slyusar claimed more than 50 drones were downed overnight over Rostov-on-Don, Taganrog, Bataysk, and five other districts. He listed damage to private houses, apartment buildings, cars, and gas pipes but made no mention of the airbase.
Ukrainian OSINT channel Supernova+ suggested the airbase was the target again. Krymsky Veter reported a fire near the airfield. However, Astra noted the published footage had not been verified by its OSINT expert, and the results of the repeat strike on the base remain unverified.
Residents told Astra they heard no air-raid sirens and did not know where shelters were located. The Moscow Times reported locals described "deafening bangs" from around 00:30.
Drones hit Rostov-on-Don for the second straight night—OSINT monitors say the military airbase was likely the target again
Russia's Defense Ministry claimed 629 Ukrainian drones downed overnight across all regions.
Ukraine's General Staff did not mention the airbase
Ukraine's General Staff reported verified results from several earlier strikes, including a hit on Kombinat Kamensky, a solid-rocket-fuel factory in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, also in Rostov Oblast. The batch did not mention the Rostov-on-Don airbase. That does not necessarily mean the second attack did not take place—the General Staff can report strike results on the same day or days later, once damage is assessed.
Previous night: reported aircraft kills
The previous strike hit the Rostov-on-Don Central military airfield overnight on 17 September. Zelenskyy reported hits on a military transport An-12, two An-26 aircraft, and three helicopters. The SBU said a fire erupted on the aircraft parking area and secondary detonation of ammunition followed, with local residents reporting a large-scale blaze visible across the city. There is no independent verification of these figures.
Drones hit Rostov-on-Don for the second straight night—OSINT monitors say the military airbase was likely the target again
Ukraine's General Staff had earlier reported strikes on the same airfield on 6 September. Ukrainian forces also reported destroying a Podlyot radar and two Pantsir-S1 air defense systems at the base, though no imagery was released.
Ukraine has been systematically targeting Russian military airfields and their air defenses with drones across the front, from occupied Crimea to Rostov Oblast. In August, a combined strike also hit a Rostov Oblast airfield alongside a major refinery.

articles.title: ‘There are no decent parties left’: Sham elections underscore Putin’s grip on Russia
articles.body:
Russia is holding its first parliamentary elections this weekend since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — a vote that sees the opposition scrambling to give voters options in a field increasingly narrowed by the Kremlin.
The shadow of the war looms large over proceedings. As Ukraine intensified strikes on Russian territory and showed greater tolerance for civilian casualties, Russia’s Supreme Court in August barred Yabloko — the country’s only openly anti-war party — from fielding a national list of candidates in the State Duma, Russia’s lower house.
And with dissenting voices all but reduced to silence, some opposition figures — including Yulia Navalnaya, widow of Russian opposition leader Alexey Navalny — are asking Russians to vote for candidates who seem at least neutral on the war.
Advertisement
But other opponents of the Kremlin say Navalnaya’s strategy is giving credibility to sham elections that are only held to justify Russian President Vladimir Putin’s maximalist war against Ukraine and tighten his grip on Russian society.
“To whoever comes to us with a sword — do not expect mercy,” Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said in a campaign ad for Putin’s United Russia party, alongside NHL superstar Alex Ovechkin and the propagandist Margarita Simonyan, who runs the state broadcaster RT.
Putin’s veterans
The Kremlin’s response to the opposition suggests it is worried that people are growing tired of the war.
By removing anti-war candidates from the ballot and promoting pro-war voices, Moscow seeks to overstate public support for the invasion of Ukraine, says Ivan Preobrazhensky, a Russian political scientist based in Prague. “By electing them, people are effectively endorsing the policies of the ruling party and the government,” he told POLITICO, even though voters have no real alternative.
Yabloko received between 1% and 2% of votes in previous parliamentary elections and was seen as “politically dead” by the Kremlin, according to Maxim Reznik, a former party leader in St. Petersburg. By allowing it to run, Reznik said, the Kremlin “wanted to show that just 1.5% of Russians oppose war.”
But reports in Russian media suggested that Yabloko’s recent positioning as “the only peace party,” as well as its advocacy for an immediate ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, had boosted its electoral support. The Nezavisimaya Gazeta reported on a July poll from an unnamed agency giving Yabloko a rating of 9.4%. Faridaily, an outlet founded by independent journalist Farida Rustamova, reported that internal government polling put the party around 5.5%.
Advertisement
A month later, the party’s deputy chairman Lev Shlosberg was sentenced to 11 years in prison for “discrediting” Russia’s army, and the party’s registration was canceled by the Supreme Court a month later after bizarre proceedings over alleged copyright violations.
Although some Yabloko candidates are allowed to compete insingle-member constituencies, the ruling lets pro-war politicians fully retain the overwhelming grip they have on the Duma.
“There are no decent parties left,” said Maxim Katz, a former municipal councilor in Moscow’s Shchukino district who later ran campaigns for key opposition figures including Navalny and is now living in exile. “They’re all giving Nazi salutes and telling how great the war is,” he told POLITICO.
Ten parties are running lists in the elections, including Putin’s United Russia party, the Communist Party, the nationalist Liberal-Democratic Party, Fair Russia and New People. Members of these five political movements unanimously backed the Kremlin’s annexation of Ukraine’s eastern regions and their inclusion into Russian territory, and have been echoing Moscow’s pro-war rhetoric.
In place of Yabloko’s ousted candidates, the Kremlin has promoted its own alternatives. More than a thousand Russian veterans of the war in Ukraine will be running — one of whom, Eduard Shonov, allegedly served in a brigade that occupied the Ukrainian town of Bucha, where Russian forces massacred several hundred civiliansat the beginning of the war.
For Russians, the war is no longer a distant reality. Recent Ukrainian strikes against Russian cities and infrastructure have caused fuel shortages and made people fearful of attacks. For a large part of the country that agreed to ignore the war as long as it “did not concern them,” the consensus expired “as soon as drones started hitting their cities,” Preobrazhensky said.
Advertisement
‘Smart voting’
The Russian opposition is still seeking to make its voice heard in an increasingly repressive environment.
Navalnaya called the upcoming elections a “propagandistic exercise” for Putin, and believes it is essential to prevent him from getting results that will legitimize his war effort in Russia and in the West.
“Our task is to convey to the majority of Russians — the anti-war majority — that, despite total censorship, fear, and repression, these ‘elections’ represent literally the last opportunity to safely express protest against the policies of Putin and his United Russia party,” she told POLITICO.
Navalnaya and Katz advocate for what they call “smart voting” — an endorsement strategy to defeat United Russia by backing candidates who are against, or at least less supportive of the war. The strategy was pioneered by Alexey Navalny himself in 2018 after he and his allies were mainly barred from running in presidential and municipal elections.
“Smart voting” relies heavily on Yabloko candidates running in single-member districts, but as they are not present in many parts of Russia, some of Navalnaya and Katz’s endorsements include candidates from the Communists and other pro-governmental parties.
This approach has been criticized by some members of the Russian opposition, including the head of Yabloko, Nikolay Rybakov. Voting for parties who are already in the Duma amounts to “supporting those who send members of Yabloko to prison,” he said at a meeting with party supporters in St. Petersburg on September 15.
Endorsing candidates is “the wrong bet,” Reznik, the former Yabloko official, told POLITICO. “The voting results are in the Kremlin’s hands. They’ll rewrite everything anyway. Just you wait and see.”

articles.title: Indonesia gets its first aircraft carrier amid debate over cost and military ambitions
articles.body:
Indonesia has received its first aircraft carrier, a former Italian warship that the government says will strengthen the archipelagic nation’s maritime security and disaster response capabilities.
The 41-year-old former ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi, with capacity for short takeoff and vertical landing aircraft and helicopters, arrived Friday morning at a naval base in North Jakarta’s Tanjung Priok port, where it was welcomed with a military ceremony.
Italy in March agreed to give the carrier, which was retired in 2024, to Indonesia in a move aimed at boosting Italy’s broader defence engagement with the south-east Asian country. Italy is seeking deals on submarines and aircraft, and gifting the carrier to Indonesia also saves it the cost of decommissioning the ship.
The transfer would make Indonesia only the second country in south-east Asia with a carrier in its fleet. The first was Thailand’s HTMS Chakri Naruebet, which was commissioned in 1997 after being procured from Spain along with carrier-capable AV-8S Matador jump-jets.
The carrier will be formally commissioned into the Indonesian Navy next week as the KRI Gajah Mada, named after the famed 14th-century Majapahit-era military leader, whose campaigns and vision of a unified archipelago have made him one of Indonesia’s most celebrated historical figures.
Defence development was one of the top priorities for president Prabowo Subianto’s administration, as he has advocated an expansion of the military through the purchase of submarines, frigates, fighter jets, missiles and pushed for more defence cooperation with various countries.
But the Garibaldi acquisition has sparked a fierce debate among defence analysts, economists and opposition politicians who question whether Indonesia needs an aircraft carrier at all and whether the government should be spending millions of dollars to refurbish and operate an ageing warship while facing mounting fiscal pressures at home.
Indonesia’s finance ministry approved $450m in financing for the aircraft carrier program in 2025. However, some lawmakers have warned the overall bill could be far higher. TB Hasanuddin, a member of parliament’s Commission I, said the cost of retrofitting the carrier alone could reach 16tn rupiah (about $900m).
Unlike major naval powers that use aircraft carriers to launch fighter jets far from home shores, Indonesia views the vessel as a mobile command centre and support hub for helicopters, drones and maritime operations across its thousands of islands.
Speaking during a disaster management meeting early this month, Prabowo said the vessel would help authorities combat forest and peatland fires that regularly blanket parts of south-east Asia with hazardous haze.
Prabowo said the carrier could accommodate up to 10 medium-sized helicopters, including aircraft with capabilities comparable to the Black Hawk and Mi-17, and could carry large quantities of water and be deployed to areas with large numbers of fire hotspots.
He also outlined plans to operate drones from the ship and use it as a mobile platform that could be rapidly deployed to help in the event of natural disasters, which are common in Indonesia, a nation that sits in the Pacific “Ring of Fire.”
Operating a carrier is extremely costly, however, and experts have questioned whether Indonesia’s leadership has thought through whether one is necessary for the country’s defence or disaster-relief needs.
The acquisition comes as Indonesia’s economy faces growing fiscal pressures. Prabowo’s government has been funding a free nutritious meals program – which has been tainted by multiple food poisoning incidents – and other costly initiatives while economists have warned about slowing growth, weaker state revenues and widening budget constraints, prompting closer scrutiny of major government spending projects.
“The plan to acquire the Garibaldi must be based on genuine operational needs and our ability to operate it, rather than being driven by pride or other considerations,” said Muhammad Fauzan Malufti, of the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
He said policymakers must weigh not only the vessel’s acquisition and modernisation costs, but also the Navy’s ability to sustain its operations, including personnel, maintenance, fuel, weapons systems and supporting infrastructure.
Fauzan said the government should be transparent about those considerations, particularly given the vessel’s age. He cited Thailand’s carrier as a cautionary example, saying it has spent much of its service life in port because of operational and budget constraints.
“The bottom line is that this should not be forced. Otherwise, the benefits could be outweighed by the costs,” Fauzan said. “The money might be better spent on other priorities, such as increasing the number of frigates in the fleet.”
Military analyst Khairul Fahmi of the Institute for Security and Strategic Studies said aircraft carriers are not a priority for Indonesia, which is focused on preventing adversaries from operating freely in the country’s territorial waters.
“Indonesia has a greater need for submarines, frigates and asymmetric weapons systems to protect its maritime sovereignty,” he said.
But he added that if Indonesia is seeking to position itself as a major maritime nation, “an aircraft carrier can be both a symbol of national power and a multifunctional platform capable of supporting a wide range of military and non-military missions.”

articles.title: IDV unveils upgraded British VIKING UGV with EW and strike roles
articles.body:
IDV has unveiled the latest generation of its British-built VIKING uncrewed ground vehicle in electronic warfare and precision-effects configurations, with the upgraded platform gaining an electric-only range of up to 30km.
The two variants were shown at DVD 2026 at Millbrook, demonstrating how the same vehicle architecture can carry significantly different payloads. One VIKING was equipped with precision effectors, while another carried Leonardo’s Guardian Vantage electronic warfare and signals intelligence system. The latest version of VIKING has been designed to improve range, usability and autonomous operation. Its electric-only range has been extended to as much as 30km, allowing the vehicle to move with a reduced acoustic and thermal signature.
The platform can be transported internally by Chinook helicopter or carried as an underslung load, and can also move under its own power or be towed.
Geoff Davis, Managing Director of IDV UK, said: “As demand for uncrewed capabilities accelerates across NATO, platforms such as VIKING are becoming an essential element of modern land operations.”
He added: “VIKING embodies this approach, offering a flexible and scalable platform that can be configured for a wide range of roles, from ISTAR, electronic warfare, counter-UAS and precision effects to logistics and casualty evacuation.”
The electronic warfare configuration pairs VIKING with Leonardo’s Guardian Vantage system, while a portable Guardian Shield unit can be carried aboard the vehicle and left in position separately. The systems are designed to passively detect transmissions, identify emitters and determine their direction before, when required, moving to active jamming.
IDV said the uncrewed vehicle could therefore carry out what it described as a “jam and scoot” role, operating away from the troops it is supporting, transmitting when required and then moving before the position can be targeted.
The VIKING’s series-hybrid powertrain is particularly relevant to that role. The electronic warfare payload can run from the vehicle’s battery while the engine is switched off, reducing both its thermal and acoustic signature while it listens passively. IDV argues that power generation is becoming an important distinction between different classes of uncrewed ground vehicle, particularly as increasingly demanding sensors, electronic warfare systems and other payloads are fitted to them.
Guardian Vantage and Guardian Shield are designed in the UK and manufactured at Leonardo’s Basildon plant. IDV said both use components and software supplied by British small and medium-sized companies and carry no US International Traffic in Arms Regulations restrictions.
VIKING itself is developed and built at IDV UK’s facility at MIRA Technology Park in Nuneaton, using a British supply chain. The company says the vehicle has undergone more than a decade of trials with armed forces in Britain, Europe and the United States, with initial orders now placed by allied armies. The vehicle’s modular architecture is intended to allow different mission systems to be fitted to the same basic platform, with IDV listing possible roles including reconnaissance, electronic warfare, counter-drone operations, precision effects, logistics and casualty evacuation.
IDV also displayed its MUV Military Utility Vehicle in an ambulance configuration and an 8×8 protected logistics vehicle from its Modular Military Range, but the upgraded VIKING represented the company’s clearest move towards higher-end autonomous battlefield roles.

articles.title: Iranians rally in biggest show of defiance since US war began
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iranians rally by the hundreds of thousands in biggest show of defiance since US-Israeli war began
Hundreds of thousands of Iranians rallied Friday in a government-organized show of defiance after months of war, pledging their readiness to take up arms in the biggest such demonstration since the United States and Israel launched the war in February.
Iran's government has sought to rally the people and stress national unity, even as the economy worsens under a US naval blockade of Iranian ports and new US sanctions meant to increase Tehran's economic pain.
Estimates varied of the number of people volunteering to receive limited military training and defend the country in an effort described as "Janfaday-e Iran," or the "ones who sacrifice their lives for Iran." They marched through downtown Tehran in combat uniform, carrying flags, as onlookers cheered.
For days, state media have encouraged Iranians to join the campaign, saying training with assault rifles would begin soon. The volunteers would be an additional layer of security to the powerful Revolutionary Guard paramilitary and its all-volunteer arm, the Basij.
Tehran’s Guard chief, Gen. Hassan Hassanzadeh, told the state broadcaster that over 600,000 people had registered to participate, with over 1 million expected to take part in the training. On Friday morning, the broadcaster estimated over 300,000 people were on the streets.
The new head of the Basij, Hossein Taeb, declared in a speech as the rally began that the volunteers will be ready for “full-fledged defense” and similar rallies will take place in other cities soon.
The new trainees will make a “nightmare” for Iran's enemies, Taeb added, as President Masoud Pezeshkian, military commanders and other senior officials watched the march.
Some participants trampled flags of the U.S. and Israel. Others chanted “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.”
"I am here to tell Trump that we Iranians have no fear about his threats against our homeland," said Marzieh Afaghi, 24, who attended the rally with her toddler and husband. "No one in history could invade Iran and remain there."
The rally was also a chance for Iran to show off military hardware. Anti-aircraft batteries were on display, while female Guard members in black headscarves sat with truck-mounted machine guns.
The Guard displayed drones that have been widely used against ships in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has asserted control since the war began, severely affecting the Gulf region’s shipments of oil and natural gas to the rest of the world.
Friday's events also suggested that hardliners like Taeb among Iran's leadership will be more prepared to suppress any future demonstration against the theocracy.
In January, shortly before the war, Iran saw some of its largest nationwide protests in history, which began over the struggling economy and turned to wider grievances. Activists have said a crackdown killed over 7,000 people and saw tens of thousands detained.
In May, government officials said more than 30 million people in Iran—home to a population of some 90 million—had volunteered via an online form or at public gatherings to lay down their lives for the theocracy.

articles.title: Russian Elites Fear Covert Mobilization as Putin Eyes 300,000 New Troops
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Elites Fear Covert Mobilization as Putin Eyes 300,000 New Troops
Russian elites and Kremlin insiders are increasingly gripped by the fear of a looming military mobilization following the upcoming State Duma elections, Bloomberg reported on September 18.
This prompted a quiet scramble to move assets and relatives out of the country.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Internal documents obtained by Bloomberg reveal that Kremlin officials—and even workers at military recruitment centers—have been advising friends and family to leave Russia in the coming months while actively seeking ways to open foreign bank accounts.
The panic coincides with Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s recent directive to slash the number of regional officials by 15% to ease the burden on a deficit-ridden budget. However, according to the documents seen by Bloomberg, there are growing internal fears that the Kremlin intends to draft these newly unemployed bureaucrats into the military.
According to a European security official cited by Bloomberg, Russia is preparing to send an additional 300,000 men to the war in Ukraine. But unlike the chaotic partial mobilization of September 2022, which triggered a massive exodus of hundreds of thousands of Russians, the Kremlin may avoid a formal public announcement this time.
Instead, authorities have completely overhauled the conscription system to handle a silent draft. Paper summonses have been replaced with a unified digital registry that is now seamlessly integrated with the tax service, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, medical records, property databases, and border control.
Once an electronic summons is issued, the recipient is automatically barred from leaving the country.
While sources indicate that Putin has not yet made a final decision on whether to pull the trigger on a mass draft, the Russian army is facing severe manpower shortages. Russian leader continues to demand the full capture of Ukraine’s Donetsk and Luhansk regions, but the human cost remains staggering.
A source in Moscow familiar with the statistics told Bloomberg that frontline fatalities are reaching up to 1,000 soldiers every week.
Furthermore, the military is struggling to attract capable volunteers. The source noted that the overall “quality” of individuals currently signing contracts with the Ministry of Defense is extremely low.
To sustain the 700,000-strong force currently deployed in Ukraine—a figure cited by Putin himself—Russia must recruit approximately 400,000 new soldiers annually.
Yet, despite raising the average sign-on bonus to a record 1.8 million rubles ($19,000), the influx of recruits is noticeably shrinking. Janis Kluge, an expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, calculates that 234,000 people signed contracts in the first half of this year, down from 260,000 during the same period last year.
This manpower deficit has directly impacted battlefield progress. Territorial gains have practically stalled; Bloomberg analyst Alex Kokcharov estimates that Russia captured just 155 square kilometers during its summer offensive—13 times less than the 2,037 square kilometers seized during the same period a year earlier.
“The military situation in recent months indicates that Russia does not have enough manpower to concentrate troops on the main axis of attack and confidently cover the front line,” said Kirill Rogov, head of the Re: Russia analytical center. “In other words, mobilization is necessary if the goal is to reach the borders of the Donbas within the next six months.”
If a mobilization is initiated, the burden is unlikely to be shared equally across the country. Political scientist Ekaterina Schulmann told Bloomberg that the Kremlin will likely focus its drafting efforts on the regions that demonstrate the highest levels of support for Putin during the upcoming parliamentary elections.
“In places where loyalty, discipline, and administrative efficiency will be demonstrated, more people will be drafted,” Schulmann explained. In the eyes of the Kremlin, she noted, regional authorities who can successfully execute an election can equally execute a mobilization.
The Kremlin’s current reliance on shadow recruitment to avoid a formal mobilization has placed immense pressure on local authorities. According to recent reports, courts in 51 Russian regions have been fining municipal officials for missing their contract-soldier quotas.
This pressure has driven administrators to drastic measures, including attempts to draft hundreds of male orphans in the Irkutsk region. To enforce compliance, the State Duma is reviewing legislation to significantly increase these financial penalties and introduce suspensions of up to three years for noncompliant bureaucrats.
