articles.title: Ukraine received $3.78 billion tranche under EU loan, says prime minister
articles.body:
Burc Eruygur
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Ukraine received a tranche of €3.3 billion ($3.78 billion) under a loan package from the EU, the country’s prime minister said Friday
“Ukraine has received another €3.3 billion tranche from the EU under the Ukraine Support Loan,” Serhii Koretskyi said in a statement on US social media company X.
Saying that the funds will go toward Ukraine’s top defense priorities, including the procurement of missiles and drones, Koretskyi thanked the European Commission and all EU member states for supporting Ukraine and strengthening its military.
According to an EU delegation statement on the funds’ disbursement, the latest tranche is the fourth payment made to Kyiv under the Ukraine Support Loan's defense window, with nearly €15 billion having been provided to the war-torn country this year.
“Europe will continue to deliver the support Ukraine needs to defend its people and its territory,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen was quoted as saying.
The Ukraine Support Loan is a €90 billion limited recourse loan for 2026-2027 agreed upon by the European Council last December, with €30 billion allocated for budgetary assistance and €60 billion for defense procurement support.

articles.title: Trump hails ‘major progress’ on setting up US Army base in Poland
articles.body:
Trump hails ‘major progress’ on setting up US Army base in Poland
The US has made major progress in negotiations to establish a military base in Poland, President Donald Trump has announced.
His remarks came as Russia warned that it would retaliate if the territory of Poland or the Baltic states were used for a NATO attack against the country.
Poland, which borders the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad to the northeast, is a key logistics hub for delivering Western military aid to Ukraine and is one of Kiev’s main supporters in Europe.
“GREAT NEWS! Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a US Army base in Poland,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday.
“If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance.”
Nawrocki responded by promising to find “the best possible location” for the base. “We are ready to continue our efforts to strengthen our defense cooperation: seriously, responsibly, and always together,” he wrote on X.
The US already maintains a permanent Army garrison and command headquarters in Poland, although most of the 10,000 US troops stationed in the country serve on a rotational basis. During Trump’s first term in 2018, Poland offered to host a permanent base tentatively named ‘Fort Trump’.
Under Trump’s successor, President Joe Biden, the US established a garrison headquartered at Camp Kosciuszko in Poznan and permanently stationed the V Corps Forward Headquarters in the city.
Tensions between Russia and NATO have flared in recent months as eastern members of the US-led military bloc have accused Russia of launching drone incursions. Moscow has dismissed the allegations as unfounded.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said during a trip to Kiev over the weekend that “if Russia attacked us and we took our gloves off, I think we would defeat Russia quite quickly.”
Russian presidential aide and former security chief Nikolay Patrushev responded to Sikorski by warning that “Polish statehood would cease to exist within two or three days” if a conflict breaks out.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov reiterated this week that the country has no intention of attacking NATO members, but said that if the bloc attacks Russia, the war would be “very short.”

articles.title: UN finds grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UN mission finds grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran, and Tehran crimes against humanity
A UN fact-finding mission on Iran said on Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school and sports facility in Iran in February, and that these constituted war crimes.
It also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.
The findings in a new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, examined US conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government's response to nationwide unrest that began in late December.
The Pentagon declined to comment on a report conducted by an outside organization.
"Our investigation remains ongoing, and we have nothing to announce at the moment," it said in a statement. White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in response to the report that the UN Human Rights Council had "accomplished nothing for human rights," adding that Iran was the only party in the current conflict that had committed war crimes.
The Iranian permanent mission in Geneva did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
U.S. officials have previously said military operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.
UN Fact-Finding missions are investigative, not judicial bodies, and therefore do not initiate any criminal cases.
Their findings, however, can be used in criminal investigations by national courts or international tribunals such as the International Criminal Court. States will discuss the findings of the report when it is presented to the Human Rights Council in Geneva on Monday.
MINAB SCHOOL STRIKE
The UN experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe U.S. forces were responsible for an attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the city of Minab, where more than 150 people were killed, including around 120 schoolchildren, according to Iranian officials.
The attack constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law, the mission concluded.
According to the report, the US failure to update information in relation to the school, which was adjacent to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval complex, in its targeting databases and to confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.
"Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen."
In June US President Donald Trump said that "nobody" purposefully attacked a girls' school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident. Reuters news agency first reported that an initial internal US military investigation showed US forces were likely responsible for the fatal strike in Minab in southern Iran.
The Pentagon has since elevated the probe but it has not published any preliminary findings.
UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found no evidence that it was being used for military purposes.
The experts reached a similar conclusion over a strike on a sports centre in Lamerd. The report said the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.
U.S. Central Command said in a statement in March that U.S. forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.
IRAN ABUSES
The UN mission probe found that the Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.
Rights groups say bystanders were among those killed during the biggest crackdown since Shi'ite Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed "terrorists and rioters" backed by exiled opponents and foreign foes the U.S. and Israel.
The probe said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was likely far higher than official figures which say 3,038 people were killed, and 25,000 people injured.
The government's response to the protests — including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of the death penalty — marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.

articles.title: U.S. Air Force joins Navy in funding Castelion hypersonic missile maker
articles.body:
- The Air Force Research Laboratory added $16.4 million to Castelion's contract for its Blackbeard hypersonic weapon, bringing that deal's total to $37.2 million.
- The Navy separately placed a production order worth up to $200 million for Blackbeard on Sept. 14, 2026, following a rapid string of earlier awards.
The Air Force Research Laboratory has added $16.4 million to a Castelion Corp. contract for developing a low-cost, mass-producible long-range strike weapon, the latest in a rapid series of government awards backing the company’s Blackbeard hypersonic missile.
The modification brings the total value of this particular contract to $37.2 million, up from $20.9 million. Work will continue at Castelion’s headquarters in Torrance, California, funded by fiscal 2025 research money, and is scheduled to run through June 30, 2028. Wright-Patterson Air Force Base’s research laboratory manages the contract, separate from a parallel string of Navy awards that have funded the same missile.
Blackbeard is designed to fly faster than Mach 5 while maneuvering within the atmosphere, built in both an air-launched version for aircraft such as the F/A-18 and a ground-launched variant compatible with the HIMARS launcher. Castelion, founded in 2022 by three former SpaceX engineers, has pitched the weapon as the first U.S. hypersonic system built from the outset for industrial-scale, commercial-style manufacturing rather than the smaller test batches typical of earlier hypersonic programs.
The Navy has moved unusually fast on the missile. After initial Army and Navy integration awards in October 2025, the Navy selected Blackbeard in February 2026 as its first weapon candidate under the Multi-mission Affordable Capacity Effector program, known as MACE, an effort to field large numbers of cheaper, longer-range strike weapons instead of relying on smaller numbers of expensive ones. That was followed in April by a $105 million contract to integrate the missile onto the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and run live-fire testing in the Indo-Pacific Command area.
In June, the Navy ordered 50 early operational capability prototypes for $23.4 million, and in August it added nearly $90 million to push the weapon toward becoming a formal program of record, including design changes meant to speed up future sales to allies. Just this month, on Sept. 14, the Navy placed a production order worth up to $200 million, moving Blackbeard out of prototype status entirely.
Congress increased MACE program funding by more than $140 million in the fiscal 2026 defense appropriations act, more than doubling its base funding. Much of Castelion’s production capacity runs through Project Ranger, a 1,000-acre manufacturing campus the company built in Rio Rancho, New Mexico, at a cost it has put above $250 million. Castelion has said its longer-term goal is producing 500 of the weapons a year.
The U.S. Army was one of the first services to back the program, placing an integration award alongside the Navy in October 2025, before the Air Force Research Laboratory and the Navy’s own contracts expanded rapidly through 2026.

articles.title: As Congress passes Russia sanctions, Trump weighs business deals with Moscow before the war ends
articles.body:
As Congress passes Russia sanctions, Trump weighs business deals with Moscow before the war ends
The Trump administration is weighing business deals with Russia even before the war in Ukraine ends, two sources close to the negotiations told The New York Times. One of the sources said such deals could show that the United States is serious about a “reset” in relations with Russia.
Since Trump began his second term, Russian officials have floated several cooperation options for Washington, including joint projects in the Arctic, development of rare earth metals, and aluminum production.
Washington had previously ruled out economic deals with Moscow before the war’s end. A year ago, during talks in Anchorage, possible energy projects were discussed, though Trump had said even before that meeting that he would not do business until “we get the war settled.” The current approach would mark a shift from Trump’s earlier stance, according to the Times.
Meanwhile, the U.S. Congress passed a bill on September 16 imposing what have been dubbed “sanctions from hell“ against Russia. The legislation calls for new restrictions on Russian officials, businessmen, energy projects, and the shadow fleet, along with 100% tariffs on the largest buyers of Russian oil and gas. Trump still has to sign the bill, and WSJ reports he intends to do so.
The Kremlin warned the new sanctions would complicate peace talks. China and India, the largest buyers of Russian oil, also opposed the bill’s passage. Beijing stated that China’s trade relations should not be subject to “interference or coercion” from third countries, while Indian authorities promised to take “all necessary measures” to protect their interests.
The bill leaves the final call on imposing the 100% tariffs to the U.S. president. Trump, who often favors a “carrot-and-stick” approach, tends to prefer the “carrot” when it comes to Russia, the NYT writes.
Balázs Jarábik, a former European Union diplomat in Kyiv, told the NYT that the United States apparently is “considering bigger concessions toward Russia.” He said that while Washington had previously refused to agree to such deals before a ceasefire, it now does not rule out moving ahead with some of them if Moscow first demonstrates “concrete restraint.”
The war in photos. Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine.
Russian forces struck a shopping mall in Zaporizhzhia overnight on September 18. The building burned to the ground by morning, and one person was injured.

Russian officials trying to move assets abroad and open foreign bank accounts amid mobilization rumors, Bloomberg reports
Amid rumors of a new mobilization, senior Russian officials have spent recent months trying to open accounts at foreign banks and move their assets abroad, Bloomberg reported, citing documents it had obtained.
According to Bloomberg, draft office employees are doing the same, and advising friends and relatives to leave Russia.
Bloomberg’s report offered no further details.
Speculation that Russia could announce a new mobilization after elections to the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, has circulated for several weeks, echoed by Meduza sources, Western media, and Ukrainian officials. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said that Russian authorities are allegedly planning to mobilize up to 300,000 people this fall.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov has said Ukrainian officials are trying to “ideologically stir up the situation” in Russia with their statements about a possible mobilization. Commenting on the rumors, Vladimir Putin has said that “there is no scenario today that would require a mobilization,” and has called the reports “utter nonsense” and an “information attack” on Russia.

articles.title: US approves sale of F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia
articles.body: The United States has approved a $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 stealth warplanes to Saudi Arabia, the State Department said Thursday, the kingdom's latest major arms purchase since the start of the Iran war. Saudi Arabia has been repeatedly targeted with drone and missile strikes by Tehran's forces since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February, and has also been hit by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

articles.title: Global: Amid mounting threats, the UN’s next Secretary-General must be a staunch defender of international law
articles.body:
Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnès Callamard will be in New York City for the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly from September 22 to 26 and available for interviews. She will be meeting with senior UN figures and focusing her visit on the following issues:
- The selection of the next UN Secretary-General, and the state of the UN, multilateralism and the rules-based order
- Artificial Intelligence and the need for a global, binding, transparent, and effective regulatory model
- The Trump administration’s continuing attacks on international justice institutions
- International and multilateral responses to Israel’s genocide in Gaza and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank
- US-Israeli unlawful attacks on Iran, violations of international law and war crimes
- Iran’s internal repression, including crimes against humanity
- Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine
- Sudan, the role of the UAE and the international community
- DRC, critical minerals and Rwanda
“The United Nations is at one of its most critical junctures since its foundation more than eight decades ago. The world is beset by genocide, war, climate collapse, rampant inequality, ascendent anti-rights movements, unprecedented corporate power, and a reckless, unrestrained and extractive race to develop ever-more advanced AI. The Security Council is mired in paralysis while powerful states are further undermining the UN’s relevance and effectiveness by subjecting it to severe political, financial, and diplomatic pressure,” said Agnès Callamard.
“The next UN Secretary-General must be a staunch defender of international law. They must be willing to confront the powerful bullies and predators that stalk the international stage. They must be prepared to resist geopolitical pressure, condemn atrocities no matter who commits them, and engage meaningfully and constructively with civil society. They cannot simply be a consensus manager whose selection is the result of a closed-door compromise by the powerful. The next Secretary-General must be someone with the conviction and the know-how to mount a robust and effective defence of human rights and the UN Charter.”
The United Nations is at one of its most critical junctures since its foundation more than eight decades ago.
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General

articles.title: Slovak PM says Slovakia should not go to war "because of some Article 5" of NATO
articles.body:
Slovak PM says Slovakia should not go to war "because of some Article 5" of NATO
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has said he does not intend to fulfil Slovakia's obligations under NATO's Article 5 or take part in defending its allies in the event of a Russian attack.
Source: Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico during a speech to students and hospital staff in Prešov
Details: Fico did not once mention Russia as an aggressor state or a source of military threat to Europe. Instead, Fico accused European leaders of using "war-mongering rhetoric" and acted as though he did not understand who exactly NATO was supposed to defend itself against.
Quote: "It seems... that sometimes there is a tendency to replace the inability to solve problems such as illegal migration, competitiveness and high energy prices with these war-mongering conversations: let's go, let's fight. For God's sake, who do we want to fight? Who?"
Details: Fico publicly expressed his unwillingness to fulfil the obligations under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, which provides for a collective military response by NATO in the event of an attack on one of its members.
Quote: "Can you imagine, ladies and gentlemen, that Article 5 of the NATO treaty would be invoked? Can anyone imagine it? Can anyone imagine being told: get 5,000 soldiers ready, or 10,000 soldiers, and they'll go off somewhere to fight? And we won't even know who we're fighting, why or what for.
I don't want Slovakia to be part of any military conflict because of some Article 5. As prime minister, I will do everything to ensure that Slovakia is never drawn into a military conflict."
Background:
- After returning to the post of Slovak prime minister in autumn 2023, Robert Fico immediately halted military aid to Ukraine and began regularly making anti-Ukrainian statements while justifying Russia's invasion.
- Throughout 2024-2025, Fico consistently opposed Ukraine's membership of NATO and threatened to veto the process. He argued that Ukraine joining NATO would be a direct route to a Third World War.
- In June 2026, ahead of the NATO summit in Ankara in July, Fico came out strongly against further large-scale financial and military support for Ukraine.

articles.title: US considering arming AUKUS submarines with nuclear warheads — Russian MFA
articles.body:
GENEVA, September 18. /TASS/. The United States is openly considering the possibility of arming SSN-AUKUS submarines with strategic nuclear warheads, Russian Foreign Ministry Ambassador-at-Large Andrey Belousov said at the 70th session of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) General Conference in Vienna.
AUKUS is a trilateral security partnership between Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States. One of its key areas of cooperation is the creation of a nuclear-powered submarine fleet for Australia.
"SSN-AUKUS submarines are technically capable of carrying strategic warheads, and the United States is openly considering them as potential carriers of such weapons. Moreover, if the relevant decision is made, all the necessary infrastructure for this purpose will already have been established in Australia. We can see from open sources that the United States and the United Kingdom are moving full steam ahead with the military development of Australian territory," he said.
The diplomat explained that military contingents are being deployed in Australia and infrastructure is being built there to accommodate the weapons of nuclear-armed states.

articles.title: UK seeks allies for space-based missile warning network
articles.body:
Britain is working with NATO allies and other partners on future sensing capabilities for missile defence, including space-based systems intended to help detect, assess and track threats across the Euro-Atlantic.
The work was outlined in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what progress had been made in finding partners for the next-generation persistent surveillance capability proposed in the 2025 Strategic Defence Review. The SDR called for an overhead intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capability able to sense, warn of and track threats across the Euro-Atlantic in support of Integrated Air and Missile Defence.
Defence Readiness and Industry Minister Luke Pollard said: “Defence is also improving the sensing capabilities that underpin Integrated Air and Missile Defence through a layered NATO-integrated approach, drawing on ground-based, airborne, maritime and space-based sensors to improve the ability to detect, assess and respond to threats across the Euro-Atlantic.”
Pollard said the money would initially be directed towards foundational elements of the system, including command and control, new radars and other sensing infrastructure.
He said: “For Integrated Air and Missile Defence (IAMD), the Defence Investment Plan invests a further £790 million in dedicated homeland IAMD, focused on improving foundational capabilities through enhanced Command and Control and sensing systems, including new radars and control systems.”
The Government is also investing in long-range weapons and Deep Precision Strike, including Precision Strike Missiles, as part of the wider effort to improve the ability of the Integrated Force to detect and respond to threats. The future sensing architecture is intended to work as part of NATO rather than as an isolated national system, bringing information from different domains into a common air and missile defence picture.
Pollard said Defence was “working closely with NATO as part of a layered and integrated approach to the defence of the UK and the Euro-Atlantic.”
On international participation, he said the National Armaments Director was already working with allies and partner nations to identify opportunities for joint development and procurement.

articles.title: U.S. Army tests a cheap missile made to intercept drones
articles.body:
- Perseus Defense tested its Mk-III interceptor, built for about $2,500 each, at Yuma Proving Ground alongside U.S. Northern Command, NORAD and JIATF-401.
- The low-cost kinetic system is part of a broader Pentagon push for cheaper counter-drone options following the 2023 Langley Air Force Base drone incursion.
A counter-drone startup tested a low-cost interceptor missile at Yuma Proving Ground this month, loading it into an eight-shot launcher during a homeland-defense experiment involving U.S. Northern Command, NORAD and the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401.
Perseus Defense, a company that went through Y Combinator’s 2025 batch, said each Mk-III interceptor it fired cost roughly $2,500 to build. The company demonstrated the system to a group of distinguished visitors at the test event, showing the launcher running what it described as Lattice-level integration, a reference to Anduril Industries’ command-and-control software, following an earlier demonstration at Fort Carson’s Operation Jailbreak exercise.
The Mk-III is built to physically strike small drones rather than jam or spoof their signals, a kinetic hit-to-kill approach the company says is harder to defeat than electronic warfare against drones flying on fiber-optic links or preprogrammed waypoints that don’t rely on jammable radio signals. Perseus has said it is targeting a cost per engagement far below the $100,000-plus kinetic interceptors currently used against drones that themselves can cost as little as a few hundred dollars.
The push for that kind of low-collateral kinetic option traces back to a specific incident. In December 2023, dozens of unidentified drones flew over Joint Base Langley-Eustis in Virginia, forcing the base to temporarily relocate its F-22 fighters and exposing gaps in how U.S. installations could legally and physically respond to drone incursions over American soil. Similar sightings followed at other bases into 2024 and 2025, and the Department of War stood up JIATF-401 in 2025 specifically to speed up counter-drone capabilities for U.S. forces and installations at home.
The Perseus system was fired at Cibola Range Site 17, Yuma Proving Ground, as part of Falcon Peak 26.2, a counter-small unmanned aircraft systems experiment run by the North American Aerospace Defense Command and U.S. Northern Command. The exercise is designed to demonstrate new counter-drone technologies, expand the military’s focus on low-collateral defeat capabilities, deepen collaboration with mission partners, and give developers fast feedback to speed up the maturity of systems with potential use across the Department of War. This was the first time the campaign was held at Yuma Proving Ground rather than its previous home at Eglin Air Force Base. Other reporting on the event described a Perseus interceptor called Harpe, a 61-centimeter missile with a stated 2-kilometer engagement range fired from a launcher weighing less than 36 kilograms (79 pounds), tested alongside other short-range counter-drone systems to help U.S. Northern Command weigh mobility, cost per shot and magazine depth for base defense.
Perseus Defense was founded in 2025 by Jason Cornelius and Steve Messinger, who studied aerospace engineering together at Penn State, and the company has raised $6.5 million in seed funding.

articles.title: U.S. approves Saudi F-35 sale after year of signals
articles.body:
- The U.S. State Department approved a possible $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia on Sept. 17, 2026.
- The notification follows a Houthi claim a day earlier that it shot down a Royal Saudi Air Force F-15 over Marib governorate.
The U.S. State Department has approved a possible sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, a $24.3 billion deal that would make the kingdom just the second country in the Middle East, after Israel, cleared to fly the stealth aircraft.
The Defense Security Cooperation Agency notified Congress of the potential sale on Sept. 17. The package covers 48 conventional-takeoff F-35A jets and 49 Pratt & Whitney F135 engines, one spare beyond the 48 needed to power the aircraft. It also includes secure communications and navigation equipment, electronic warfare support, training simulators, spare parts and years of maintenance and logistics support. Lockheed Martin Aeronautics in Fort Worth, Texas, and Pratt & Whitney Military Engines in East Hartford, Connecticut, would be the main contractors.
A congressional notification is not a signed contract. It starts a review period during which lawmakers can object to the sale before formal negotiations between the U.S. and Saudi governments can begin, and the State Department’s release included standard language saying the deal would not disrupt the regional military balance and would not require sending additional U.S. personnel to Saudi Arabia.
The move follows nearly a year of on-again, off-again signals from the Trump administration. President Trump first said the U.S. would sell F-35s to Saudi Arabia in November 2025, ahead of a Washington visit by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, when the two countries also signed an agreement designating Saudi Arabia a major non-NATO ally. Trump repeated the commitment in March 2026, calling the F-35 “perhaps the most capable fighter jet ever built.” The sale had drawn scrutiny inside the administration over concerns about preserving Israel’s military edge in the region and the risk that F-35 technology could eventually reach China, concerns that also stalled a similar proposed sale to the United Arab Emirates.
Saudi Arabia’s current fighter fleet, built mainly around F-15 variants and Eurofighter Typhoons, has taken losses in the kingdom’s long war against Yemen’s Houthi movement. The Defence Blog reported on Sept. 16 that Houthi forces said they shot down a Royal Saudi Air Force F-15 over Marib governorate, the latest in a string of aircraft losses Riyadh has suffered during years of fighting. That vulnerability adds a practical dimension to Saudi Arabia’s interest in a stealth aircraft that carries none of the current fleet’s radar signature.
The State Department’s notification says the sale would strengthen Saudi Arabia’s homeland defense and improve its ability to operate alongside U.S., regional and NATO forces, describing the kingdom as capable of absorbing the new aircraft into its military without difficulty. No offset agreement, the arrangement where a seller commits to investment or work-share in the buyer’s economy, has been proposed yet; any such deal would be negotiated separately between Saudi Arabia and the contractors.

articles.title: S. Korean president rejects Trump to send troops to ME
articles.body:
South Korea has maintained a naval presence off the coast of Somalia in an anti-piracy mission, while resisting calls from U.S. President Donald Trump to play a more active military role in supporting Washington over the war in Iran, NBC News reported.
“There won’t be deployment that would involve or enter war. I can tell you that very clearly,” Lee said at a news conference. “We won’t deploy military assets in any form to that end.”
He added, however, that it “is also clear that we must do the minimum as other countries do to protect our commercial shipping and crude shipments, and also the safety of our people.”
Trump has criticized Seoul for what he called insufficient support for the Iran war and scaled back major joint military drills by the two countries’ armed forces this summer, a move that unsettled the U.S. ally.
Asked about progress in reaching an agreement with the United States on Seoul’s U.S. investment commitments under its trade deal with Washington, Lee said concern over the commercial viability of the package was the main sticking point.

articles.title: Poland deploys its military aircraft in response to Russian strikes on targets in central Ukraine
articles.body:
Poland has deployed military aircraft in its airspace in response to Russian strikes on targets in central Ukraine.
"In connection with subsequent strikes carried out by the Russian Federation using airborne assault means on targets in the central part of Ukraine, military aviation is operating preventively in Polish airspace," the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces reported on the X platform.
According to the statement, the necessary forces and assets at the disposal of the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces were deployed through the Air Operations Center – Air Component Command.
Poland's ground-based air defense and radar reconnaissance systems have been placed on alert.
The Operational Command said these measures are preventive in nature and aimed at ensuring the security and protection of Polish airspace, particularly in the eastern part of the country.
"The Operational Command of the Armed Forces is monitoring the current situation, and the subordinate forces and means remain ready for immediate response," the statement reads.

articles.title: In the Arctic, the ice is moving – and so is the India-Russia agenda
articles.body:
In the Arctic, the ice is moving – and so is the India-Russia agenda
Russian-Asian rapprochement in the Arctic is currently unfolding along two distinct tracks: the first driven by logistics and operations, and the second focused on resources and investment.
Russia’s new Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor (TATC), whose key section is the Northern Sea Route (NSR) running along its Arctic coast, is intended domestically to connect major Russian ports – from St. Petersburg through Murmansk to Vladivostok – and link them to inland cities and towns via land, rail, sea and inland waterway networks.
On the international front, the larger TATC is aimed at linking the consumer markets of Europe and Asia via shorter, safer, more cost-effective, and alternative maritime routes. Similarly, on the resource and investment side, Russia remains keenly interested in developing Arctic and Siberian potential in critical minerals, energy resources, and infrastructure projects that require capital and technology.
The overall Russian approach in the Arctic remains focused on linking its energy and mineral projects in mainland Russia, the Arctic, Siberia, and the Far East to the TATC through multimodal transport connectivity.
The ice is moving
Last month marked a turning point for container transit along the NSR when Sea Legend Shipping launched its regular container service – the China-Europe Arctic Express – consisting of eight voyages, that are scheduled between August and early October 2026. The first shipment, which set sail from China’s Ningbo-Zhoushan port on August 15 via the Northern Sea Route, reached the Port of Teesport in the United Kingdom on September 9 – in just 25 days.
The goal is to deliver high-value and time-sensitive cargo including electronics, lithium batteries, electric vehicle components and photovoltaic modules to multiple European ports (Felixstowe, United Kingdom; Rotterdam, Netherlands; Hamburg, Germany and Gdynia, Poland). Sea Legend Shipping is making use of Russian ice breaking services, and is delivering good to its European clients in far less time than via traditional routes. So far it hasn't faced any kind of criticism or sanctions from Europe.
Similarly, South Korea’s PanStar Group has conducted its own pilot voyage along the NSR to European ports, carrying chemical products. South Korea’s Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and Panstar reported on Monday that the containership Panstar Arco has completed the first leg of its demonstration voyage, reaching the UK and Rotterdam on September 12 and 13 respectively – successfully covering the route in 21 days. The vessel will then sail to Gdynia, Poland, where it is expected to load additional cargo before beginning the return trip. The vessel is currently scheduled to return to Busan on October 12.
While Seoul hopes this pilot test will position Busan as a leading Arctic shipping hub, currently there are no plans to move regular commercial traffic along the NSR until 2030.
India’s logic of engagement
Against this backdrop, India’s interest in the Russian Arctic is positioned quiet differently. It is primarily about integrating into the resource and investment aspect of the region. The economic viability of sending goods to Europe from India by transiting the entire NSR remains unfavorable for the foreseeable future, but it does offer a secure, strategic alternative maritime route to the traditional shipping lanes, given ongoing geopolitical challenges.
For India, in shipping terms, Russia’s proposed TATC offers greater potential if cargoes are picked up from, or delivered to, Vladivostok and then sent either to other points in Russia via the TATC’s multimodal transport network or to India through the Eastern Maritime Corridor (EMC), also known as the Chennai-Vladivostok Maritime Corridor.
Similarly, some segments or shipping connectivity between India and Eastern ports of Russia along the NSR can become viable options for enhancing point-to-point shipping connectivity between both the countries, if Russia becomes successful in integrating those with its energy and mineral development projects in the region.
New prospects for India-Russia partnership
The India-Russia partnership dates back to the 1971 Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation. Despite contemporary global geopolitical challenges, the underlying character of India-Russia bilateral cooperation has remained intact.
On bilateral trade and economic fronts, it in fact has grown exponentially. Despite western pressures, India’s oil imports for Russia have continued and it has emerged as a significant factor in supporting the Russian economy in challenging times. In 2022, India’s oil imports from Russia surged to $45.9 billion and crossed $79 billion last year.
Russia’s Pivot to the Arctic and its planned large-scale projects in terms of shipping, energy, and mineral development need Indian industrial attention to take these trade figures between the countries to new highs in the future.
Critical minerals
India’s projected demand for rare and critical metals is expected to increase four to tenfold by 2047. India is heavily dependent on imports of lithium, cobalt, nickel, and a number of other rare-earth elements. Furthermore, India’s net cumulative demand for minerals such as copper, graphite, silicon, and nickel is also expected to increase exponentially between 2025 and 2070. Russia’s resource base appears almost ideally complementary to such Indian needs.
The Pavlovskoye lead-zinc deposit in the Novaya Zemlya archipelago; the Tomtor deposits, which constitute one of the largest deposits of niobium and rare-earth elements in Yakutia; and the Angara-Yenisey cluster for the deep processing of non-ferrous and rare metals in Siberia are some of the potential projects that could fulfill India’s future mineral resource demands. Any significant progress in terms of joint investments and partnership could open new prospects for India-Russia economic partnership and reduce Indian reliance on traditional hegemons for these resources.
Energy imports to refined exports
India’s demand for oil is expected to be around 14 million barrels per day by 2050, while its gas consumption is also expected to rise to 103 billion cubic meters annually by 2030. Of this, around 65 billion cubic meters would be supplied by India’s LNG imports.
Crude continues to remain the key commodity in the India-Russia trade basket, and Russia’s vast LNG potential, mainly its Arctic projects, remains largely untapped by India. LNG imports require specialized vessels, and longer distances add to its transportation costs, which ultimately affect its final price. New investments in Russian Arctic LNG projects could offer a strategic diversification and long-term solutions for meeting India’s energy demands in any future geopolitical scenarios in West Asia if both sides are successful in factoring in pricing and transportation aspects.
India, on the other hand, possesses substantial refining capabilities in terms of crude and its related derivatives while Russia is currently facing difficulties in meeting its own demand for refined petroleum products. This is opening another avenue for greater cooperation between the two sides. India has recently scaled up deliveries of refined petroleum products to Russia to meet its domestic needs.
Shipping synergy
In March this year, New Delhi allocated approximately $8.4 billion to bolster shipbuilding, shipbreaking, and maintenance infrastructure under the ‘Make in India’ initiative. Concurrently, Russia’s growing demand for vessel construction and maintenance presents high-value opportunities for Indian shipbuilding and ship-repair enterprises. Synergizing these capabilities directly aligns with both nations’ strategic interests, offering a mutually beneficial avenue for bilateral maritime cooperation. Both Russia and India are placing significant emphasis on developing sustainable maritime operations for the future.
Both countries are pursuing major reforms to build greener ports and cleaner maritime infrastructure, promote alternative fuels, deploy hybrid and electric vessels, and launch green shipping corridors. They are also focusing on advanced technologies and AI to modernize ports and improve logistics and cargo handling – creating strong potential for high-value economic cooperation between India and Russia.
In its efforts to advance its artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities, India has recently allocated about $1.25 billion to the IndiaAI mission. Similarly, India’s ‘Semicon India Programme’ aims to build a self-reliant semiconductor ecosystem in the country. Such initiatives create new avenues for collaboration in high-growth digital sectors between India and Russia.
A way forward
Russia’s Arctic pivot to the East is the sum of several parallel experiments at different stages of maturity. Container shipping along the NSR remains niche, seasonal, and dependent on who ultimately assumes the commercial risks. Russia’s Atomflot tariff depends on a vessel’s gross tonnage, ice class, distance, and the period of escort. Added to this are the higher costs of icebreaker escorts, high insurance premiums for Arctic voyages, and the need for crews trained to operate in Arctic conditions. Despite these challenges, countries like China and South Korea are already sending test consignments to Europe via the NSR and are competing for the benefits of first movers.
Russia’s total foreign trade turnover reached $697.3 billion in 2025, of which 73.4% was accounted for by Asia. India contributed approximately $63.6 billion, and remains Russia’s second-largest trading partner after China, significantly ahead of the UAE, Brazil, Iran, and South Africa.
India has highlighted its plans to send its first cargo via the NSR by 2027, but its broader comprehensive plans for the region are still at the nascent stage of development. Opening up of the Russian Arctic offers immense new untapped business potential for India and Russia, requiring a stronger government push and greater Indian industrial exposure.
This would not only help India and Russia to reach their bilateral trade target of $100 billion by 2030, but to surpass it in the future.
